baseline.text:
Two I/O nodes on R43-M0 logged a FATAL `kernel panic` within half a second of each other at 13:56. Nothing else was logged on that midplane before or after.

**What failed**

| Time (2005-08-19) | Node | Component / severity | Message |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13:56:00.281 | R43-M0-NC-I:J18-U01 | KERNEL / FATAL | `kernel panic` |
| 13:56:00.628 | R43-M0-N8-I:J18-U11 | KERNEL / FATAL | `kernel panic` |

Both are I/O nodes (the `I:J18` cards). This is one kind of message (pattern 576). The owning team is node-platform, and the stored judgment classes it as a system software failure (p_problem 0.88).

**Just before and after**
- **R43-M0:** I searched 13:30–14:30 and these two lines are the only ones. The midplane logged no warning, error or precursor in the 26 minutes before, and no follow-up or recovery in the 34 minutes after.
- **Rest of the machine:** the closest earlier line anywhere is at 13:17:11, 2,329 s before. It is an INFO "1 ddr error detected and corrected" on R73-M1, which has no evident link to this event. The closest later line is at 17:11:25, 11,725 s after. It is an APP FATAL `ciod: LOGIN chdir(...) failed: No such file or directory` on R56-M1, also with no evident link.
- **Cause:** the logs give no cause or consequence for the panic. I can't say why the nodes panicked or what happened to them afterwards.

**Is it new?** No. `kernel panic` was first seen on 2005-08-15. Across the dataset it has 18 lines in 13 bursts on 18 nodes, with the last one on 2005-11-11. Two bursts and 3 lines came before this one, so it was already recurring.

I didn't run a precursor analysis across all occurrences of the pattern, so I can't say whether it usually has an early warning sign.

Session report with every call: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-191815-f302. Its automatic number check showed 0 of 8 numbers found in tool results, so verify the figures through the individual calls.

product.text:
On R43-M0, two FATAL KERNEL "kernel panic" log lines (pattern 576) hit two different nodes within the same second, at 2005-08-19 13:56:00. R43-M0 logged no other lines in the 3600 s before or after; the nearest neighbouring lines are the same midplane's ciod LOGIN errors at 12:26 and 17:12.
Scope: bgl, 2005-08-19 (searches 13:10 → 14:30 machine-wide; context for R43/R43-M0 12:56:00 → 14:56:00; R43 whole day 2005-08-19; pattern 576 over the whole dataset 2005-06-03 → 2006-01-04). The location filters 'R43/M0' and 'R43-M0' returned 0 log lines; the 'R43/R43-M0' form matched. The machine-wide window and the R43-M0 context were not truncated; the R43 day sample was truncated (10 of 37).
First failure: 2005-08-19 13:56:00.280831, KERNEL, FATAL, node R43-M0-NC-I:J18-U01, line_id 3069219, body "kernel panic" (pattern 576).
Second failure (last line of the burst): 2005-08-19 13:56:00.628434, KERNEL, FATAL, node R43-M0-N8-I:J18-U11, line_id 3069220, body "kernel panic".
The two lines form burst 3 of pattern 576, with 2 lines on 2 nodes, from 2005-08-19T13:56:00.280831 to 2005-08-19T13:56:00.628434. Pattern 576's owner team is node-platform.
Before: R43/R43-M0 had 0 log lines in the 3600 s before the first panic. The nearest earlier line is 2005-08-19 12:26:12.894104 on node R43-M0-NC-I:J18-U01, APP FATAL "ciod: LOGIN chdir(/home/auselton/testing) failed: No such file or directory", 5387.4 seconds before the anchor.
Before, elsewhere on the machine: the closest earlier lines in the 13:10 → 14:30 search are INFO ddr/CE/torus corrected-error lines (patterns 4, 70, 6 and 7) from 2005-08-19 13:17:10.179621 to 13:17:11.356019 on nodes in R30, R35, R55, R73 and R44, none on R43. Every line before the panics in that window belongs to that 13:17 group.
After: the only line after the first panic on R43/R43-M0 within the 3600 s after window is the second panic (after_total 1). The nearest later line is 2005-08-19 17:12:37.933881 on node R43-M0-N8-I:J18-U11, the same ciod LOGIN chdir(/home/auselton/testing) failure message, 11797.7 seconds after the anchor.
Machine-wide, the 13:10 → 14:30 search returned 15 log lines on 7 distinct nodes; the last one (last_ts 2005-08-19 13:56:00.628434) is the second panic, so no other line was logged anywhere after the panics in that window.
R43 rack on 2005-08-19: 37 log lines on 17 distinct nodes between 2005-08-19 12:24:41.458315 and 2005-08-19 23:28:05.646975. The sampled first 10 are ciod LOGIN chdir failures (pattern 586) and 'Link has been severed' errors (pattern 435) from 12:24–12:26, including R43-M0 nodes R43-M0-N4-I:J18-U11, R43-M0-N4-I:J18-U01, R43-M0-N0-I:J18-U11 and R43-M0-N0-I:J18-U01.
Recurring, not new: pattern 576 has 18 log lines, 13 bursts, 18 nodes and 8 weeks_active, from 2005-08-15T16:31:53.274944 to 2005-11-11T13:51:11.907657. Before this burst there were 2 bursts and 3 lines (new_as_of false). The median gap between bursts is 5 days, 1:01:37.812071.
Rate vs usual: the week starting 2005-08-15 has 3 bursts and 5 log lines for pattern 576, and the week starting 2005-08-22 has 2 bursts and 5 log lines. Weeks before 2005-08-15 show 0, and most later weeks show 0 or 1 burst.
Spread: pattern 576 is read as 'widespread' (18 nodes, top_node_share 0.056). R43 accounts for 2 log lines on 2 nodes, matching this burst; the panic is not confined to R43.
Hypothesis: The two panics within the same second on two nodes of one midplane (names containing '-I:', possibly I/O nodes) may share one cause, such as a common job, software state or midplane-level hardware/service-card event, rather than two independent failures. Would confirm: Check the console/RAS output of both nodes at 13:56:00 for the panic reason, and the job scheduler for what ran on R43-M0 then. A different job or cause on each node would rule out a shared cause.
Hypothesis: The ciod LOGIN chdir failures on R43-M0 nodes at 12:24–12:26 and 17:12 are probably a separate user/job-directory problem and unrelated to the panics, since they are hours away and have a different message. Would confirm: Compare the jobs/users behind both events and see whether pattern 586 also precedes the other panic bursts.
Unknown: The root cause of the panic: the log line is only 'kernel panic' with no reason or stack.
Unknown: Whether the nodes rebooted or recovered: no lines from them follow until 17:12:37.933881 (ciod error on R43-M0-N8-I:J18-U11).
Unknown: What job was running, and any customer impact, downtime or cost: none of this is in the logs.
Unknown: Why the R43-M0 filter forms 'R43/M0' and 'R43-M0' matched 0 log lines.
Next step: Run get_context or search_logs with location R43/R43-M0, widened well beyond the first window (before_s and after_s up to 86400) around 2005-08-19 13:56, and add node filters for R43-M0-NC-I:J18-U01 and R43-M0-N8-I:J18-U11 to see whether any non-FATAL lines (reboot, boot, RAS) exist. — The 3600 s window shows no earlier line on R43-M0, and the nearest neighbours are 5387.4 s before and 11797.7 s after.
Next step: Pull the console/RAS records and scheduler job allocation for R43-M0 at 2005-08-19 13:56:00 outside this log set. — The two panic lines carry no cause, and node-platform owns pattern 576.
Next step: Run burst_timeline for the other bursts of pattern 576 and compare precursors, for example whether they are also paired nodes in one midplane. — The pattern has 13 bursts over 8 weeks_active with a median gap of 5 days, 1:01:37.812071, so a recurring precursor may be findable.

baseline.text:
**"Data TLB error interrupt" in June 2005: two separate episodes**

There were 152,659 matching lines in June. All were KERNEL component, FATAL severity, pattern 31. They hit 467 nodes. They fall into two different episodes:

| | Episode 1 | Episode 2 |
|---|---|---|
| When | Started **2005-06-05 00:08:13**. This is also the first occurrence in the whole dataset. | **2005-06-11 17:17:44 → 23:39:33**, about 6.4 hours |
| Lines | 477 | 152,182, which is 99.7% of June's lines |
| Nodes | 466, at most 3 lines each | 1 node: `R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01` |
| Reading | Widespread (the `spread` tool's rule) | One node logging the same line over and over |

**Episode 1: where it started and how it spread**
- The first lines came from rack R20 (midplane R20-M0). The first node was `R20-M0-N2-C:J10-U11`, followed within seconds by other nodes on R20-M0 and R20-M1.
- That day it appeared on 13 racks, R20 to R37. The rack counts, in nodes with at least one line, were:
  - R21: 74
  - R24: 62
  - R25: 60
  - R20: 55
  - R22: 30
  - R32 and R35: 28–29 each
  - R30: 17
  - R34: 14
- Almost no node repeated. I did not trace how fast it spread beyond the first few seconds.
- The 466 nodes in this episode plus the one flooding node on June 11 give the 467 total.

**Episode 2: the flood**
- Node `R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01` (rack R30, midplane M0) emitted 152,182 identical lines. The first two came about 0.1 s apart.
- R30 had 17 nodes in episode 1, and `R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01` was not among the nodes reported by `spread` for episode 1.
- No lines appear from June 12 to the end of June.

**Context:** the message is rare outside these episodes. It came back in July, August and November with only a few dozen lines in total, and 541 nodes were affected over the whole dataset.

**Caveat:** this is raw line counts. By the log's own burst measure, the whole of June is only about 5 bursts. The flood is one burst from a single node, so it should not be read as a fleet-wide problem. I did not look at what happened just before either episode, so I can't say what triggered them.

product.text:
The first 'data TLB error interrupt' line in June 2005 was on node R20-M0-N2-C:J10-U11 at 2005-06-05 00:08:13.410695. It was spread thinly then (254 log lines on 251 nodes in the first burst). On 2005-06-11 it became a flood on a single node, R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01, which accounts for 152182 of the 152659 log lines.
Scope: bgl dataset, 2005-06-01 00:00:00 → 2005-07-01 00:00:00, query "data TLB error interrupt" (pattern_id 31). Search samples were truncated (10 and 3 rows shown), but totals, first/last times and node breakdowns come from full counts. Pattern history covers the whole dataset (2005-06-03 → 2006-01-04) for context.
152659 log lines matched in June 2005, all component KERNEL, all severity FATAL, all pattern_id 31, on 467 distinct nodes. First match 2005-06-05 00:08:13.410695, last 2005-06-11 23:39:32.877740.
The first line (line_id 17742) was on node R20-M0-N2-C:J10-U11: 'data TLB error interrupt' at 2005-06-05 00:08:13.410695.
It was new: before 2005-06-05 00:08:13 there were 0 bursts and 0 log lines of this pattern in the dataset.
The first burst ran 2005-06-05 00:08:13.410695 → 2005-06-05 01:19:44.542323 with 254 log lines on 251 nodes. Racks seen in the first sample rows include R20-M0 and R20-M1.
On 2005-06-05, 4 bursts started with 477 log lines in total. On 2005-06-11, 1 burst started with 152182 log lines. Every other day of June 2005 shown has 0 bursts and 0 log lines.
Node R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01 emitted 152182 log lines (share 0.9969), from 2005-06-11 17:17:44.898186 to 2005-06-11 23:39:32.877740. The spread tool reads this as 'concentrated on one node' (top_node_share 0.997, entropy_norm 0.007).
The other nodes each had only a few log lines: the next highest, R22-M0-N7-C:J04-U01, R22-M0-N7-C:J09-U01 and R25-M0-NA-C:J14-U01, had 3 each.
Rack R30 had 152199 log lines on 18 nodes. Racks such as R21 (74 log lines, 74 nodes), R24 (63 log lines, 62 nodes) and R25 (62 log lines, 60 nodes) had one or a few log lines per node.
Timeline, first line: in the window 2005-06-04 23:58:13.410695 → 2005-06-05 00:18:13.410695, node R20-M0-N2-C:J10-U11 had no other log lines. Closest earlier line on that node: 2005-06-03 17:32:29.059469, INFO 'generating core.3757', 110144.4 s before. Closest later line: 2005-06-05 00:35:57.659828, INFO 'generating core.3757', 1664.2 s after.
Cluster-wide just before the first line, pattern 3 'generating core.<N>' (INFO) first appeared at 2005-06-05 00:08:05.726278 with 16093 log lines on 4096 nodes in the examined window. The first TLB line followed at 2005-06-05 00:08:13.410695.
Timeline, hot node R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01. Before: 2005-06-11 17:17:44.605961 FATAL 'machine check interrupt (bit=0x10): L2 DCU read error'. At: 2005-06-11 17:17:44.898186 FATAL 'data TLB error interrupt'. After: 2005-06-11 17:17:45.004402 'data TLB error interrupt', then more at 17:17:45.103186, 17:17:45.353061 and so on. 406 log lines on that node fall in the 16-minute context window around the anchor.
Nearest earlier line on the hot node before the context window: 2005-06-07 15:32:14.647834, INFO 'generating core.1536', 351930.3 s before the anchor.
Recurring over the dataset: the pattern has 22 bursts over 8 weeks active, 541 nodes and 152734 log lines in total, last seen 2005-11-28T10:01:47.587002. Median gap between bursts is 2:11:48.168741, longest gap 92 days, 1:51:31.855776. The pattern is owned by team node-platform.
Hypothesis: The 2005-06-11 flood on R30-M0-N9-C:J16-U01 may come from a hardware fault on that node. The line just before it was an L2 DCU read error machine check, and the TLB error may then repeat in a loop on the same node. Would confirm: Check whether pattern 173 'machine check interrupt (bit=0x10): L2 DCU read error' and other FATAL lines precede each burst on that node, and whether the node stopped logging after 2005-06-11 23:39:32 because it was reset, removed or the job ended.
Unknown: The root cause of the 2005-06-05 spread across 251 nodes and of the 2005-06-11 flood is not established by these logs.
Unknown: Why the 2005-06-11 flood ended at 2005-06-11 23:39:32.877740 (reboot, job end, node removal) is not shown.

baseline.text:
The instance was built and then deleted about 30 seconds later, all within 44 seconds on 2017-05-16. Its lifecycle log has no errors or warnings. I found 28 lines for it, all INFO. 25 come from nova-compute and 3 from nova-api, so the timeline tool shows only the compute lines. Only those two services logged it. No scheduler or conductor lines mention this instance.

**Build (22:51:36 – 22:51:58)**

| Time | Service | Event |
|---|---|---|
| 22:51:36.968 | nova-compute | Attempting claim: 2048 MB memory, 20 GB disk, 1 vCPU (request `req-3ac9b75e…`). |
| 22:51:36.969–.971 | nova-compute | Host resource checks: 64,172 MB total memory with 512 MB used, 15 GB total disk, 16 vCPUs. Disk and vCPU limits are unlimited. |
| 22:51:37.003 | nova-compute | Claim successful. |
| 22:51:37.261 | nova-api | `GET /v2/…/servers/9fafc51c…` returned 200 in 0.20 s. |
| 22:51:37.619 | nova-compute | Creating image. |
| 22:51:51.023 | nova-compute | VM Started, then VM Paused 0.06 s later (lifecycle events, request `req-3ea4052c…`). |
| 22:51:51.201 | nova-compute | sync_power_state skipped because the instance had a pending task (spawning). |
| 22:51:57.910 | nova-api | Created the event `network-vif-plugged:4bbe198c…` for the instance, so the network port was plugged. |
| 22:51:57.927 | nova-compute | VM Resumed. |
| 22:51:57.936 | nova-compute | Instance spawned successfully. |
| 22:51:57.937 | nova-compute | Took 20.32 s to spawn on the hypervisor. |
| 22:51:58.054–.055 | nova-compute | A second sync_power_state skip and a second VM Resumed event. |
| 22:51:58.074 | nova-compute | Took 21.12 s to build the instance. |

The longest step was between "Creating image" and "VM Started", about 13.4 s. Another 6.7 s passed before the resume.

**Delete (22:52:05 – 22:52:20)**

| Time | Service | Event |
|---|---|---|
| 22:52:05.334 | nova-api | `DELETE /v2/…/servers/9fafc51c…` returned 204 in 0.26 s (request `req-6dc007d0…`). |
| 22:52:05.374 | nova-compute | Terminating instance. |
| 22:52:05.590 | nova-compute | Instance destroyed successfully. |
| 22:52:06.285–.287 | nova-compute | Deleted the files in `/var/lib/nova/instances/9fafc51c…_del`. |
| 22:52:06.405 | nova-compute | Took 1.03 s to destroy on the hypervisor. |
| 22:52:06.858 | nova-compute | Took 0.45 s to deallocate the network. |
| 22:52:20.587 | nova-compute | VM Stopped (lifecycle event), 13.7 s after the last step. |

The instance lived about 7 seconds after the build finished before the delete request arrived. The logs don't show who or what issued the delete. The sync_power_state "Skip" lines are normal during spawning.

nova-api returned HTTP 503 on only 2 log lines (pattern 100103), at 2017-05-16 06:25:02.870 and 2017-05-17 06:25:03.049. Both were GET /servers/detail requests that failed immediately after nova-api got a 503 from the identity server while validating the token. The 503 is a downstream identity failure, not a nova-api fault by itself.
Scope: openstack dataset, whole corpus (2017-05-14 19:39:01 → 2017-05-17 12:02:35). Filter status = 503, then ±120 s context around each hit, plus pattern_id 100100 and pattern_history for 100103. Results were not truncated for the 503 and pattern searches. The context windows were truncated at 30 lines per side.
There are 2 log lines with status 503, all from component nova-api (pattern 100103), first at 2017-05-16 06:25:02.870000 and last at 2017-05-17 06:25:03.049000. No node value is recorded (distinct_nodes 0).
Both 503 lines are the same request shape: 10.11.10.1 "GET /v2/54fadb412c4e40cdbaed9335e4c35a9e/servers/detail HTTP/1.1" status: 503 len: 323, with time 0.0080531 (request req-1cc7d50c-25a2-46b0-a668-9c00f589160c) and time 0.0101860 (request req-abcdb287-429c-40a5-8e79-d490d4fb7410).
Timeline BEFORE the first 503: on the same request_id, line 70743 at 06:25:02.867 (ERROR) says 'Bad response code while validating token: 503'. baseline.text:
nova-api returned HTTP 503 only twice in the whole dataset. In both cases the identity service gave nova-api a 503 when it tried to validate the caller's token. The logs don't show why the identity service failed, because its own logs aren't in this dataset.

**When it happened**
- **First 503:** 2017-05-16 06:25:02.870, request `req-1cc7d50c-25a2-46b0-a668-9c00f589160c` (line 70746).
- **Second 503:** 2017-05-17 06:25:03.049, request `req-abcdb287-429c-40a5-8e79-d490d4fb7410` (line 194065).
- Both were `GET /v2/54fadb412c4e40cdbaed9335e4c35a9e/servers/detail` from 10.11.10.1. Each took about 8–10 ms and returned a 323-byte body.
- The two events are almost exactly 24 hours apart, at the same minute.

**Why**
Each 503 came with the same three nova-api lines, logged within about 3 ms of each other just before it:
1. ERROR: `Bad response code while validating token: 503`
2. WARNING: `Identity response: <!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC …>`, which looks like an HTML error page returned instead of token data.
3. CRITICAL: `Unable to validate token: Failed to fetch token data from identity server`

So nova-api was working normally. It could not authenticate the request because the identity service returned a 503. A search for the "validating token" message finds exactly these two occurrences and no others.

**What happened around the requests**
- Each failing request ID had a successful `servers/detail` call (status 200) about 1 s earlier. That is 278 ms on 05-16 and 262 ms on 05-17. The 503 came on the next call under the same request ID.
- Other `servers/detail` calls in the minutes before were all 200, at roughly 250–450 ms. No other errors appeared in nova-api around either 503.
- The surrounding nova-compute activity was routine: periodic base-image checks and resource audits, and on 05-17 a VM spawn that completed in about 22 s.
- On 05-16, the next log line in the whole dataset after the 503 comes about 8.8 hours later.

**Caveats**
- Two events is a small sample.
- The 24-hour spacing at the same minute suggests something scheduled, such as a daily job or restart of the identity service. That is only a hypothesis, and the logs here can't confirm it.
- To find the root cause, check the identity service (keystone) and web-server logs for about 06:25 on those two days.

baseline.text:
**What failed:** On each affected I/O node, `ciod` lost its CioStream socket to `172.16.96.116`. Every line is pattern 968, severity FATAL, component APP, owned by hpc-workloads. The logs show that the sockets dropped. They don't show why.

**Where and when it started:**
- The first line is at **2005-11-17 05:33:24.623**, on `R77-M0-NC-I:J18-U11`. R77, R40, R41, R54 and R56 follow within seconds.
- Across 11-17 there are 1,008 lines on 504 I/O nodes, two per node, between 05:33:24 and 06:17:09.
- The first burst ran 05:33:24 to 05:37:00 and covered all 504 nodes (504 lines). Every node in the burst is an I/O node (`-I:J18-…`).
- This is new. The message never appeared before this moment. It then recurred in 82 bursts (26,546 lines, 1,024 nodes) through 2006-01-03.

**What happened just before:**
- **Per node:** each node logged `ciod: Received signal 15, code=0, errno=0, address=0x000001b0` (INFO) about 0.1–0.5 s before its own "Link has been severed" line. For the first node, that is 05:33:24.49 and then 05:33:24.62. Signal 15 is SIGTERM, so `ciod` was probably being terminated. Signal-15 lines first appear at 05:14:17.
- **Earlier, from 05:12:38:** 64 nodes logged `ciod: Error loading /bgl/apps/followup/HPL/xhpl.…: invalid or missing program image, Permission denied` (FATAL). This is the earliest problem-level line in the window, and the job being launched was an HPL run.
- **05:09:34–05:09:38:** the SystemController started and began controlling the BG/L rows.
- **05:19:02–05:19:04:** one node logged a machine-check register dump (PLB, TLB and cache parity lines), all FATAL.
- **Immediately before 05:33:24:** the busiest lines were INFO messages about corrected torus errors on rack R63 (compute nodes, `-C:` locations). I read them as background noise, since they are corrected and on different nodes.

**Hypothesis, not proven:** a job launch failed on the HPL image with a permission error, and `ciod` was then SIGTERMed across the I/O nodes. That would drop the sockets to `172.16.96.116`. The data shows the order of events but not who sent the signal. The machine check on one node looks unrelated, since it affects a single node and the failure covers 504.

The session report is at http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-191813-15ef. Its number check found none of the 12 numbers in tool results, and the page shows 0 recorded tool calls. The figures above come from the tool results earlier in this session, so verify them against those.

Pattern 968 (ciod 'Error reading message prefix … Link has been severed', APP, FATAL, owner hpc-workloads) first appeared at 2005-11-17 05:33:24.623263 on R77-M0-NC-I:J18-U11. Just before that, the same node logged 'ciod: Received signal 15' at 2005-11-17 05:33:24.491562. The pattern is new (no earlier lines) and spread across 504 I/O nodes, so it is not local to one node.
Scope: bgl dataset, 2005-11-17 00:00:00 → 2005-11-18 00:00:00 for search and spread; whole dataset (2005-06-03 → 2006-01-04) for history; context window 05:23:24 → 05:33:54. The search rows are a truncated sample of 10 of 1008 matches; the counts come from the totals. The burst_timeline and context lists are also truncated.
First matching line: 2005-11-17 05:33:24.623263, node R77-M0-NC-I:J18-U11, APP FATAL: 'ciod: Error reading message prefix on CioStream socket to 172.16.96.116:43572, Link has been severed'. On 2005-11-17 there were 1008 log lines on 504 distinct nodes, the last at 2005-11-17 06:17:09.268580.
Burst 1 of pattern 968 ran 2005-11-17 05:33:24.623263 → 2005-11-17 05:37:00.983282 with 504 log lines on 504 nodes.

baseline.text:
**Summary:** BGL logged 61 "machine check interrupt" lines in October 2005. All were KERNEL FATAL, spread across 54 nodes with no single hot spot.

**When**
- The first was on 2005-10-01 at 11:02:23 and the last on 2005-10-31 at 20:43:30.
- They arrived at a steady 0–6 lines a day (most days 1–3), with no storm. The peak was 6 lines on 10-09.
- There were no lines on 10-14, 10-15, 10-17, 10-20, 10-21, 10-24 and 10-26.

**Where**
- The lines came from 54 distinct nodes. The top node had only 4 lines (R02-M0-N4-C:J04-U11, 6.6%), followed by R51-M0-N8-C:J13-U11 with 3.
- They hit many racks (R01, R02, R04, R12, R15 through R17, R21 through R23, R25, R27, R30, R33, R35, R45, R51, R52, R75 through R77 and others). Spread's own rule reads this as "widespread" rather than one bad node or rack.
- The messages are on compute-chip locations, for example `R04/R04-M0/R04-M0-N3-C:J17-U11`. The `-U01` and `-U11` suffixes both appear.

**Message variants**

| Variant | Lines |
|---|---|
| Plain "machine check interrupt" | 37 |
| "(bit=0x1d): L2 dcache unit data parity error" | 14 |
| "(bit=0x06): L3 major internal error" | 10 |

The first L2 dcache line was on 10-07 at R06-M1-NE-C:J11-U11.

**Around the first one**
- It was `machine check interrupt (bit=0x06): L3 major internal error` on node R04-M0-N3-C:J17-U11 (rack R04, midplane M0), on 2005-10-01 at 11:02:23.73.
- Nothing preceded it on that node. The node's previous line was a harmless INFO from 2005-07-26 ("generating core.37344"), over two months earlier.
- Within 0.1 s, the same node logged an INFO line: "9 L3 EDRAM error(s) detected and corrected".
- From 11:02:25 to about 11:02:33 the node then wrote a FATAL register dump. It started with "instruction address: 0x0001f0b8" and "machine check status register: 0xa0000000". The rest was one line per register, such as "data read plb error...1", "machine state register: 0x00003000" and "machine check enable...1". Most of the error flags showed 0. The data-read PLB error and the summary line showed 1.
- That node had 123 lines in the next 15 minutes, so the dump was long. I only read the first 20 lines.

Yes. Six VMs had spawn and build times above the threshold, and the slowest was a445709b-6ad0-40ec-8860-bec60b6ca0c2: 50.72 seconds to spawn against a median of 19.74, a ratio of 2.57. Five of the six were slow within a short window on 2017-05-14, and one more on 2017-05-16.
Scope: openstack dataset (nova-api / nova-compute / nova-scheduler), corpus start to corpus end (2017-05-14 to 2017-05-17). Baseline is each message pattern over the whole dataset; flag threshold is max(median + 6×MAD, median + 2 s). Results were not truncated. Context for a445709b covers 2017-05-14 21:28:33 to 21:48:33, filtered to that VM.
Flagged lines: 16 (total_matches), covering 6 distinct VM objects. Each VM is flagged on both its 'Took N seconds to spawn the instance on the hypervisor' line and its 'Took N seconds to build instance' line, 2 flagged lines per VM.
Normal spawn time (pattern 100016, n=2066): median 19.74 s, p95 21.008 s, MAD 0.42 s, flag threshold 22.26 s. Normal build time (pattern 100017, n=2066): median 20.55 s, p95 21.81 s, flag threshold 23.07 s. 6 of the 2066 lines were flagged for each of the two patterns.
Slowest VM a445709b-6ad0-40ec-8860-bec60b6ca0c2 (nova-compute, 2017-05-14 21:43:33): 'Took 50.72 seconds to spawn the instance on the hypervisor.' (ratio 2.57 vs median 19.74) and 'Took 51.59 seconds to build instance.' (ratio 2.51 vs median 20.55).
Other flagged VMs, spawn time vs the 19.74 s median: 544fd51c-4edc-4780-baae-ba1d80a0acfc 41.81 s (ratio 2.12, first flagged 2017-05-14 21:08:19); 1643649d-2f42-4303-bfcd-7798baec19f9 31.27 s (1.58, 21:47:20); ae651dff-c7ad-43d6-ac96-bbcd820ccca8 29.46 s (1.49, 21:09:11); d7d68893-c44f-4e7c-8d4b-0e7801d62776 26.69 s (1.35, 21:45:04); f0ff0b46-b3cd-43e6-97eb-839fd1cdaa87 22.56 s (1.14, 2017-05-16 16:49:11).
Five of the six VMs were flagged on 2017-05-14, with first-flagged times from 21:08:19.736 to 21:47:20.593. The sixth, f0ff0b46, was flagged on 2017-05-16 at 16:49:11.697, only just over the threshold (spawn 22.56 s vs 22.26 s; build 23.34 s vs 23.07 s).

The lines carry no node value: the search for a445709b returned distinct_nodes 0, so these results do not show which compute node each slow spawn ran on. The component is nova-compute.

Hypothesis: The slow spawns may come from a transient slowdown in the hypervisor spawn step (image or disk preparation, or host contention) during 2017-05-14 21:08 to 21:47. Would confirm: Find which compute host and image each of the six slow VMs used. Check whether other VMs spawned in the same window on those hosts were also slow, and look at libvirt / image-cache / disk I/O metrics for that host at that time.
Hypothesis: The dataset description says some VMs had injected anomalies (labels for evaluation only), so the 2017-05-14 cluster may be an injected slow-VM fault rather than organic load. Would confirm: Compare the six flagged VM ids with the dataset's anomaly labels, if available.

rows.title: OpenStack nova logs (cloud VM lifecycle and API)
rows.description: Loghub OpenStack: nova-api / nova-compute / nova-scheduler logs of a small cloud, 2017-05-16 to 2017-05-17, with request ids, tenant ids, VM instance ids, HTTP status and request latency inline. Some VMs had injected anomalies (labels for evaluation only).

rows.object_meaning: VM instance uuid: follows one VM across requests and services (spawn, build, delete)

rows.duration_meaning: HTTP request time (time: N) and VM lifecycle step times (Took N seconds to spawn / build / delete)

sql: WITH b AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS n, median(v) AS med, mad(v) AS mad, quantile_cont(v, 0.95) AS p95 FROM (SELECT pattern_id, duration_ms / 1000.0 AS v FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND pattern_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT pattern_id FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND duration_ms IS NOT NULL)) WHERE v IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), t AS (SELECT *, greatest(med + 6.0 * mad, med + 2.0) AS threshold FROM b ), f AS ( SELECT l.line_id, l.ts, l.pattern_id, l.object_id, l.request_id, l.duration_ms / 1000.0 AS value_s, l.body FROM logs l WHERE l.dataset = 'openstack' AND l.pattern_id IN (SELECT pattern_id FROM t) ) SELECT f.line_id, f.ts, f.pattern_id, f.object_id, f.request_id, round(f.value_s, 3) AS value_s, round(t.med, 3) AS median_s, round(f.value_s / t.med, 2) AS ratio, f.body FROM f JOIN t USING (pattern_id) WHERE f.value_s > t.threshold ORDER BY ratio DESC, f.ts LIMIT 30

WITH b AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS n, median(v) AS med, mad(v) AS mad, quantile_cont(v, 0.95) AS p95 FROM (SELECT pattern_id, duration_ms / 1000.0 AS v FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND pattern_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT pattern_id FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND duration_ms IS NOT NULL)) WHERE v IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), t AS (SELECT *, greatest(med + 6.0 * mad, med + 2.0) AS threshold FROM b ), f AS ( SELECT l.line_id, l.ts, l.pattern_id, l.object_id, l.request_id, l.duration_ms / 1000.0 AS value_s, l.body FROM logs l WHERE l.dataset = 'openstack' AND l.pattern_id IN (SELECT pattern_id FROM t) ) SELECT t.pattern_id, p.template, t.n, round(t.med, 3) AS median_s, round(t.p95, 3) AS p95_s, round(t.mad, 3) AS mad_s, round(t.threshold, 3) AS threshold_s, count(*) FILTER (WHERE f.value_s > t.threshold) AS flagged FROM t JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'openstack' AND p.pattern_id = t.pattern_id LEFT JOIN f ON f.pattern_id = t.pattern_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY flagged DESC, t.n DESC

WITH b AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS n, median(v) AS med, mad(v) AS mad, quantile_cont(v, 0.95) AS p95 FROM (SELECT pattern_id, duration_ms / 1000.0 AS v FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND pattern_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT pattern_id FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND duration_ms IS NOT NULL)) WHERE v IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), t AS (SELECT *, greatest(med + 6.0 * mad, med + 2.0) AS threshold FROM b ), f AS ( SELECT l.line_id, l.ts, l.pattern_id, l.object_id, l.request_id, l.duration_ms / 1000.0 AS value_s, l.body FROM logs l WHERE l.dataset = 'openstack' AND l.pattern_id IN (SELECT pattern_id FROM t) ) SELECT count(*) AS total_matches, count(DISTINCT f.object_id) AS flagged_objects FROM f JOIN t USING (pattern_id) WHERE f.value_s > t.threshold

WITH b AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS n, median(v) AS med, mad(v) AS mad, quantile_cont(v, 0.95) AS p95 FROM (SELECT pattern_id, duration_ms / 1000.0 AS v FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND pattern_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT pattern_id FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'openstack' AND duration_ms IS NOT NULL)) WHERE v IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), t AS (SELECT *, greatest(med + 6.0 * mad, med + 2.0) AS threshold FROM b ), f AS ( SELECT l.line_id, l.ts, l.pattern_id, l.object_id, l.request_id, l.duration_ms / 1000.0 AS value_s, l.body FROM logs l WHERE l.dataset = 'openstack' AND l.pattern_id IN (SELECT pattern_id FROM t) ) SELECT f.object_id, max(round(f.value_s / t.med, 2)) AS max_ratio, count(*) AS flagged_lines, min(f.ts) AS first_ts FROM f JOIN t USING (pattern_id) WHERE f.value_s > t.threshold AND f.object_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 50

baseline.text:
Yes. Six of the 2,066 VMs that logged a spawn time started abnormally slowly. Five of them were within about 40 minutes of each other on 2017-05-14.

**Normal startup times**
- **Spawn on the hypervisor:** median 19.74 s, p95 21.0 s.
- **Total instance build:** median 20.55 s, p95 21.8 s.
- **Flagging rule:** a VM was flagged if its time was more than 6 median absolute deviations above the median, and at least 2 s above it.

**Slow VMs**

| VM (instance uuid) | Time (UTC) | Spawn | Build | Slowdown vs. median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a445709b-6ad0-40ec-8860-bec60b6ca0c2 | 2017-05-14 21:43 | 50.72 s | 51.59 s | about 2.6× |
| 544fd51c-4edc-4780-baae-ba1d80a0acfc | 2017-05-14 21:08 | 41.81 s | 42.81 s | about 2.1× |
| 1643649d-2f42-4303-bfcd-7798baec19f9 | 2017-05-14 21:47 | 31.27 s | 32.12 s | about 1.6× |
| ae651dff-c7ad-43d6-ac96-bbcd820ccca8 | 2017-05-14 21:09 | 29.46 s | 30.32 s | about 1.5× |
| d7d68893-c44f-4e7c-8d4b-0e7801d62776 | 2017-05-14 21:45 | 26.69 s | 27.61 s | about 1.35× |
| f0ff0b46-b3cd-43e6-97eb-839fd1cdaa87 | 2017-05-16 16:49 | 22.56 s | 23.34 s | about 1.14× (marginal, just over the threshold) |

- **Cause:** nearly all the extra time is in the hypervisor spawn step. The build time is only about 1 s longer than the spawn time in each case. The logs don't say why these VMs were slow.
- **Pattern:** the 2017-05-14 cluster suggests a temporary slowdown on that evening rather than six unrelated problems. That is my reading of the timing, not something the logs state.
- **Other slow operations:** a few API calls were also slow around 2017-05-17 06:25, including a 4.2 s server-list query and a 2.1 s external-events POST. These are not VM starts.

Session report with every tool call and number check: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192029-7fc6. The report page shows 0 of 19 numbers matched to tool results, so don't treat it as verified. The figures above come straight from the `value_outliers` output.

Yes, moderately. The 245 FATAL KERNEL log lines in the hour are 5.1 times the prior 7-day average of 47.881 per hour, but 5 of the 168 earlier hourly windows were at or above 245, and the busiest reached 4097. About 195 of the 245 lines come from one node, R36-M1-N0-C:J16-U11, in a machine-check register dump.
Scope: bgl, component KERNEL, severity FATAL, window 2005-11-17 05:00:00 → 06:00:00 (1 h) vs 168 earlier 1 h windows from 2005-11-10 05:00:00 → 2005-11-17 05:00:00. Counts are log lines. The rate comparison is complete. Search, facet and context rows are samples (truncated), but their totals are complete.
The window has 245 log lines, a rate of 245.0 per hour. The 7-day baseline has 8044 log lines, a rate of 47.881 per hour, so the ratio is 5.1.
Of the 168 baseline windows, 5 had 245 or more log lines (share 0.0298), and the baseline maximum per window was 4097.
The first FATAL KERNEL line in the window is at 2005-11-17 05:19:02.164718 and the last at 2005-11-17 05:42:58.164108, out of 245 total matches.
Node R36-M1-N0-C:J16-U11 accounts for 195 lines (share 0.7959). R50-M1-NC-I:J18-U11 has 32 lines and R73-M1-N5-C:J09-U11 has 2. 16 lines have no node value. The facet reports 4 node values, while the search tool reports distinct_nodes 3.
The top patterns are pattern_id 963 (36 lines), 957 (32 lines), 975 (12 lines) and 912 (8 lines). The facet shows 149 distinct pattern_ids, and the top-8 list is truncated.
The burst starts on node R36-M1-N0-C:J16-U11 with verbatim lines: 05:19:02.164718 'Machine Check Status Register: 0xa0800000', 05:19:02.270231 'machine check summary.............1', 05:19:02.397563 'instruction plb error.............0', 05:19:02.521684 'data read plb error...............1'. The sequence continues with tlb, i-cache and d-cache parity lines, then 05:19:03.806093 'Machine State Register: 0x00003000'.
Before the first line, the node had no lines in the preceding 600 s window (before_total 0). The nearest earlier line on that node is at 2005-11-17 04:32:53.275980, FATAL KERNEL, 'rts panic! - stopping execution', 2768.9 s before.
After the first line, the same node has 194 lines in the context window (after_total 194, truncated). The nearest later line on that node is at 2005-12-01 06:42:49.017759, INFO, 'ciod'-free text '0 microseconds spent in the rbs signal handler during 0 calls...', 1214626.9 s later.
At rack/midplane level R36/R36-M1, FATAL lines show the same 194 matches in the window, with no earlier lines in the 600 s window. The nearest later FATAL line is at 2005-11-18 04:36:16.345889 (APP, node R36-M1-NC-I:J18-U11, pattern 985, 'ciod: Error loading /bgl/apps/followup/SPaSM_static/SPaSM.V1R2M0: invalid or missing program image, Permission denied'), 83834.2 s later.
Hypothesis: This may be a single machine-check event on node R36-M1-N0-C:J16-U11. The node dumped its register and error-status lines (patterns 906, 907, 36 and others), and that dump produced most of the lines. A second, smaller source on R50-M1-NC-I:J18-U11 (32 lines) may be a separate cause. Would confirm: Run pattern_history for pattern_ids 906/907/36/963/957 to see whether they occurred in earlier weeks, and run precursors on pattern 906 to see what precedes it. If each dump is about the same number of lines, the 245 reflects a few dumps, not a sustained error rate.
Hypothesis: The 'rts panic! - stopping execution' line at 04:32:53 on the same node, about 2768.9 s earlier, may be related to the later machine check. Would confirm: Widen get_context on the node to before_s 86400 and check whether panics and machine checks recur together.
Unknown: The logs do not show the root cause of the machine check, such as hardware fault vs software.
Unknown: They do not show whether the pattern_ids in this burst are new or recurring: the baseline count covers all FATAL KERNEL lines, not these patterns.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Unknown: The facet and search disagree on distinct nodes (4 vs 3), and 16 lines have no node value, so how many nodes were affected is uncertain.

Next step: Count lines per minute on R36-M1-N0-C:J16-U11 for 05:00–06:00 on 2005-11-17, then inspect node R50-M1-NC-I:J18-U11 (32 lines) with get_context. — Shows whether the burst is one dump starting at 05:19:02 or repeated, and whether the second node is a separate event.
Next step: Inspect the baseline windows at or above 245 lines (the maximum was 4097) to see which node and pattern drove them. — Tells you whether the larger prior bursts have the same signature as this one.

baseline.text:
Yes, but only moderately. The rate is above the 7-day average, though it is not rare.

- **Window:** 2005-11-17 05:00–06:00 had 245 KERNEL FATAL lines.
- **Baseline:** The previous 7 days (2005-11-10 05:00 to 2005-11-17 05:00, 168 one-hour windows) had 8,044 such lines. That is about 47.9 per hour.
- **Ratio:** The window ran at about 5.1 times the usual hourly rate.
- **History:** 5 of the 168 earlier hours (about 3%) had as many lines or more. The busiest earlier hour had 4,097 lines.

The baseline average is pulled up by a few storm hours. A hurricane of FATAL lines in one hour, like the 4,097 one, can inflate the mean. Most ordinary hours are probably well below 48 per hour, so 245 is likely a larger outlier than the 5.1× ratio suggests. I didn't check the median hour.

These are log lines, not incidents. One fault can log many lines. To see whether this was one burst or a widespread problem, I can check how the lines spread across nodes, or which message patterns they came from.

baseline.text:
**Investigate first: the new `ciod … Link has been severed` error (pattern 968), owned by hpc-workloads.** The logs show what happened and when, but not why. Cost, downtime and root cause aren't in them.

**What recurred most, 1–29 Nov 2005**

"Bursts" are recurrences separated by more than 30 minutes of quiet. They are not confirmed incidents.

| Problem | Bursts | Lines / nodes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Kill job … timed out. Block freed.` | 34 (41 in the previous 4 weeks) | 48 lines | node-platform |
| `rts panic! - stopping execution` | 33 (up from 27) | 45 lines, 33 nodes | node-platform |
| **`ciod: Error reading message prefix on CioStream socket … Link has been severed`** | **27 (0 before)** | **10,408 lines, 1,024 nodes** | **hpc-workloads** |
| `machine check interrupt` | 17 (down from 30) | 18 lines | node-platform |
| `invalid operation exception` (software, sqrt and int cnvt variants) | 14 each (0 before) | 24 lines, 15 nodes | node-platform |
| `Node card is not fully functional` and `Can not get assembly information for node card` | 9 each (down from 19) | 561 lines, 456 nodes | cluster-control |
| `rts: kernel terminated for reason` | 7 (up from 2) | 5,120 lines, 3,584 nodes | node-platform |
| `Error receiving packet on tree network` | 7 (up from 1) | 5,120 lines, 3,584 nodes | node-platform |

Three kernel lines (`wait state enable`, `critical input interrupt enable` and `external input interrupt enable`) had 40 bursts each. I left them out because Jev, the model that judges which patterns are real faults, rates them as unlikely problems (probability 0.02–0.32). They look like register dumps.

**By team** (problem bursts in November, with the previous 4 weeks in brackets)
- **node-platform:** 256 (197), across 47 problem patterns.
- **hpc-workloads:** 96 (5), across 53 patterns. This is the biggest jump.
- **cluster-control:** 55 (42), across 26 patterns.

The owner table lists node-platform as a disputed owner for the hpc-workloads `ciod` patterns. Check that table before you assign them.

**Why the `ciod` link error goes first**
- It ranks first in the computed priority table, with a score of 97.8.
- It first appeared on 17 Nov and was new this month.
- It hit 1,024 nodes, with no single node above 0.1% of the lines.
- Daily lines were 1,008 on 17 Nov, quiet around 19–20 Nov, then 2,047 on 24 Nov, 2,045 on 25 Nov, 3,466 on 26 Nov, 1,022 on 27 Nov and 512 on 28 Nov. So it is recurring and flaring, not a one-off.
- A related new pattern, `Connection reset by peer`, had 5 bursts across 1,014 nodes (2,256 lines).

**Candidate precursors (association only, not cause)**
- Before 14 of the 27 `ciod` link-severed bursts, within 30 minutes, DDR error-correction messages appeared (`CE sym`, `ddr error(s) detected and corrected`). Their lift over a control window was 3.5, with a median lead of about 25 seconds.
- Before 12 of the 27, a `ciod: Received signal` message appeared about 1 second earlier (lift 2.0).
- Before 11 of the 27, the kernel register-dump lines appeared (lift 2.8).

This points to a node-side fault, or to compute-node crashes, feeding the I/O link errors. That is a hypothesis to test.

**Next, for node-platform**
1. `rts: kernel terminated` and `tree network packet error`. Each had 5,120 lines across 3,584 nodes, 7 bursts each, and both are rising. They are probably the same fleet-wide events.
2. `rts panic`. It recurs in every week of the period.
3. The three `invalid operation exception` patterns. They are new since 17 Nov, which is also the day the `ciod` link error started.

The session report with every query is at http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192032-9fa5. Its check of the numbers in this answer found 0 of 23 in the recorded tool results, because the report logged no tool calls (tool_calls: 0). Treat the figures above as unchecked by that page. They come from the tool outputs I read earlier.

baseline.text:
The "machine check interrupt" problem peaked in the first full week of October 2005 and then held steady at a lower level. The team that owns it is **node-platform**.

**Weekly trend** (phrase search, log lines, weeks start Monday):

| Week starting | Lines |
|---|---|
| 26 Sep (only 1–2 Oct is in range) | 4 |
| 3 Oct | 21 |
| 10 Oct | 11 |
| 17 Oct | 11 |
| 24 Oct | 11 |
| 31 Oct (only 31 Oct is in range) | 3 |

- There were 61 lines in October in total.
- The week of 3 Oct was the peak, with 21 lines. It then fell by about half, to 11 lines, and stayed at exactly 11 for the next three weeks.
- The first and last rows are partial weeks, so their low counts only reflect the days in range.
- Overall the problem is not growing. It spiked early in the month and then settled into a steady, lower rate.

**Ownership:**
- The main pattern, "machine check interrupt" (pattern 33), is logged by the KERNEL component, which node-platform owns.
- The same team also owns the variants, such as "…(bit=N): L‹N› major internal error" (pattern 93).
- Jev judged pattern 33 a hardware fault, with a problem probability of 0.78.
- Over the whole dataset, pattern 33 has 161 lines across about 150 nodes. It is therefore a widespread, low-volume hardware symptom, not one bad node.

The weekly counts come from a phrase search, so they include the variant messages that contain "machine check interrupt". They are not pattern 33 alone. I did not check ownership confidence with `owner_of`, so I can't say whether the owner is curated or inferred.

In the OpenStack nova logs, 3,969 requests failed with HTTP 404 and 2 failed with HTTP 503. All of them were on **nova-api**, the Nova REST API service. The **cloud-api** team owns nova-api. That ownership comes from the curated ownership table, with confidence 1.0.

|---|---|---|---|
| 404 | 3,969 | nova-api | cloud-api |
| 503 | 2 | nova-api | cloud-api |

- **Other statuses:** nova-api is the only component that logs an HTTP status in this dataset. The only other statuses logged are 200, 202 and 204.

product.text:
Across the whole openstack dataset, 3969 log lines carry HTTP 404 and 2 log lines carry HTTP 503. Both come only from nova-api, and the curated owner of nova-api is cloud-api.
Scope: Dataset openstack, whole corpus 2017-05-14 19:39:01 to 2017-05-17 12:02:35 (first_ts / last_ts from describe_corpus). Filters: status = 404 and status = 503, grouped by component. Counts are log lines. Neither count_by result was truncated. No previous-period comparison was run for these statuses.
HTTP 404 appears on 3969 log lines in openstack, all from one component, nova-api.
HTTP 503 appears on 2 log lines in openstack, all from one component, nova-api.
nova-api is owned by team cloud-api (source: curated, confidence 1.0). Its description is 'Nova REST API (request handling and latency)'.
The openstack corpus holds 207820 log lines between 2017-05-14 19:39:01.445000 and 2017-05-17 12:02:35.320000, from the components nova-compute, nova-api and nova-scheduler.
1. HTTP 404 responses from nova-api. Investigate first because it is by far the larger volume of the two failure statuses. — owner cloud-api (curated, confidence 1.0) — 3969 log lines with status 404, all on nova-api, against 2 log lines for 503. Bursts, nodes, weeks active and change vs the previous period were not measured for this status. — Break the 404 log lines down by request path and pattern to see whether they cluster on one endpoint. Then decide whether they are expected not-found results or a fault.
2. HTTP 503 responses from nova-api. Rare, but a 503 is a server-side status. — owner cloud-api (curated, confidence 1.0) — 2 log lines with status 503, all on nova-api. Bursts and change vs the previous period were not measured. — Pull the 2 log lines and their request ids, and check what the same request did on nova-compute and nova-scheduler.
Hypothesis: The 404 volume may be mostly routine not-found responses, such as lookups for VMs that no longer exist, and not a service fault. Would confirm: Group the 404 log lines by request path and instance uuid, and check whether the same requests succeeded earlier or were preceded by a delete.
Hypothesis: The 2 503 log lines may be a short-lived backend or availability problem behind nova-api. Would confirm: Check log lines around the 2 timestamps for nova-api, nova-compute and nova-scheduler errors, and see whether the 503 repeats.
Unknown: The counts are log lines with a status, not distinct requests. Distinct request ids were not counted.
Unknown: Bursts, weeks active and change vs the previous period for the 404 and 503 patterns were not measured, so no trend can be stated.
Unknown: The logs do not show root cause, cost, downtime or customer impact.
Unknown: Whether the 404 responses are expected behaviour is not established by these results.
Next step: Run top_patterns filtered to status 404, then status 503, on nova-api to get bursts and change vs the previous period. — The ledger gives only line counts (3969 and 2); a trend needs burst counts.
Next step: List the 2 nova-api 503 log lines with their request ids and trace each request across services. — Only 2 log lines carry 503, so each one can be checked individually.
Next step: Group the 3969 404 log lines by request path and tenant. — This shows whether the 404s are concentrated or spread out.

baseline.text:
It's fleet-wide, not one bad node. There is one mild hotspot in rack R30.

In October 2005 (2005-10-01 to 2005-11-01), "rts panic! - stopping execution" appeared in 46 log lines. All are KERNEL FATAL, under pattern 69. The first was 2005-10-01 11:02 and the last was 2005-10-31 20:44, so it recurred through the whole month.

- **Nodes:** The 46 lines came from 38 distinct nodes. The busiest node logged only 2 lines, which is 4.3% of the total. The tool's rule calls a pattern "concentrated" at 50% or more from one node, so this is nowhere near that.
- **Evenness:** The spread is almost even across nodes (normalized entropy 0.986). The tool's rule labels this "widespread".
- **Racks:** It hit at least 20 racks. The first five hits were on R04, R52, R22, R21 and R62.
- **R30 hotspot:** R30 has the most lines, 10 across 7 nodes. R31 is next with 3 lines on 2 nodes. R30 is the only rack with a clear cluster. It is still spread over several nodes, so it does not point to a single faulty node.

Counts are log lines, not incidents. Some of the 46 lines could come from the same event, for example the two lines on 2005-10-02 09:10 on different nodes. This shows where and how widely the message appeared. It doesn't show why. R30 would be the place to look first for a shared cause, such as a midplane or job issue. The logs I checked don't show whether that is the case.

The biggest single FATAL pattern by lines is KERNEL 'data TLB error interrupt': 152734 log lines, 541 nodes, 22 bursts, 8 weeks active, top-node share 0.996.

baseline.text:
Two components, KERNEL and APP, account for almost all FATAL lines in BGL. KERNEL is owned by node-platform and APP by hpc-workloads.

BGL has 855,501 FATAL lines in total. Only four components logged any:

| Component | FATAL lines | Share | Owning team |
|---|---|---|---|
| KERNEL | 626,756 | 73.3% | node-platform |
| APP | 228,536 | 26.7% | hpc-workloads |
| LINKCARD | 206 | <0.1% | node-platform |
| MMCS | 3 | <0.1% | cluster-control |

By team, node-platform owns 626,962 FATAL lines (KERNEL plus LINKCARD), hpc-workloads 228,536 and cluster-control 3.

- **Ownership confidence:** All four owners come from the curated ownership table, so they are not inferred.
- **APP dispute:** Jev's hints say most APP lines belong to node-platform (probability 0.939). The curated owner is hpc-workloads, so I've kept that. If the dispute is right, node-platform would own about 99.9% of all FATAL lines.
- **Unit:** These are log lines, not incidents. One fault can log thousands of lines, so the numbers show volume rather than how often problems occurred.

baseline.text:
**October 2005 was worse than September for a group of recurring hardware and kernel faults, and node-platform owns every one of them.** Ownership is curated, with confidence 1.0, for all of them.

I compared problem bursts in 2005-10-01 → 2005-11-01 with the previous period. A burst is a recurrence after more than 30 minutes of quiet. The tool's "previous period" starts on 2005-08-31, so it includes one extra August day.

**Largest increases**

| Pattern | Kind | Bursts, Oct vs prev. | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Kill job N timed out. Block freed." (#261, KERNEL) | job or application failure | 44 vs 29 (+15) | 47 lines, active in 6 weeks |
| "machine check interrupt (bit=N): L3 major internal error" (#93, KERNEL) | hardware failure | 10 vs 5 (+5) | 8 nodes |
| "NodeCard is not fully functional" (#318, HARDWARE) | hardware failure | 3 vs 1 (+2) | one node only, 5 lines |
| "Microloader Assertion" (#467, KERNEL) | system software failure | 2 vs 0 (+2) | 18 nodes, first seen in August, so not new |

- **Uncorrectable and parity errors (+2 each):** each of the patterns below went from 2 bursts to 4. Each touched about 4 nodes, and all are KERNEL-level FATAL messages.
  - uncorrectable error in directory (#120)
  - uncorrectable error in EDRAM bank (#122)
  - parity error in bank (#123)
  - uncorrectable error in external DDR (#124)
  - parity error in read queue (#125) and in read queue PLB (#126)
  - memory manager uncorrectable error (#135)
  - generic uncorrectable error (#153)
  - address parity error (#154)
  - DDR failing data registers (#158)
  - DDR failing address register (#160)

  They share first-seen times in June and the same 4-node footprint. That points to one repeated memory/DDR fault episode that logs many messages, not a dozen separate problems. That is my reading, not something the logs prove.

**Owner:** node-platform, for the KERNEL and HARDWARE components. Every top-growth pattern belongs to it, so no other team shows a comparable increase in this ranking. I read only the 15 largest of 86 candidates. Those 15 are the ones with the biggest increase (+2 or more), so patterns outside them grew by 2 bursts or less.

**Caveats**
- The "Kill job … timed out" pattern is the clear mover. Its 15-burst increase is far larger than any other. It is also the only one that is a job-level failure, not a hardware fault.
- Several kernel patterns were left out by the problem filter as probably not real faults. Examples are "instruction address", "machine check status register" and "summary…". They recurred about 55–58 times in October, and I did not check whether they grew.
- The counts are bursts and log lines, not confirmed incidents. They say nothing about downtime or impact.

I didn't call `session_report`, so there's no session report link for this answer.

product.text:
Counting problem bursts across all teams, October (345) was below September (446), but several node-platform KERNEL and HARDWARE patterns recurred more often. The largest is 'Kill job <N> timed out. sql: WITH now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS lines, count(DISTINCT node) AS nodes, count(DISTINCT date_trunc('week', ts)) AS weeks_active, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500 OR severity IS NULL)) AS problem_lines, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500)) AS error_lines FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' AND pattern_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), top_node AS ( SELECT pattern_id, max(n) AS top_node_lines FROM ( SELECT pattern_id, node, count(*) AS n FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' AND node IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ), b_now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), b_prev AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts_prev FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-10-04 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-11-01 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), base AS ( SELECT p.pattern_id, p.template, p.component, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team, o.source AS owner_source, o.confidence AS owner_confidence, o.disputed_by AS owner_disputed_by, p.severity, now.lines, now.problem_lines, now.error_lines, now.nodes, now.weeks_active, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) AS bursts, coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS bursts_prev, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) - coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'bgl' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'bgl' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'bgl' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = 'bgl') THEN now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE now.error_lines > 0 END) ), inputs AS ( SELECT *, round(weeks_active::DOUBLE / 5, 3) AS persistence, round(problem_lines::DOUBLE / lines, 3) AS problem_share, p_problem AS severity_input FROM base ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY bursts) AS pr_frequency, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY change) AS pr_trend, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY nodes) AS pr_spread, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY persistence) AS pr_persistence, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY severity_input) AS pr_severity FROM inputs ) SELECT *, round(100 * (0.3 * pr_frequency + 0.2 * pr_trend + 0.25 * pr_spread + 0.15 * pr_persistence + 0.1 * pr_severity), 1) AS score FROM ranked ORDER BY score DESC, bursts DESC, pattern_id

WITH now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS lines, count(DISTINCT node) AS nodes, count(DISTINCT date_trunc('week', ts)) AS weeks_active, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500 OR severity IS NULL)) AS problem_lines, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500)) AS error_lines FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' AND pattern_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), top_node AS ( SELECT pattern_id, max(n) AS top_node_lines FROM ( SELECT pattern_id, node, count(*) AS n FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' AND node IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ), b_now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-11-29 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), b_prev AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts_prev FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-10-04 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-11-01 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), base AS ( SELECT p.pattern_id, p.template, p.component, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team, o.source AS owner_source, o.confidence AS owner_confidence, o.disputed_by AS owner_disputed_by, p.severity, now.lines, now.problem_lines, now.error_lines, now.nodes, now.weeks_active, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) AS bursts, coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS bursts_prev, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) - coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'bgl' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'bgl' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'bgl' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND coalesce(j.p_problem, 0) < 0.5 ) SELECT pattern_id, template, component, team, bursts, lines, nodes, p_problem, kind FROM base ORDER BY bursts DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 3

baseline.text:
**Recommendation for November 2005: fix the ciod "link severed" socket failures first, then the kernel terminations and tree-network errors.** The priority score (0–100) is computed from frequency, trend, spread, persistence and judged severity. The logs don't show cost, downtime, customer impact or root cause, so those are not part of the ranking.

**Priorities, in order**

1. **ciod "Error reading message prefix on CioStream socket… Link has been severed"** (pattern 968, hpc-workloads, score 97.8).
   - It is new this period: 27 bursts in November against 0 in the previous four weeks.
   - It hit 1,024 nodes, with 10,408 lines spread almost evenly (top node about 0.1% of lines). That points to a systemic problem, not one bad node.
   - The related "Connection reset by peer" variant (pattern 988) is also new. It had 5 bursts across 1,014 nodes and scores 85.6. I'd treat the two as one network/I/O problem.
2. **"rts: kernel terminated for reason…"** (pattern 562, node-platform, score 93.5).
   - It had 7 bursts, up from 2, and touched 3,584 nodes.
   - It is a kernel failure, so it is more serious than most of the others.
3. **"rts panic! – stopping execution"** (pattern 69, node-platform, score 91.8).
   - This is the most persistent problem. It was active in all 5 weeks, with 33 bursts against 27 before.
   - It is limited to 33 nodes.
4. **Tree-network receive errors** (pattern 806, node-platform, score 88.7).
   - It had 7 bursts, up from 1, across 3,584 nodes.
   - It has the same burst count and node count as pattern 562 (5,120 lines each), so the two may come from the same events. That is only a hypothesis; I haven't checked it. Check them together.

**Lower priority, but worth a ticket**
- **Application load failures** (hpc-workloads, all new this month):
  - a "program image too big" error in a user's test binary (pattern 822, 5 bursts, 16 nodes);
  - a missing program image for `ddcMDbglV` (pattern 829, 2 bursts, 128 nodes).
  These look like job or user errors, not platform faults.
- **Floating-point "invalid operation exception" messages** (patterns 943, 944 and 945, node-platform):
  - All three are new, with 14 bursts each, but only on 15 nodes.
  - Their fault probabilities are weaker (0.84–0.87, against 0.91–0.96 for the top items).

**By team**
- **hpc-workloads** has the sharpest deterioration: 96 bursts against 5 in the previous period, and 27,859 lines. Most of that comes from the new ciod socket errors.
- **node-platform** has the most problem patterns (47) and the most bursts (256, up from 197). It owns three of the top four items.
- **cluster-control** is steadier, with 55 bursts, up from 42. Its top item is "Temperature Over Limit on link card" (score 78.8).

**Caveats**
- The ciod patterns are owned by hpc-workloads, but the ownership table flags a dispute: the judged hints point to node-platform. A "link severed" error is a network failure, so the two teams should look at it together.
- Bursts are recurrences separated by more than 30 minutes of quiet, not confirmed incidents.
- Three kernel start-up messages (patterns 45, 46 and 47, "wait state enable", "critical input interrupt enable", "external input interrupt enable") recur often, with 40 bursts each. The judgment model rated them as routine and not faults, so I left them out of the ranking.

baseline.text:
**Answer: October 2005 on Blue Gene/L (BGL), where to look first and what to do**

The logs show how often, how widely and how severely each problem occurred. They don't show cost, downtime, customer impact or root cause. The ranking below uses the tool's computed score. It weights burst frequency, change from the previous period, number of nodes, persistence and the stored fault judgment. A "burst" is a recurrence separated by more than 30 minutes of quiet.

**1. Memory and cache hardware faults on compute nodes (node-platform team)**
- These are the top five items in the computed ranking, scored 74–82 out of 100.
- Patterns:
  - Uncorrectable errors in external DDR memory, EDRAM and directory.
  - DDR failing address and data registers.
  - Parity errors.
  - "machine check interrupt … L3 major internal error", which had 10 bursts on 8 nodes, up from 5 bursts the month before.
- Each memory-error pattern appeared in 4 bursts on 4 nodes, up from 2 bursts the previous period. They recurred in 4 of the 6 weeks.
- They are rare (4–10 bursts each) but all are judged real hardware faults, and all are rising.
- A quick check of the nearby lines would show whether these are the same four nodes. The ranking doesn't establish that. Each pattern's top node holds 25% of its lines, which is consistent with 4 equal nodes.
- Next steps:
  - Pull the affected node and midplane locations.
  - Replace or isolate the repeat offenders.
  - Check whether the memory-error patterns are one failure logged in several ways, using `similar_patterns` or `co_occurrence`.

**2. "Kill job … timed out. Block freed." (node-platform team)**
- This is the most frequent real fault: 44 bursts in October, against 29 before (+15). It was active in all 6 weeks.
- The node count is 0 because the log lines carry no node, so spread can't be judged.
- Next steps:
  - Find out why jobs time out and are killed. Ask whether the cause is hardware, the scheduler or user jobs.
  - Check whether it lines up with the hardware faults above, using `precursors` or `co_occurrence`.
- Related patterns also recur, though they are falling month on month:
  - "rts panic! - stopping execution": 33 bursts, down from 51.
  - Plain "machine check interrupt": 34 bursts, down from 38.

**3. Job-loading failures from one user's HPCC benchmark runs (hpc-workloads team)**
- These are new in October. They are the largest source of log lines, but each is a single burst, so they look like a few bad submissions rather than hardware.
- Examples:
  - `vnm.rts`: 5,120 lines across 1,024 nodes, starting 5 Oct.
  - COP `vnm.rts`: 2,048 lines, starting 12 Oct.
  - EPStreamTriad: 2,048 lines, starting 15 Oct.
- The messages say "invalid or missing program image, Permission denied" or "No such file or directory".
- The team's burst count rose from 18 to 43 (+25).
- Next steps:
  - Have the job owner fix file permissions and paths, and check that the executables exist.
  - Don't treat these as machine failures.
  - Confirm that these jobs are not also feeding the "Kill job timed out" count.

**4. Link severed on the I/O stream (`ciod`, hpc-workloads team)**
- 3,434 lines across about 1,013 nodes, in 8 bursts. That is down from 14, so it is improving but widespread.
- The ownership table gives this to hpc-workloads, but the model's hints point to node-platform. Confirm the owner before assigning it.

**5. Node card discovery warnings (cluster-control team)**
- "Node card is not fully functional" and "Can not get assembly information for node card" each logged about 1,120 lines on 254 nodes, in 20 bursts. That is down slightly from 24 and 23.
- This is a steady background hardware-inventory problem rather than a spike. Have cluster-control check the node cards involved.

**Not prioritised:** the most frequent KERNEL patterns, "instruction address", "machine check status register" and "summary…", have 55–58 bursts. The judgment model rates them as diagnostic dump lines rather than faults (problem probability 0.08–0.13). They are probably the register dump that follows a machine check. They are useful as evidence for item 1, not as separate problems.

**Team view:** node-platform has 43 problem patterns and 251 bursts, up from 217 (+34). Start there. hpc-workloads has the largest volume, but it comes from a handful of user-level errors.

**Suggested order of action:**
1. node-platform: investigate the memory and machine-check nodes and the job-timeout surge.
2. hpc-workloads: fix the job-submission errors.
3. cluster-control: follow up on the node cards.
4. Decide who owns the severed-link errors.

The top three priorities for October 2005 are all node-platform kernel hardware-error patterns: uncorrectable DDR error, uncorrectable EDRAM error, and L-level major machine check interrupt. Each recurred in bursts across several nodes and weeks, and more often than in the previous period. The overall weekly burst trend reads as no clear change.
Scope: bgl dataset, 2005-10-01 to 2005-11-01 (compared with 2005-08-31 to 2005-10-01). Filter: problem patterns (jev real-fault filter). The priority table is truncated: top 10 shown of 86 matches, so the top 3 are reported here. The weekly trend and ownership results are not truncated.
Team roll-up, node-platform: 43 problem patterns, 251 bursts (previous period 217, change 34), 4150 log lines.
Team roll-up, cluster-control: 10 problem patterns, 51 bursts (previous period 56, change -5), 2338 log lines.
Team roll-up, hpc-workloads: 33 problem patterns, 43 bursts (previous period 18, change 25), 36295 log lines.
Weekly problem bursts total 345 for the period, and the trend reading is 'no clear change'.
Three high-burst patterns were excluded by the problem filter because of low p_problem; all are node-platform KERNEL: pattern 32 (58 bursts), pattern 34 (55 bursts), pattern 35 (55 bursts).
The APP component is owned by hpc-workloads (curated) but the ownership is disputed by node-platform (dispute confidence 0.939). It covers 228536 log lines, a 0.0481 share of the dataset.
58 problem patterns were first seen in the period (list truncated to 20). The first listed (pattern 745, ciod core files, node-platform) had 5 bursts and 2560 log lines over 512 nodes.
1. Uncorrectable error detected in external DDR (hardware failure judgment) — owner node-platform — score 82.1; 4 bursts (previous 2, change 2); 4 nodes; 4 weeks active — Decide whether node-platform should triage the affected hardware first and fund a memory-error investigation.
2. Uncorrectable error detected in EDRAM bank (hardware failure judgment) — owner node-platform — score 81.6; 4 bursts (previous 2, change 2); 4 nodes; 4 weeks active — Treat together with rank 1 as one memory-error review under node-platform.
3. Machine check interrupt (L-level major internal error) (hardware failure judgment) — owner node-platform — score 80.2; 10 bursts (previous 5, change 5); 8 nodes; 5 weeks active — Have node-platform confirm whether the 8 nodes overlap with ranks 1 and 2 and decide on remediation.
Hypothesis: Ranks 1-3 may share a common underlying node memory or hardware fault. Would confirm: Check whether the same nodes and time windows appear across the DDR, EDRAM and machine check patterns.
Hypothesis: The excluded patterns 32, 34 and 35 may be real hardware problems that the problem-probability filter understated. Would confirm: Engineer review of those patterns' log lines across the 53 to 55 nodes affected.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: Root cause is not established by these logs.

Unknown: The ranking covers only the top 10 of 86 matching patterns.

Next step: Resolve ownership of the APP component between hpc-workloads and node-platform. — APP ownership is disputed, and hpc-workloads shows the largest rise in bursts (change 25) in the team roll-up.
Next step: Review the excluded high-burst patterns 32, 34 and 35 to confirm they can be deprioritised. — They had 58, 55 and 55 bursts but were excluded by the problem filter.

baseline.text:
**node-platform carried the most risk in September 2005. Its trend is flat to slightly better, so I wouldn't call it clearly improving or worsening.**

**Why node-platform**
- It had 268 of the 446 problem bursts in the month (60%). hpc-workloads had 106 and cluster-control had 72. A burst is a recurrence of a problem message after more than 30 minutes of quiet, so it is not a confirmed incident.
- The two top-ranked problems in the computed priority table are both node-platform's:
  - **Lustre mount failures** (`Lustre mount FAILED : bglio… point /p/gb…`) scored 98.4. They came in 40 bursts, up from 2 in the prior period. They hit all 1,024 nodes and logged 23,505 lines.
  - **"rts panic! - stopping execution"** scored 95.9. It came in 49 bursts, up from 24, on 279 nodes, and was active in all 5 weeks.
- Hardware-type faults also sit in its area, for example machine check interrupts (38 bursts, up from 26).

**Is it getting better or worse?**
- **Versus August:** node-platform went from 275 bursts (2 Aug–1 Sep) to 268, a change of −7. Its weekly slope within September is −1.0 bursts per week.
- **Individual problems are moving the other way:** the Lustre mount and rts panic problems both grew sharply versus August. The team total stays flat only because other patterns declined.
- **Whole system:** September's weekly problem bursts were 130, 89, 48, 99 and 80. The first week is a partial week that starts 29 Aug. The tool's verdict is "no clear change", with half-month means of 89 and 89.5.

**Other teams**
- **hpc-workloads** is the one to watch. Its bursts rose from 23 to 106 versus August. Most of that is job-load failures (`ciod: Error loading … invalid or missing program image`) that appeared for the first time in September, each as a single burst across about 1,000 nodes. Its weekly slope inside September is −7.9, so these look like early-month events rather than a continuing climb.
- **cluster-control** improved, from 107 to 72 bursts.

**Limits**
- The logs measure frequency, spread, trend and persistence. Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in them.
- The Lustre mount and rts panic problems are the first things to look at.

Ownership of the hpc-workloads ciod patterns is disputed: the model's hints point to node-platform. If those were reassigned, node-platform's lead would grow.

baseline.text:
**Fix this one first: the "rts: kernel terminated for reason <N>" error (pattern 562).** It comes from the KERNEL component, which the node-platform team owns.

This is the priority table's computed ranking for August 2005. It scored 96 out of 100 and ranked first among 148 problem patterns.

- **It is new.** It had no bursts in July and appeared in 13 separate bursts in August. A "burst" is a recurrence after more than 30 minutes of quiet. Something changed that month.
- **It is widespread.** It hit 2,666 distinct nodes with 11,349 log lines. No single node accounts for more than 0.2% of them. That points to a systemic software problem, not one bad machine.
- **It persisted.** It showed up in 3 of the 5 weeks in the period.
- **It is judged a real fault.** The stored model judgment gives a 0.91 probability that this is a genuine problem, classed as a system software failure. This is a model judgment, not a confirmed root cause.
- **Its owner is clear.** The ownership table assigns KERNEL to node-platform directly, with full confidence. node-platform also carries the most problem bursts of any team: 460 in August, up from 136 in July.

**Runners-up**
- **"Node card is not fully functional" and "Can not get assembly information for node card"** (cluster-control, scores about 91). They are probably one hardware-discovery problem that appears as two messages. They are the most frequent and the longest-running: 37 and 36 bursts, active in all 5 weeks. They are a close second.
- **"ciod … Link has been severed"** (hpc-workloads, score 89). It is new in August, with 13 bursts across 865 nodes.

**Caveats**
- The ranking weighs frequency, trend, spread, persistence and judged severity. Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in the logs, so I can't say which fault hurt users most.
- The weights are fixed: frequency 0.30, spread 0.25, trend 0.20, persistence 0.15, severity 0.10.
- The runners-up score close to the winner. If the node-card hardware errors affected more jobs in practice, they could be the better pick.

I didn't open the session report page.

sql: WITH now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS lines, count(DISTINCT node) AS nodes, count(DISTINCT date_trunc('week', ts)) AS weeks_active, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500 OR severity IS NULL)) AS problem_lines, count(*) FILTER (WHERE (severity IN ('FATAL', 'FAILURE', 'SEVERE', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL') OR severity IN ('WARN', 'WARNING') OR status >= 500)) AS error_lines FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-09-01 00:00:00' AND pattern_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ), top_node AS ( SELECT pattern_id, max(n) AS top_node_lines FROM ( SELECT pattern_id, node, count(*) AS n FROM logs WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AND ts < '2005-09-01 00:00:00' AND node IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ), b_now AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-09-01 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), b_prev AS ( SELECT pattern_id, count(*) AS bursts_prev FROM bursts WHERE dataset = 'bgl' AND start_ts >= '2005-07-01 00:00:00' AND start_ts < '2005-08-01 00:00:00' GROUP BY 1 ), base AS ( SELECT p.pattern_id, p.template, p.component, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team, o.source AS owner_source, o.confidence AS owner_confidence, o.disputed_by AS owner_disputed_by, p.severity, now.lines, now.problem_lines, now.error_lines, now.nodes, now.weeks_active, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) AS bursts, coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS bursts_prev, coalesce(b_now.bursts, 0) - coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'bgl' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'bgl' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'bgl' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = 'bgl') THEN now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE now.error_lines > 0 END) ), inputs AS ( SELECT *, round(weeks_active::DOUBLE / 5, 3) AS persistence, round(problem_lines::DOUBLE / lines, 3) AS problem_share, p_problem AS severity_input FROM base ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY bursts) AS pr_frequency, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY change) AS pr_trend, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY nodes) AS pr_spread, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY persistence) AS pr_persistence, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY severity_input) AS pr_severity FROM inputs ) SELECT *, round(100 * (0.3 * pr_frequency + 0.2 * pr_trend + 0.25 * pr_spread + 0.15 * pr_persistence + 0.1 * pr_severity), 1) AS score FROM ranked ORDER BY score DESC, bursts DESC, pattern_id
