coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'bgl' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'bgl' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'bgl' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND coalesce(j.p_problem, 0) < 0.5 ) SELECT pattern_id, template, component, team, bursts, lines, nodes, p_problem, kind FROM base ORDER BY bursts DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 3

SELECT team, round(regr_slope(n, i), 3) AS slope, sum(n) AS bursts FROM (SELECT t.team, s.i, count(x.t) AS n FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY b) - 1 AS i, b FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-08-01 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2005-09-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b)) s CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'bgl' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2005-09-01 00:00:00') t LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'bgl' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-08-01 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2005-09-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b AND x.team = t.team GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY bursts DESC

baseline.text:
The November logs show how often and how widely problems occurred. They don't show what the problems cost us or why they happened.

**What the logs don't contain**
- **Cost, downtime and customer impact.** The tool's own caveat says these "are not in these logs." We can't say how many jobs were lost, how many node-hours were unavailable, or who was affected.
- **Root cause.** The logs show symptoms and sequences, and "earlier" is not the same as "caused by." Take the biggest November item, `ciod: Error reading message prefix on CioStream socket…Link has been severed`. It first appeared in November, with 27 bursts across 1,024 nodes and 10,408 lines. The logs can't tell us whether the cause was the network, the I/O nodes, user jobs or a software change. The same goes for `rts: kernel terminated` and `rts panic`.
- **Incident counts.** A "burst" is a recurrence of one message after more than 30 minutes of quiet. It is not a confirmed incident. Line counts are skewed by storms:
  - 200,937 lines were logged on Nov 3.
  - 150,957 lines were logged on Nov 4.
  - Only 595 lines were logged on Nov 6.
  - A busy day therefore doesn't mean a worse day.
- **Severity of each message type.** Whether a message type counts as a "problem" comes from a stored model judgment (Jev), not from an engineer. Some messages that carry error-level severity were judged not to be faults. Examples are `wait state enable…`, `critical input interrupt enable…` and `external input interrupt enable…`, each with 40 bursts. Those judgments are probabilities, so they can be wrong in either direction.

**Ownership is partly uncertain**
- Ownership of the APP component is disputed. The table assigns it to hpc-workloads, but the model hints point to node-platform with confidence 0.939.
- APP covers 228,536 lines, 4.8% of the dataset. Several top November problems sit in it, including the `ciod` link-severed errors, the "program image too big" error and the "No such file" error.
- Which team should act on those is therefore uncertain.

**Other blind spots**
- The ranking measures frequency, spread, trend and persistence, using the weights shown in the tool output. It says nothing about which fault matters most to the business.
- The "trend" compares November only with the 4 weeks before it (Oct 4 to Nov 1). That is a short baseline.
- The data has no request IDs, durations or status codes, so we can't follow a job end to end or measure slowness. Only the node location is available.
- The logs are filtered to RAS events, so faults that never logged an event are invisible.

The tool-call record and number checks for this session are at http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192241-7e1a. The page reported that none of the 10 numbers in my summary text were matched to tool results, so check them against the tool outputs there.

baseline.text:
**No. Reliability on BGL did not clearly improve from September to November 2005.** The tool's verdict is "no clear change".

I counted problem bursts per week. A burst is a recurrence of a problem message after more than 30 minutes of quiet. Only messages judged to be real faults were counted. There were 1,198 bursts in total, and the bursts are recurrences, not confirmed incidents.

- **Slope:** The fitted line falls slightly, by about 1.3 bursts per week each week. The average was 87 per week in the first half of the period and 84 in the second half. That drop is far too small to count as improvement, because the tool's rule needs a difference of more than 20% and beyond normal noise.
- **Weekly counts:** The weeks of 9/5 to 10/31 ran between 46 and 115 bursts. The first and last weeks of the period are partial: 130 in the week of 8/29, which includes some August days, and only 18 in the week of 11/28.
- **Late rise:** The late-November weeks were the worst of the period, with 154 bursts in the week of 11/14 and 117 in the week of 11/21. That is the opposite of a steady improvement.
- **Teams:** Every team's slope was slightly negative, but all of them are small and within the noise.

| Team | Bursts | Weekly slope |
|---|---|---|
| node-platform | 775 | −0.40 |
| hpc-workloads | 245 | −0.58 |
| cluster-control | 178 | −0.36 |

Problem activity is high and uneven from week to week, with no sustained downward trend. The logs show frequency and trend only. They don't show downtime or customer impact.

In 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08, 214 distinct IPs appear in log lines matching "Failed password root". The heaviest were ip:59.63.188.30 (28766 log lines), ip:183.63.110.206 (17340), ip:58.242.83.25 (14383), ip:183.192.189.131 (8670) and ip:218.65.30.30 (8374). These are log-line counts, not exact attempt counts, because some lines are collapsed "message repeated 5 times" summaries.
Scope: Dataset ssh (OpenSSH auth log, host LabSZ, one node). Period 2018-01-01 00:00:00 → 2018-01-08 00:00:00; the corpus ends 2018-01-07 17:22:01. Filter: full-text "Failed password root". The IP ranking is truncated to the top 30 of 214 IPs, so the other IPs are not listed.
102039 log lines matching "Failed password root" were found in the window, all on node LabSZ, split across 2 patterns: 400011 with 66646 log lines and 400015 with 35393 log lines.
214 distinct IPs appear in those log lines. The top 30 were shown (truncated).
Top entities by log lines (entity values as given in the result): ip:59.63.188.30 = 28766 (first 2018-01-03 10:07:06, last 2018-01-05 12:22:59); ip:183.63.110.206 = 17340 (first 2018-01-02 19:15:56, last 2018-01-03 10:08:41); ip:58.242.83.25 = 14383 (first 2018-01-01 08:48:42, last 2018-01-02 17:13:42); ip:183.192.189.131 = 8670 (first 2018-01-03 00:57:51, last 2018-01-03 12:36:43); ip:218.65.30.30 = 8374 (first 2018-01-01 14:23:31, last 2018-01-02 11:12:24).
Next in the ranking: ip:218.87.109.156 = 7135 log lines; ip:182.100.67.120 = 6179; ip:182.100.67.52 = 3389; ip:183.192.189.133 = 614; ip:139.219.239.13 = 566; ip:123.235.32.19 = 499, spread from 2018-01-01 02:18:48 to 2018-01-07 13:38:16.
Every one of the top 30 IPs was seen on 1 node (LabSZ). Most were active in windows of hours to about two days, while ip:123.235.32.19 and ip:114.112.48.155 recur across several days at low volume (499 and 320 log lines).
Pattern 400015 lines are collapsed summaries, e.g. "message repeated 5 times: [ Failed password for root from 74.82.254.191 port 44521 ssh2]" (2018-01-01 00:12:43). One log line therefore stands for several attempts.
Timeline for the first failed-root connection in the window, request sshd-3117, node LabSZ. Before, 2018-01-01 00:12:28: "reverse mapping checking getaddrinfo for 74.82.254.191.ifibertv.com [74.82.254.191] failed - POSSIBLE BREAK-IN ATTEMPT!" and "pam_unix(sshd:auth): authentication failure; logname= uid=0 euid=0 tty=ssh ruser= rhost=74.82.254.191  user=root". At, 00:12:30: "Failed password for root from 74.82.254.191 port 44521 ssh2". After, 00:12:43: "message repeated 5 times: [ Failed password for root from 74.82.254.191 port 44521 ssh2]", "Disconnecting: Too many authentication failures for root [preauth]", and "PAM service(sshd) ignoring max retries; 6 > 3".
On node LabSZ the closest earlier line before that window is 2017-12-31 23:56:30, "Received disconnect from 202.107.207.123: 11: Bye Bye [preauth]" (sshd-3101), 960.0 seconds before the anchor. The closest later line is 2018-01-01 00:28:52, "Invalid user  0101 from 5.188.10.180" (sshd-3146), 982.0 seconds after.
The first matching lines in the period are on 2018-01-01, at 00:12:30 for pattern 400011 and 00:12:43 for pattern 400015. The last are 2018-01-07 17:07:13 and 2018-01-07 16:21:28 respectively.
Hypothesis: The top IPs may be separate automated brute-force campaigns that each ran for hours to about two days. Several sit in adjacent address ranges (218.65.30.x, 182.100.67.x, 183.192.189.x), which could mean the same operator or botnet. Would confirm: Group the IPs by /24 and compare their start and stop times, usernames tried and ports; check whether the ranges rotate in sequence.
Unknown: The logs do not give an exact attempt count: pattern 400015 lines each stand for repeated attempts (the sampled lines say 5 times), and summing those repeats was not done.
Unknown: The full-text match on "Failed password root" may include lines that are not literally "for root", and the ledger does not verify this. The per-pattern counts also differ between the facet (400011 = 66646 in the window) and the unbounded search (66928), which was not reconciled.
Unknown: The 184 IPs beyond the top 30 are not listed, so the total attempts per IP outside the ranking are unknown.
Unknown: The usual (baseline) rate of failed root logins outside this week was not measured, so whether this week is abnormal is not established.
Unknown: Whether any login succeeded, plus impact, downtime or cost, is not in these results.
Next step: Re-run top_entities for ip with pattern_id 400011 and pattern_id 400015 separately, limit 50, for 2018-01-01 → 2018-01-08, and add the repeat counts ("message repeated N times") to get true attempts per IP. — The 102039 log lines undercount attempts because pattern 400015 collapses repeats (ev-d1f4d843ec, ev-0b880f1043).

baseline.text:
Seven IP addresses account for most of the failed root logins in the week of 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08, though my counts are log lines and understate the real number of attempts. The log has 102,039 lines reading "Failed password for root from <ip> …" in that period. They came from 214 distinct source IPs, all against host LabSZ.

**Undercount:** 35,393 of those lines are sshd summaries of the form "message repeated N times: [Failed password for root …]". Each stands for N attempts but counts as one line, so the true attempt count is higher than 102,039. I didn't sum the N values, so I can't give an exact total.

**Top sources, in log lines:**

| IP | Lines | Active (first → last line) |
|---|---|---|
| 59.63.188.30 | 28,766 | Jan 3 10:07 → Jan 5 12:22 |
| 183.63.110.206 | 17,340 | Jan 2 19:15 → Jan 3 10:08 |
| 58.242.83.25 | 14,383 | Jan 1 08:48 → Jan 2 17:13 |
| 183.192.189.131 | 8,670 | Jan 3 00:57 → Jan 3 12:36 |
| 218.65.30.30 | 8,374 | Jan 1 14:23 → Jan 2 11:12 |
| 218.87.109.156 | 7,135 | Jan 3 15:01 → Jan 4 12:17 |
| 182.100.67.120 | 6,179 | Jan 1 20:32 → Jan 2 11:31 |
| 182.100.67.52 | 3,389 | Jan 4 03:43 → Jan 5 07:32 |

- **Concentration:** these eight IPs account for about 94,200 lines, roughly 92% of the 102,039.
- **Long tail:** the other 206 IPs each have fewer than about 620 lines. The next largest are 183.192.189.133 (614), 139.219.239.13 (566), 123.235.32.19 (499), 119.7.221.129 (462), 60.2.12.12 (435) and 115.238.230.180 (432).
- **Subnet clusters:** several sources sit in the same ranges, for example 218.65.30.x (.30, .43, .61, .122, .123, .124), 182.100.67.x (.4, .52, .120) and 218.87.109.x (.154, .156). That looks like coordinated brute-forcing from the same networks. This is my inference from the addresses, not something the logs state.
- **Pattern:** each IP's activity runs in a window of hours to a couple of days, which fits sequential password-guessing bursts.

The per-IP figures are the top 30 of 214 from `top_entities`. They also count the "message repeated" lines once each, so they understate attempts in the same way.

baseline.text:
Block `blk_-1608999687919862906` was written, copied to 10 datanodes, read many times, and deleted about an hour later. I found no ERROR or problem-level lines. The log has 269 lines for it in two sessions. I read only the first 50 of the 249 lines in the first session, so the read burst is summarised rather than listed line by line.

**Session 1: 2008-11-09 20:35:18 → 20:36:26 (249 lines)**

1. **20:35:18, allocation and first write.**
   - The NameNode (`dfs.FSNamesystem`) allocated the block for `/mnt/hadoop/mapred/system/job_200811092030_0001/job.jar`.
   - At the same second, datanode 10.250.19.102 logged "Receiving block".
2. **20:35:19, initial pipeline finishes.**
   - 10.250.10.6 and 10.250.14.224 also logged "Receiving block".
   - The PacketResponders for the first three copies terminated, and each logged "Received block … of size 91178".
   - The NameSystem recorded `addStoredBlock` for 10.250.10.6, 10.251.111.209 and 10.250.14.224, each with size 91178.
3. **20:35:21 → 20:35:27, chained replication.** The NameNode repeatedly asked a datanode that already held the block to copy it to two more. Each hop shows an "ask … to replicate" line, a "Starting thread to transfer" line, "Transmitted block", then "Received block" and `addStoredBlock` on the target.
   - 10.250.14.224 → 10.251.215.16 and 10.251.71.193 (20:35:21)
   - 10.251.215.16 → 10.251.74.79 and 10.251.107.19 (20:35:24–26)
   - 10.251.107.19 → 10.251.31.5 and 10.251.71.240 (20:35:27)
   - 10.251.31.5 → 10.251.90.64 (20:35:30)
4. **20:35:23 → 20:36:26, read burst.**
   - Many "Served block … to /<client>" lines (pattern 500012) appear from the datanodes holding the block. They start at 20:35:23, peak around 20:35:27–31, and the session ends at 20:36:26.
   - The block is a job jar, so this is probably tasks fetching it, but the logs don't say that.
   - `dfs.DataNode$DataXceiver` accounts for 220 of the 249 lines, mostly these reads.

**Session 2: 21:38:09 → 21:38:40 (20 lines), deletion**

- **21:38:09:** `NameSystem.delete` added the block to the invalidSet of 10 datanodes: 10.250.10.6, 10.250.14.224, 10.251.107.19, 10.251.111.209, 10.251.215.16, 10.251.31.5, 10.251.71.193, 10.251.71.240, 10.251.74.79 and 10.251.90.64.
- **21:38:10 → 21:38:40:** `dfs.FSDataset` logged 10 "Deleting block … file /mnt/hadoop/dfs/data/current/blk_-1608999687919862906" lines, one per replica. Most fall in the first 4 seconds, and the last few come about 30 seconds in.

The block ended up with 10 replicas, more than the usual default of 3. That fits a job jar, but the logs don't say why.

The replica list comes from the invalidSet lines. The write and replication trail is partly cut off in the output I read, so it may not match that list exactly.

I haven't generated the session report page.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** Two teams own the recurring problems. client-connectivity owns the most frequent one, and coordination-platform owns the rest. I'd start with the quorum election-channel failures, because they were still firing when the data ends.

The data covers 2015-07-29 17:41 to 2015-08-25 11:26, and the log has no node or host field. I can't say which ensemble member a line came from, or how widespread a problem was. Bursts are recurrences separated by more than 30 minutes of quiet. They are not confirmed incidents.

**Top recurring problems, ranked by the computed priority score**

| # | Problem | Owner | Bursts | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `caught end of stream exception` (NIOServerCnxn, WARN) | client-connectivity | 18 | 1,670 |
| 2 | `Cannot open channel to N at election address /IP` (QuorumCnxManager, WARN) | coordination-platform | 8 | 2,584 |
| 3 | `Unexpected Exception:` (NIOServerCnxn, ERROR) | client-connectivity | 9 | 27 |
| 4 | `Unexpected exception causing shutdown while sock still open` (LearnerHandler, ERROR) | coordination-platform | 7 | 590 |
| 5 | `Exception when following the leader` (Follower) | coordination-platform | 6 | 11 |
| 6 | `Connection broken for id N, my id = N` (RecvWorker) | coordination-platform | 6 | 32 |
| 7 | `Unexpected exception, tries=N, connecting to /IP` (Learner) | coordination-platform | 5 | 8 |

Further down the ranking:
- `ZooKeeperServer not running` session closes (client-connectivity): 159 lines.
- A single burst of `Connection broken for id <HEX>` (coordination-platform): 10,356 lines.

**Owners:**
- **coordination-platform:** 7 problem patterns, 35 bursts, 13,585 lines. This is the quorum, election and leader/follower layer. Its ownership comes from the dataset's default row (confidence 0.95), not a component-specific entry.
- **client-connectivity:** 4 problem patterns, 30 bursts, 1,864 lines. Ownership is curated (confidence 1.0).

**What happened over time**
- Almost all the noise came on 2015-07-29. That day had 42,668 of the 48,507 WARN lines, including the 10,356-line burst of broken quorum connections. Several related errors first appear around 19:03–19:54: session closes, "exception when following the leader", and "shutdown while sock still open". That points to a leader/quorum disruption.
- After that, WARNs are sporadic: 1,589 lines on 07-30, 840 on 07-31, 371 on 08-10 and 518 on 08-20.
- The election-channel failures came back on 08-24 and 08-25, with 1,039 and 1,404 WARN lines. One burst began at 2015-08-24 15:26 and ran until the end of the data (2,417 lines). It started with `Cannot open channel to 2 at election address /10.10.34.12:3888`. That pattern was active in all 5 weeks.
- The "end of stream" exceptions (18 bursts) have no regular schedule: the median gap between bursts is about 4 hours, and only 18% of gaps are regular. They fall mostly on Thursdays and Fridays (13 of 18).

**What to investigate first**
1. **coordination-platform: election-channel failures to peer 2 (10.10.34.12:3888, pattern 200018).**
   - It was the only problem still active at the end of the data.
   - It recurs across the whole period.
   - It affects leader election and quorum health.
   - Check whether that peer, its port 3888 or the network path to it was down on 08-24 and 08-25. Also check what happened on 07-29 around 19:00, when the same connection-broken family spiked.
   - Whether those two events are linked is a hypothesis. The tools show timing only, not cause.
2. **client-connectivity: `caught end of stream exception` (pattern 200062).** It is the most frequent pattern by bursts. It is usually a client disconnecting abruptly. Check whether the same clients repeat, and whether the bursts line up with the quorum disruptions above. I didn't check either.

**Caveats**
- Every problem shows as "new", with change equal to its burst count. That is because the dataset starts on 07-29, so the previous period is empty. It does not mean they truly appeared for the first time.
- Three frequent patterns were filtered out as not real faults. They are the "old client … r-o mode" notice (14 bursts, 1,861 lines) and two Leader "not first" / "First is 0x0" messages (9 bursts each).
- Cost, downtime and customer impact aren't in these logs.

I didn't call `session_report`, so there is no report page for this session.

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2015-07-29 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = 'zookeeper') THEN now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE now.error_lines > 0 END) ) SELECT *, count(*) OVER () AS candidates FROM base ORDER BY bursts DESC, nodes DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 15

product.text:
Between 2015-07-29 and 2015-08-26 there were 65 problem bursts in the Zookeeper logs: 35 owned by coordination-platform and 30 by client-connectivity. Investigate first the election-channel failure "Cannot open channel to <N> at election address" (coordination-platform): it was active in 5 weeks and had 1039 and 1378 log lines on the last two days. Each problem pattern had 0 bursts in the previous period, so the previous period gives no baseline.
Scope: Dataset zookeeper, 2015-07-29 00:00 to 2015-08-26 00:00, compared with 2015-07-01 to 2015-07-29. Problem patterns only (Jev filter, p_problem >= 0.5). The top-patterns result had 11 matches and was not truncated. The log has no node or host field, so nodes = 0 means the spread across nodes is unknown.
Problem bursts in the period total 65: coordination-platform 35 and client-connectivity 30.
Weekly problem bursts (week starting 2015-07-27, 08-03, 08-10, 08-17, 08-24): coordination-platform 25, 1, 2, 3, 4; client-connectivity 22, 0, 2, 6, 0.
Pattern 200062 "caught end of stream exception" (NIOServerCnxn, client-connectivity) has 18 bursts, 1670 log lines, 3 weeks active, and 0 bursts in the previous period (change 18).
Pattern 200089 "Unexpected Exception: " (NIOServerCnxn, client-connectivity) has 9 bursts and 27 log lines, 2 weeks active, 0 bursts in the previous period.
Pattern 200018 "Cannot open channel to <N> at election address" (QuorumCnxManager, coordination-platform) has 8 bursts, 2584 log lines, 5 weeks active, 0 bursts in the previous period (change 8).
Daily log lines for pattern 200018: 71 on 2015-07-30, 14 on 2015-08-07, 8 on 2015-08-10, 10 on 2015-08-18, then 1039 on 2015-08-24 and 1378 on 2015-08-25.
Pattern 200048 "Unexpected exception causing shutdown while sock still open" (LearnerHandler, coordination-platform) has 7 bursts and 590 log lines, 2 weeks active, p_problem 0.903.
Pattern 200050 "Connection broken for id <HEX>" has 1 burst but 10356 log lines. The watched phrase "connection broken" matched 10388 log lines in the window and 0 in the previous period.
Weekly WARN log lines for coordination-platform: 42304, 16, 19, 27, 2443 (week starting 2015-07-27, 08-03, 08-10, 08-17, 08-24). For client-connectivity: 2793, 0, 355, 550, 0.
Pattern 200055 (old-client connection requests, 14 bursts, 1861 log lines) was excluded by the problem filter (p_problem 0.15, kind "not a problem").
1. Quorum members cannot open election channels to peers ("Cannot open channel to <N> at election address"). INVESTIGATE FIRST: it recurred in all 5 weeks and reached its highest daily volume at the end of the period. — owner coordination-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 8 bursts (previous period 0, change 8), 2584 log lines, 5 weeks active, p_problem 0.733; 1039 log lines on 2015-08-24 and 1378 on 2015-08-25. — Check election-port connectivity and peer availability around 2015-08-24 to 2015-08-25 and around 2015-07-29 to 2015-07-31, and decide whether the two episodes share a cause.
2. Client connections ending with "caught end of stream exception". — owner client-connectivity (curated, confidence 1.0) — 18 bursts (the most of any problem pattern; previous period 0), 1670 log lines, 3 weeks active, p_problem 0.551. — Review which clients are dropping connections and whether it correlates with the server-side quorum disruption in the same weeks.
3. Unexpected exceptions in NIOServerCnxn ("Unexpected Exception: "). — owner client-connectivity (curated, confidence 1.0) — 9 bursts (previous period 0), 27 log lines, 2 weeks active, p_problem 0.664. — Pull the stack traces for these 27 log lines and confirm whether they share a cause with rank 2.
4. Learner handler shutting down with the socket still open ("Unexpected exception causing shutdown while sock still open"). — owner coordination-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 7 bursts (previous period 0), 590 log lines, 2 weeks active, p_problem 0.903. — Check whether these shutdowns line up with the election-channel failures in rank 1.
Hypothesis: Most patterns were first seen between 19:03 and 19:54 on 2015-07-29, and 25 coordination-platform bursts fall in the week starting 2015-07-27. This may be a single disruption event (for example a network partition or restarts) rather than several independent problems. Would confirm: Compare timelines of the patterns around 2015-07-29 19:00 to 20:00 and check for restart or network events in the surrounding log lines.
Hypothesis: The rise in pattern 200018 on 2015-08-24 and 2015-08-25 may be a second disruption of the same kind as the first. Would confirm: Check which peer ids and election addresses appear in those log lines, and whether a restart or network change occurred around 2015-08-24.
Unknown: Node spread: the logs contain no node or host field, so which ensemble members were affected is not known.
Unknown: Root cause of any pattern is not established by these logs.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Unknown: Why client-connectivity bursts are 0 in the week starting 2015-08-24 while coordination-platform bursts are 4 is not explained.
Next step: Open the log context around 2015-08-24 to 2015-08-25 for pattern 200018 and identify the unreachable peer addresses. — The pattern's highest daily volume (1039 and 1378 log lines) is at the end of the period.
Next step: Build a single timeline of patterns 200018, 200048, 200050 and 200062 starting from their first-seen times on 2015-07-29. — Many patterns were first seen within minutes of each other on 2015-07-29, which suggests one event.
Next step: Review the 18 bursts of "caught end of stream exception" by time and client, and confirm whether they follow the quorum disruption. — This is the most frequently recurring problem pattern (18 bursts, 1670 log lines).

## What to prioritise next (Apache error log, 2005-12-01 → 2006-02-28)

The log ends on 2006-02-28, so the period is covered in full. This server doesn't log hostnames, so I can't say whether any problem is spread across machines. The logs also don't show cost, downtime or customer impact. The ranking below uses frequency, trend, spread, persistence and severity.

**1. Requests for CGI scripts that don't exist (web-platform), which looks like scanning**
- The message is "script not found or unable to stat" (patterns 300042 and 300033).
- It came in 127 bursts, up from 32 in the previous three months. It ranked first in the priority table, with a score of 88.9 out of 100.
- Almost all of it is requests for `/var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl` and `/var/www/cgi-bin/awstats`. These account for about 1,100 lines each, and a few IPs repeat. Short bursts of about 46 lines from a single IP also appear, for example on 2006-01-08 and 2006-02-08.
- Weekly volume rose from none in December to about 470–640 lines per week in January and February.
- This reads as automated probing for a known awstats vulnerability. That is my interpretation, not something the log states.
- **Action:** check that awstats isn't exposed or is patched. Then block or rate-limit the repeat IPs, and quiet the log noise.

**2. mod_jk/jk2 integration errors (app-integration)**
- The message is "jk2_init() Can't find child N in scoreboard" (pattern 300022). It scored 86.8.
- It was active in 13 of the 14 weeks and came in 69 bursts, up from 54 before.
- It is rising again: 107 lines in the week of 2006-02-20, against 9 in the week of 2006-02-06.
- This is the most persistent real fault in the period. It points to the Apache–Tomcat connector's worker or child-process handling. The log doesn't show the cause.
- **Action:** have app-integration investigate it.

**3. Lower priority: mod_jk2 startup failures (web-platform)**
- These are the "Can't create worker.jni / channel.jni" and "Factory error creating …" messages (patterns 300006–300013).
- Each has 11 bursts and only 11 lines, down from 16 bursts before. They look like one startup problem that is shrinking, so fix them alongside item 2.

**What to deprioritise**
- "File does not exist" is the loudest message, with 13,882 lines and 156 bursts. The fault judgment rates it unlikely to be a real fault (p_problem 0.25), so it is mostly routine 404 noise. Its mass is worth skimming for the same scanners as item 1.

Every apache component has a curated, undisputed owner.

product.text:
On combo, the morning of 2005-12-06 was dominated by repeated kernel Out of Memory kills, which continued until 12:02:46. After a quiet gap, a clean-looking reboot started at 12:20:03 (gdm "Master rebooting...") and the kernel booted again at 12:22:57. The logs do not show what triggered the reboot.
Scope: Dataset linux, node combo (the only node), 2005-12-06 00:00:00 → 12:30:00, plus a check of everything before 00:00 and the first line after 12:30. The 837-line window and the later windows were truncated samples (limit 50), so counts come from totals and listed lines are examples. Nothing after 12:30 was inspected beyond the first 15 lines.
The window 2005-12-06 00:00:00 → 12:30:00 holds 837 log lines from 1 node (combo), first at 00:00:16 and last at 12:28:50. 639 of them are from the kernel component.
Pattern 700495 (kernel "Out of Memory: Killed process ...") accounts for 397 of the 837 log lines, first at 00:00:16 and last at 12:02:46.
The OOM lines are not new. Before 2005-12-06 00:00:00 there are 9932 matching log lines from 2005-11-15 04:30:29 to 2005-12-05 23:55:28. The last one before midnight is "Out of Memory: Killed process 7394 (python)." and the first of the day is "Out of Memory: Killed process 7395 (httpd)." at 00:00:16. A rate against the usual rate was not computed.
In the listed morning lines, OOM kills of httpd and python repeat in clusters at about 00:00, 00:05, 00:10, 00:15, 00:20 and 00:25. The same cluster pattern appears from 09:00 to 10:25, with sendmail and mrtg also killed at 10:16:36 and 10:16:43.
At 00:27:00 to 00:27:09 the OOM killer took out sendmail (7135, 7270) and mrtg (7472). At 00:27:23 the kernel logged "httpd: page allocation failure. order:0, mode:0x1d2" followed by a "Call Trace:" through __alloc_pages, do_page_cache_readahead, filemap_nopage and do_page_fault. A second "httpd: page allocation failure" follows at 00:27:23, again with a Call Trace.
Right before the reboot, the last OOM lines are: 12:02:40 "Out of Memory: Killed process 9715 (sendmail).", 12:02:41 "Out of Memory: Killed process 9853 (mrtg)." and 12:02:46 "Out of Memory: Killed process 9864 (diskcheck)."
No log lines exist on combo between 12:02:46 and 12:20:01. The first line after the OOM burst is gpm "*** info [mice.c(1766)]: " at 12:20:01, followed by gpm "imps2: Auto-detected intellimouse PS/2" at 12:20:02.
The reboot starts with gdm "Master rebooting..." at 12:20:03, shutdown "shutting down for system reboot" at 12:20:08, and init "Switching to runlevel: 6" at 12:20:14.
During shutdown several services logged failure: "messagebus shutdown failed" (12:20:20), "xfs shutdown failed" and "jserver shutdown failed" (12:20:29), "Stopping MySQL:  failed" (12:20:31), "sm-client shutdown failed" (12:20:50), "named shutdown failed" (12:21:10), "rpc.statd shutdown failed" and "portmap shutdown failed" (12:21:21). Others, such as httpd, squid, sshd, sendmail, smartd, snmpd, xinetd and ntpd, logged "succeeded" or exited normally.
The old kernel stopped logging at 12:21:22 with "Kernel log daemon terminating." The new boot is visible at 12:22:57 with "Linux version 2.6.5-1.358 (bhcompile@bugs.build.redhat.com) (gcc version 3.3.3 20040412 (Red Hat Linux 3.3.3-7)) #1 Sat May 8 09:04:50 EDT 2004". It also logs "126MB LOWMEM available." and "ACPI disabled because your bios is from 2000 and too old".
After the boot, "httpd startup succeeded" is logged at 12:24:08. ntpd logs "synchronized to LOCAL(0), stratum=10" and "kernel time sync disabled 0041" at 12:27:44, then "kernel time sync enabled 0001" at 12:28:50, the last line before 12:30.
No Out of Memory line appears after 12:02:46 up to 12:30:00, so the OOM kills stopped before the reboot began and did not resume within the window. Only 3 log lines fall in 12:25:00 → 12:30:00.
The first log line after 12:30:00 is at 2005-12-06 17:24:19 (named "starting BIND 9.2.3 -u named -t /var/named/chroot"). There are 4143 log lines from then to 2006-02-28 04:48:54, all on 1 node.
Hypothesis: The reboot may have been an operator-initiated restart to clear chronic memory exhaustion. The clean sequence (gdm "Master rebooting...", runlevel 6, services stopped in order) fits a deliberate reboot rather than a crash, and it follows weeks of OOM kills on this node. Would confirm: Check the login history (last/wtmp, su and sshd sessions) and any change record around 12:20 to see who ran reboot or shutdown. Then compare the OOM rate on combo before and after 12:22:57 over the following days: if OOM kills resume, the reboot did not fix the cause.
Unknown: Who or what initiated the reboot at 12:20 is not stated in these logs.
Unknown: The root cause of the memory exhaustion (a leak in httpd or python, too little RAM, or something else) cannot be established from these lines. The logs show only the kills and the page allocation failures.
Unknown: The sampled lines only show a fragment of the 397 OOM lines. Per-process kill counts and per-hour rates were not computed.
Unknown: Whether OOM kills resumed after 12:30 was not checked, and the gap between 12:28:50 and 17:24:19 was not examined.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Next step: Run count_by (or trend) on pattern 700495 for dataset linux, node combo, bucketed per hour from 2005-12-06 12:22:57 to the corpus end, and compare it with the hourly rate from 2005-11-15 to 2005-12-05. — This shows whether the reboot ended the OOM kills or whether they resumed (9932 OOM lines before 2005-12-06, 397 in the morning window).
Next step: Inspect the services that logged shutdown failures (mysqld, named, messagebus, xfs, portmap/nfslock, sm-client) on combo, and check their startup lines after 12:22:57 (for example search named startup after 12:30). — Eight services logged "shutdown failed" or "failed" during the 12:20 shutdown, and the first line after 12:30 is named startup at 17:24:19.
Next step: Check host-side memory data (free/vmstat or sar history) and the per-process footprint of httpd, python, sendmail and mrtg on combo, since the machine reports only "126MB LOWMEM available." — The OOM kills repeatedly hit httpd and python, with sendmail and mrtg also killed, and the 00:27:23 allocation failures show memory pressure.

baseline.text:
The morning was dominated by memory exhaustion on combo. The server then went quiet, and at 12:20 someone or something ordered a clean reboot. It came back up by about 12:23–12:25.

## Morning, 00:00 to ~12:02: out-of-memory kills
- The window holds 837 log lines. 639 are from the kernel, and the next busiest component is udev with 61.
- 397 of the lines are `Out of Memory: Killed process …`. The first is at 00:00:16 and the last at 12:02:46.
  - 301 victims were `httpd`, 72 were `python`, and 23 were `sendmail`, `mrtg` or `diskcheck`.
  - The kills came in bursts roughly every five minutes, each a few `httpd` processes followed by a `python`. That looks like a recurring job pushing memory over the limit.
  - Counts per hour stayed between 15 and 52, with no clear build-up toward noon.
  - Around 00:27 the system-level services were hit too: `sendmail` was killed at 00:27:00 and 00:27:04, and `mrtg` at 00:27:09.
- There were 5 `httpd: page allocation failure` events with kernel call traces, from 00:27:23 to 05:01:26. These are the kernel failing to get memory for `httpd`, which fits the same shortage.
- The last victims, at about 12:02, were `httpd`, `sendmail`, `mrtg` and `diskcheck`.

## Right before the reboot (12:02:46 to 12:20)
- Nothing was logged for about 17 minutes after the last OOM kill. I don't know why the log is silent for that gap.
- At 12:20:01 `gpm` (the console mouse service) logged. At 12:20:03 `gdm` logged `Master rebooting...`.
- At 12:20:08 `shutdown` logged `shutting down for system reboot`, and at 12:20:14 `init` logged `Switching to runlevel: 6`.
- Most services stopped cleanly: `atd`, `privoxy`, `cupsd`, `gpm`, `httpd`, `squid`, `sshd`, `sendmail`, `spamd`, `smartd`, `snmpd`, `xinetd`, `crond`, `apmd` and `ntpd`. The random seed was also saved.
- These reported `shutdown failed`: `messagebus`, `xfs`, `jserver` (FreeWnn), MySQL (`Stopping MySQL: failed`), `sm-client`, `named`, `rpc.statd` and `portmap`.
- The kernel log daemon stopped at 12:21:22 and syslog exited at 12:21:26.

## Right after the reboot (12:22:57 onward)
- `syslogd` restarted at 12:22:57. The kernel then booted as Linux 2.6.5-1.358 with 126 MB of low memory and no high memory.
- The boot messages include ACPI disabled (BIOS from 2000, "too old") and `register_security failed` (a security framework was already initialized). The `register_security` line is probably routine boot noise.
- Other boot problems:
  - 12:23:07: `cdrom: open failed`.
  - 12:23:19: `xinetd` could not bind telnet ("Address already in use"), so the telnet service was deactivated.
  - 12:24:35: `mdmpd failed`.
  - 12:24:33–12:24:35: `rsyncd` started on port 873 and `mdadm` reported success.
  - 12:24:37–12:24:54: udev removed and recreated the virtual console device nodes, which accounts for the 61 udev lines.
  - 12:27:44–12:28:50: `ntpd` reported `synchronized to LOCAL(0), stratum=10`, meaning it was running on its own local clock rather than an external time source. It then logged `kernel time sync enabled`.
- The next log line, `named` starting BIND, is stamped 17:24:19. Its line ID falls in the middle of the boot sequence, so I think it is a boot-time line with a timestamp about five hours off. That is an inference, not something I confirmed.
- Normal logging resumes the next morning, with an `sshd` line at 2005-12-07 03:28:16.

## Caveats
- The logs show the reboot was an orderly `shutdown` to runlevel 6 triggered through `gdm`. They don't show who triggered it.
- The OOM storm before it is the obvious suspect for why, but the logs don't say that.
- The machine is low on RAM (126 MB), which is consistent with the OOM kills. I have no memory-usage data from the morning to confirm it.
- The OOM kills may be the reason for the reboot, but this is only timing evidence.

baseline.text:
The logs for 2005-11-15 to 2005-12-01 don't show any kernel panics or reboots on combo. What they do show is the kernel running out of memory and killing processes, mostly httpd.

**Panics and reboots**
- Searching for "panic", "oops", reboot, restart and shutdown wording returned no panic or oops lines in the window.
- There is no kernel boot banner either, which a reboot would normally log.
- The only restart-like lines are `cupsd shutdown/startup` and `syslogd 1.4.1: restart` on Sun 2005-11-20 (about 04:09) and Sun 2005-11-27 (about 04:06). A `logrotate ... exited abnormally` line follows on 11-20. This looks like a weekly maintenance job, not a crash. The 11-20 context shows that, and I only inspected the 11-27 restart through the search hit, not its surrounding lines. The kernel was still logging OOM kills about an hour later.
- I can't rule out a hard reset that left no trace, but nothing in the logs shows one.

**What the logs show instead: an out-of-memory storm**
- The kernel logged `Out of Memory: Killed process N (...)` 6,709 times, from 2005-11-15 04:30:29 to 2005-11-30 13:56:48, in 94 separate bursts. That pattern was new this period, with none in the prior two weeks.
- It grew steadily from 88 lines on 11-15 to 328 on 11-19 and 848 on 11-20. It peaked at 1,750 on 11-21 and dropped to about 400 a day on 11-22 and 11-23. It fell further to 77 on 11-27, then climbed again to 514, 727 and 530 on 11-28 to 11-30.
- Most kills were `httpd`. 1,153 were other processes: `python` (first on 11-17 19:22), plus `sendmail` and `mrtg`, for example in the 11-21 12:40 burst.
- On 11-21 at 12:41 the kernel also logged `httpd: page allocation failure` and `Call Trace:` dumps going through the swap-in path (`read_swap_cache_async`, `do_swap_page`). This means the machine was swapping with no memory left. Later bursts, from 11-22 07:35 on, show ext3/jbd journal calls in their traces.
- A single `hda: drive not ready for command` appeared on 11-10, before the window.

**Trigger (a hypothesis, not proven)**
The best-supported trigger is memory exhaustion, with Apache httpd workers as the main consumer. A runaway or leaking Apache process, or too many workers, would fit. The logs record the symptom but not the cause. I found nothing showing why memory ran out, such as a traffic spike or a deployment, and I didn't check Apache's own error log in this dataset.

If you saw real panics or reboots, they probably come from another source, such as console output, a hardware watchdog or another host's logs. This syslog doesn't contain them.

product.text:
These logs do not show any kernel panic or reboot on combo between 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-01. What they do show is an out-of-memory episode: OOM kills from 2005-11-15 04:30:29 and page-allocation failures from 2005-11-21 12:41:10. The only restarts are two syslogd restarts, not reboots.
Scope: Dataset linux, 2005-11-15 00:00:00 → 2005-12-01 00:00:00, node combo (the only node in the matches). The panic search, the Oops/klogd search and the restart search were not truncated. The OOM, page-allocation and facet results are samples or truncated, so counts come from total_matches.
A prefix search for 'panic' in the window returned 0 matches.
A search for syslogd restart, 'kernel: Linux version', klogd and Oops returned 0 matches.
A search for reboot, restart, shutdown, kernel panic, syslogd, Linux version and Kernel command line returned 4 log lines, all on node combo. They are 'cupsd shutdown succeeded' at 2005-11-20 04:08:59 and 'syslogd 1.4.1: restart.' at 2005-11-20 04:09:36. The same pair repeats at 2005-11-27 04:06:06 and 2005-11-27 04:06:31.
Pattern 700495 'Out of Memory: Killed process <N> <*>' has 6709 log lines in the window on 1 node (combo). The first is at 2005-11-15 04:30:29 ('Out of Memory: Killed process 28473 (httpd).') and the last at 2005-11-30 13:56:48.
The OOM pattern is new: as of 2005-11-15 it had bursts_before 0 and lines_before 0. Bursts started per week: 33 (1667 log lines) in the week of 2005-11-14, 41 (3271 log lines) in the week of 2005-11-21, 38 (4178 log lines) in the week of 2005-11-28 and 21 (1288 log lines) in the week of 2005-12-05. Over the whole dataset it has 133 bursts, with a median gap between bursts of 1:14:50.
Pattern 700499 (kernel call-trace lines) has 998 log lines on 1 node, first at 2005-11-21 12:41:10 and last at 2005-11-29 04:43:48. The first trace lines are __alloc_pages, read_swap_cache_async, swapin_readahead, do_swap_page and handle_mm_fault.
Timeline around 2005-11-21 12:41:10. Before: OOM kills roughly every 5 to 7 seconds, e.g. 12:39:48 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28871 (httpd).', 12:40:29 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28881 (python).', 12:40:39 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28330 (sendmail).' and 12:40:57 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28852 (mrtg).'. At: 12:41:10 'httpd: page allocation failure. order:0, mode:0xd2', then 'Call Trace:' and ' [<0212ebf3>] __alloc_pages+0x274/0x281'. After: more call-trace lines through do_swap_page, handle_mm_fault and do_page_fault, then at 12:41:12 another 'httpd: page allocation failure. order:0, mode:0xd2'. The nearest earlier line outside the window is at 2005-11-21 12:39:03 on combo ('Out of Memory: Killed process 28853 (python).', 127.0 seconds before). The nearest later line outside the window is at 2005-11-21 14:15:23 on combo ('Out of Memory: Killed process 28886 (httpd).', 5653.0 seconds after).
In the window the linux dataset has 8675 log lines, of which kernel is 8051. Pattern 700495 accounts for 6709 and pattern 700499 for 998.
Hypothesis: Memory exhaustion on combo (httpd, sendmail, python and mrtg processes being OOM-killed, with swap-in paths in the call traces) may have hung the machine. Any hangs or reboots that followed may not have been logged. Would confirm: Look for gaps in combo's log timeline right after OOM bursts, boot lines in other sources (console, wtmp/last), and memory and swap metrics. Per-process OOM victim counts would show which service is growing.
Hypothesis: The syslogd 'restart.' lines on 2005-11-20 and 2005-11-27 may be routine daemon restarts, since cupsd shutdown precedes each at the same time of day, rather than reboots. Would confirm: Check logrotate and cron entries around 04:06 to 04:09 on those dates, and whether a boot banner follows the restart.
Unknown: Whether any kernel panic or reboot occurred. There are no panic, Oops or boot-banner lines in the logs for this window.
Unknown: The root cause of the memory exhaustion (a leak, a traffic spike or a misconfigured service) is not established by these logs.
Unknown: Service or customer impact and downtime are not in the logs.
Next step: Run a count_by on body or process name for pattern 700495 on node combo, and a trend by hour for 2005-11-15 to 2005-12-01. Then compare the bursts against the syslogd restart times (2005-11-20 04:09:36 and 2005-11-27 04:06:31). — Identifies which process is killed most often and whether OOM bursts coincide with restarts. 6709 OOM log lines with 0 panic matches points to memory pressure rather than a logged panic.
Next step: Check outside these logs (console or serial logs, last/wtmp, monitoring) for actual reboot times on combo, and look for log gaps after OOM bursts. — The searches for panic, Oops, klogd and Linux version returned 0 matches, so the claimed panics and reboots cannot be confirmed from this dataset.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** In December 2005 it recurred once a day, every day. It runs on a fixed daily schedule at about 04:00, and `linux-ops` owns it.

**How often**
- I found 31 matching lines between 2005-12-01 and 2006-01-01, one per day from 12-01 to 12-31.
- All of them come from the `logrotate` component on the single host `combo`.
- The message is always the same: `ALERT exited abnormally with [1]`. It is one message pattern, id 700263.

**Schedule**
- It is regular. Over the whole dataset (2005-06-09 to 2006-02-28) the pattern has 231 occurrences, one per day. The gap between them is about 86,401 s (24 h), and every gap falls within ±20 % of that.
- Every occurrence starts in the 04:00 hour. In December the times run from 04:02:06 to 04:15:11.
- It does not depend on the weekday: each weekday has 33 occurrences.
- From 12-12 onward it fires at almost exactly 04:02:06–04:02:17. That fits a daily cron-driven log rotation job that fails each time with exit code 1.
- Before 12-12, the start times were a few minutes later and less even (04:03 to 04:15). I did not look into why they changed.

**Ownership**
- `linux-ops` owns `logrotate`. That comes from the curated default row, which assigns every program on this server to `linux-ops`, with confidence 0.95. It is not a specific hand-written assignment for `logrotate`.
- Its functional area is kernel/OS, chosen by a rule (common programs: log rotation) at 0.9 confidence.

**Caveats**
- The logs show the failure but not the reason. The message gives only the exit code 1, so the cause needs a look at the logrotate configuration and the job's own output on `combo`.
- I did not check what other messages appear around 04:02 on those days, for example with `get_context` or `precursors`.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** This was new. The memory trouble began on 2005-11-15 and ended on 2005-12-09. The logs show no memory problem of this kind before or after that period.

**New or long-standing?**
- The kernel message "Out of Memory: Killed process …" first appears on 2005-11-15 04:30. Before that date it appears 0 times in the 5 months of logs from 2005-06-09.
- It last appears on 2005-12-09 04:58 and does not return before the logs end on 2006-02-28.
- It was therefore a single episode of about 3.5 weeks.
- The only earlier memory-related lines are routine boot messages, such as the memory size report. They appear 8 times, once per reboot, and are not faults.

**How big was it?**
- **Volume:** There were 10,404 out-of-memory kill lines. They came in 133 separate bursts, meaning recurrences separated by more than 30 minutes of quiet. The median gap between bursts was about 75 minutes, and the longest quiet stretch was about 2.3 days.
- **Shape:** It grew and then faded.
  - The week of 11-14 had 33 bursts and 1,667 lines.
  - The week of 11-21 had 41 bursts and 3,271 lines.
  - The week of 11-28 had 38 bursts and 4,178 lines.
  - The week of 12-05 had 21 bursts and 1,288 lines.
- **Peak:** The worst day was 2005-11-21, with about 1,750 out-of-memory and allocation-failure lines. Other bad days were 12-03 to 12-05, at roughly 800 to 1,200 lines each.
- **Who was hit:** Mostly `httpd`, the web server. About 1,500 of the kills hit other processes, such as `python`. Because the kernel kept killing processes, memory was clearly exhausted.
- **Related errors:** There were also 30 "page allocation failure" lines from 11-22 to 12-06, 21 from `httpd` and 9 from `sendmail`. The kernel failed to allocate memory for those services.
- **Scope:** It is one machine, so this is not a fleet-wide issue. All the lines come from the kernel component, owned by linux-ops.
- **Caveat:** These are log lines and bursts, not confirmed incidents. A burst of kills can come from one underlying squeeze.

**What the logs can't tell us**
- **Impact:** Nothing here says whether users saw errors, how long the website or mail service was down, or whether the killed processes were restarted. A kill line shows a process died, not what that cost.
- **Cost:** There are no customer, revenue or SLA figures.
- **Cause:** No reliable early-warning sign shows up. The message types that came before the kills were weak and no more common than on a normal day. Two obvious guesses, a traffic or load surge and a leak in the web application, can't be confirmed or ruled out. The logs have no memory-usage figures, load data or record of configuration changes.
- **Why it stopped:** The logs don't show whether someone fixed it, whether the workload changed, or whether it simply went away.
- **Coverage:** The logs show only what the system chose to write to syslog. Any memory pressure that didn't trigger a kill or an allocation failure is invisible.

You can check each number and tool call here: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192454-1e02. The page's automatic number check matched none of the answer's figures, because I submitted a shortened summary of the answer. The figures above come from the tool results.

product.text:
This looks new rather than long-standing. The kernel 'Out of Memory: Killed process' pattern first appeared on 2005-11-15 with 0 bursts in the prior two months, then produced 133 bursts and 10404 log lines on the single host in the period. Memory-related log lines stopped after the week starting 2005-12-05.
Scope: Dataset linux (host combo, linux-ops), 2005-11-01 to 2006-01-01, compared with 2005-09-01 to 2005-11-01. The problem filter is the Jev real-fault filter. The pattern lists are truncated (20 of 40 and 20 of 60 shown); the ranking and team roll-up were computed over all 40 problem patterns. The memory keyword trend covers the whole corpus.
The pattern 'Out of Memory: Killed process <N> <*>' was first seen 2005-11-15 04:30:29. In the period it had 133 bursts (0 in the previous period), 10404 log lines, 1 node and was active in 4 weeks.
Memory-keyword log lines per week were 0 up to the week of 2005-11-07, then 1667 (week of 2005-11-14), 3271 (2005-11-21), 4178 (2005-11-28) and 1294 (2005-12-05), then 0 for the weeks starting 2005-12-12, 2005-12-19, 2005-12-26 and 2006-01-02. Earlier weeks had at most 12 such log lines.
Related new kernel patterns first seen 2005-11-21 and 2005-11-22 include 'VM: killing process httpd' (14 bursts, 26 log lines) and 'httpd: page allocation failure' variants (14, 10 and 8 bursts), plus 'sendmail: page allocation failure' (4 bursts) and 'VM: killing process sendmail' (2 bursts).
Weekly problem bursts across all patterns peaked at 104 in the week of 2005-11-21, against 21 in the week of 2005-11-07, and fell to 7 in each of the weeks starting 2005-12-12, 2005-12-19 and 2005-12-26.
Team roll-up: linux-ops has 40 problem patterns, 331 bursts (176 in the previous period, change 155) and 11294 log lines in the period. It is the only team in the results.
1. Kernel out-of-memory killer repeatedly killing processes (new pattern) — owner linux-ops (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 133 bursts (0 previous), change 133, 1 node, 4 weeks active, 10404 log lines, score 97.5 — Decide whether to fund a memory root-cause review and capacity or limits fix for this host, and who owns it.
2. sshd authentication failures (long-standing, not memory-related) — owner linux-ops (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 25 bursts (20 previous), change 5, 1 node, 6 weeks active, 195 log lines, not new, score 94.9 — Decide whether this recurring pattern needs a security or hygiene review. It is separate from the memory problem.
3. httpd killed by the kernel VM (new, linked to memory pressure) — owner linux-ops (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 14 bursts (0 previous), change 14, 1 node, 3 weeks active, 26 log lines, score 89.1 — Ask linux-ops to confirm whether web-service restarts or protections are in place, and decide on follow-up.
Hypothesis: A memory-hungry workload, possibly httpd or sendmail, may have exhausted memory from mid-November until some change around 2005-12-12. Would confirm: Per-process memory accounting and any config, deployment or reboot changes around 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-12.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: The root cause is not established by these logs.
Unknown: The logs cover one host, so they cannot show whether other servers were affected.
Unknown: Pattern lists were truncated, so lower-ranked patterns were not individually reviewed.
Next step: Review changes and deployments around 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-12 against the memory log pattern. — The pattern first appeared 2005-11-15 and the memory log lines were 0 from the week of 2005-12-12.
Next step: Pull memory, swap and process metrics for the host, if they exist, to size business impact. — Impact (downtime, customers, cost) is not in these logs.

sql: SELECT s.b AS bucket_start, count(x.t) AS bursts FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-06-09 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2006-03-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b) LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

SELECT round(regr_slope(bursts, i), 3) AS slope, round(avg(bursts) FILTER (WHERE i < 39 / 2.0), 2) AS first_half_mean, round(avg(bursts) FILTER (WHERE i >= 39 / 2.0), 2) AS second_half_mean, sum(bursts) AS total FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY bucket_start) - 1 AS i, bursts FROM (SELECT s.b AS bucket_start, count(x.t) AS bursts FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-06-09 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2006-03-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b) LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1))

SELECT team, round(regr_slope(n, i), 3) AS slope, sum(n) AS bursts FROM (SELECT t.team, s.i, count(x.t) AS n FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY b) - 1 AS i, b FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-06-09 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2006-03-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b)) s CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') t LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = p.dataset) THEN p.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE p.error_lines > 0 END) AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b AND x.team = t.team GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY bursts DESC

baseline.text:
**The log has no exception for this crash.** HealthApp logs no severity levels. A search of 22:00–00:00 for "exception", "crash", "fatal" and "died" returned 0 lines. The log does show the app going silent for about 11 minutes and then starting up again.

**Before the crash (22:00 to about 22:27)**
- The app was running normally. Its process id is 30002312, and that same id appears after the restart.
- The last real activity was a screen-on at 22:20:23. It triggered a step flush and step and calorie updates. The step counter read 23,697 steps (`onStandStepChanged 23697`).
- After that, the only lines were the once-a-minute `TIME_TICK` broadcasts from `Step_LSC`.
- The last line before the gap is the `TIME_TICK` at 22:27:00.111. I found no error, shutdown or warning line before it.

**The gap (22:27:00 to 22:38:02)**
- No lines were logged for about 11 minutes. This is where the crash or kill happened. That fits the "around 22:30" you gave, but the log doesn't say what caused it.

**After the crash (22:38:02 onwards)**
- At 22:38:02.977 `Step_StaticReceiver` logged `onReceive action: android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED`. That is a device boot broadcast, so this may have been a phone reboot or power-off rather than an app-only crash. That is my reading.
- The app then re-initialised. It logged:
  - `setDeviceShutDownValue shutDownTime=0,isShutDown=false` and `setServiceRestartRecord=1514558283026`.
  - `FAILED_ERROR_DATA` from `Step_ReportController`, twice (22:38:03.092 and .118).
  - `updateBasicRestartStepsInfo restart but same day`.
  - `MyGetDetailDataCallback onResult bundle == null`.
  - `registersensorsuccess: true`, then the step counter was started.
- From 22:38:03.262 the step counter read 0 (`onStandStepChanged 0`), and the calorie and altitude totals were 0. This is consistent with a counter reset after the restart, though the logs don't say so outright.
- `TIME_TICK` broadcasts resumed at 22:39:00 and the app logged normally through 23:59, with no further errors. The window holds 955 lines in total. 629 fall in the 22:00 hour and 326 in the 23:00 hour.

**Caveat:** If you need the actual exception, check the Android system logcat on the phone. The `android` dataset in this database is from a different date, so I didn't use it.

baseline.text:
**ERR_DATA_INSERT started on 2018-01-02 at 08:11:53 and ran until 22:33:41. The day's volume is unusual: 51 lines, higher than every day in the previous 7 days.**

**Start**
- The first line was at 08:11:53.395 (line_id 215430). Nothing matched earlier that day.
- All 51 lines come from one component, `HiH_HiHealthBinder`. They carry the message `insertHiHealthData() bulkSaveDetailHiHealthData fail errorCode = 4, errorMessage = ERR_DATA_INSERT`, which is pattern 800029.
- The first 10 matches, all from process 30002312, fall between 08:11 and 08:59. That is a burst of 9 lines in under an hour. The next sampled line is at 11:17, so the errors continued through the day.
- Process 30002312 is the only one I checked, and I only looked at the first 10 lines.

**Volume against the previous 7 days (2017-12-26 to 2018-01-01)**

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| 2018-01-02 | 51 lines (2.1 per hour) |
| Previous 7 days | 97 lines in total (0.58 per hour, about 13.9 per day) |
| Ratio | about 3.7 times the baseline daily average |
| Highest earlier day | 25 lines |
| Earlier days with 51 or more | 0 of 7 |

- The previous days were 12, 13, 11, 10, 25, 21 and 5 lines.
- 2018-01-02 had about twice as many lines as the busiest earlier day, 2017-12-30.

**Context**
- The error is not new. It appears on every day of the dataset, starting on 2017-12-23.
- The earlier days also reached 32 lines (12-24) and 28 lines (12-25), both before your baseline window.
- 2018-01-02 is the peak of the whole dataset, but the problem was already recurring at lower levels.
- 2018-01-03 had only 3 lines, so the burst appears to have subsided.

These are log-line counts, not separate incidents. I did not look for a cause.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** The sync problem recurs. It was not a one-off. The mobile-health team owns it. One caveat: the logs have no message that says "cloud sync failed", so I used the closest matches.

**Closest match: "ifCanSync not! no cloud version"**
- This comes from `HiH_HiSyncControl` (pattern 800045). It says the app skipped a sync because it found no cloud version.
- It appears on 792 log lines, grouped into 116 separate bursts (a burst is a recurrence after more than 30 minutes of quiet). The first line is 2017-12-23 22:19 and the last is 2018-01-03 09:12.
- It shows up on every day of the span. The daily counts are:

| Date | Lines |
|---|---|
| 12-23 (partial day) | 4 |
| 12-24 | 125 |
| 12-25 | 100 |
| 12-26 | 47 |
| 12-27 | 50 |
| 12-28 | 49 |
| 12-29 | 40 |
| 12-30 | 81 |
| 12-31 | 74 |
| 01-01 | 50 |
| 01-02 | 159 (peak) |
| 01-03 (partial day) | 13 |

- The median gap between bursts is about 87 minutes (5,219 s). It does not follow a fixed schedule or a time of day. The period check calls it "no regular schedule".
- It looks like a persistent condition, not an incident. Most gaps between bursts are 1–6 hours.

**Caveats**
- The stored judgment rates this message only 0.42 likely to be a real fault, and classes it as configuration-related. It may be normal "nothing to sync yet" behaviour rather than an actual failure.
- The data ends 2018-01-03 09:59, so the last day of your range (01-04) has no data.
- A related message, `uploadStaticsToDB failed` (`Step_LSC`, pattern 800031), is an explicit failure. It has 212 lines in 60 bursts over the same span, with a judged fault probability of 0.39.

**Owner:** `mobile-health`. This comes from the curated default owner for all health-app modules, with confidence 0.95. The related `Step_LSC` component is also assigned to mobile-health. It is a catch-all default, not a team assigned specifically to sync.

Session report with every tool call: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192616-b33c. Its number check shows 0 of 6 numbers matched. I wrote the report's answer as a short summary and left out most of the figures above.

product.text:
The clearest failure signal is "uploadStaticsToDB failed message=true" (pattern 800031): 212 log lines in 60 bursts between 2017-12-23 and 2018-01-03, so it recurs rather than being a one-off. The owner is mobile-health (curated default, confidence 0.95). The logs have no explicit "cloud upload failed" message, so linking this pattern to cloud sync is an inference.
Scope: Dataset healthapp; period 2017-12-23 00:00 to 2018-01-04 00:00 (log data ends 2018-01-03 09:59:00.095); previous period 2017-12-11 to 2017-12-23. Pattern-level queries covered the whole corpus. The Step_LSC top_patterns result is truncated (20 of 32 shown); the other lookups were not truncated apart from sample rows. healthapp logs no node or host, so spread is unknown.
Pattern 800031 "uploadStaticsToDB failed message=true" (component Step_LSC) has 212 log lines in 60 bursts, from 2017-12-23 22:19:58.411000 to 2018-01-03 09:12:05.830000.
Daily log lines for pattern 800031 are non-zero on all 12 days from 2017-12-23 to 2018-01-03, for example 1 on 2017-12-23, 32 on 2017-12-24, 5 on 2018-01-01, 51 on 2018-01-02 and 3 on 2018-01-03.
Gaps between the 59 burst starts of pattern 800031: 12 under 1 h, 36 between 1-6 h, 11 between 6-24 h. The median gap is 6346.0 s and the regular share is 0.237. The tool reads this as "no regular schedule".
Pattern 800031 had 60 bursts in the period against bursts_prev 0 in the previous period (change 60) and 3 weeks active. It is flagged as first seen 2017-12-23 22:19:58.411000.
The only message mentioning "cloud" is "ifCanSync not! no cloud version" (pattern 800045): 792 log lines in 116 bursts, judged cause "configuration" with p_problem 0.421.
Pattern 800044 "sendSyncFailedBroadcast" (HiH_HiBroadcastUtil) has 792 log lines in 116 bursts, bursts_prev 0, change 116, 3 weeks active, kind "network or I/O failure".
Component Step_LSC is owned by mobile-health (source: curated default, confidence 0.95). The HiH_ and Step_ components of the failure patterns also list mobile-health. No dispute is reported.
1. sendSyncFailedBroadcast: the sync-failure broadcast fires on every sync attempt. This is the broadest sync-failure signal and the one to investigate first. — owner mobile-health — 116 bursts, 792 log lines, bursts_prev 0, change 116, 3 weeks active, nodes 0 (spread unknown); p_fault 0.86, kind network or I/O failure — Find which sync step triggers sendSyncFailedBroadcast and whether it matches the upload failures in item 2. Check its cause.
2. uploadStaticsToDB failed message=true (Step_LSC): the upload of step statistics fails repeatedly with no regular schedule. — owner mobile-health — 60 bursts, 212 log lines, bursts_prev 0, change 60, 3 weeks active, nodes 0; median gap 6346.0 s — Inspect the failure reason behind "message=true", and check the bursts on 2018-01-02 (51 log lines that day).
3. FAILED_SCREEN_OFF block report (Step_ReportController) failures — owner mobile-health — 68 bursts, 185 log lines, bursts_prev 0, change 68, 3 weeks active — Determine whether it shares a cause with the sync and upload failures.
4. Data insert failures (saveHealthDetailData saveOneDetailData fail, and bulkSaveDetailHiHealthData ERR_DATA_INSERT) — owner mobile-health — saveHealthDetailData: 60 bursts, 288 log lines, change 60; bulkSaveDetailHiHealthData: 60 bursts, 212 log lines, change 60; both bursts_prev 0 — Check whether the insert failures precede the upload failure. Pattern 800029 has the same line and burst counts as 800031.
Hypothesis: The uploadStaticsToDB failures may be linked to the local data-insert failures (ERR_DATA_INSERT), since pattern 800029 shares 800031's first timestamp and its counts of 212 lines and 60 bursts. Would confirm: Run precursors or co-occurrence analysis for pattern 800031 against 800029 and check whether they fall in the same bursts.
Hypothesis: The "no cloud version" message may point to a configuration condition behind the sync failures rather than a cloud outage. Would confirm: Check the app's sync-eligibility code (ifCanSync) and whether the message coincides with sendSyncFailedBroadcast bursts.
Unknown: Root cause of the failures is not established by these logs.
Unknown: Whether uploadStaticsToDB is the cloud upload or only a local database write is not stated in the logs.
Unknown: The number of affected users or devices is unknown, because healthapp logs no node or host.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Unknown: The previous period shows 0 bursts for these patterns, but this may reflect where the corpus starts (2017-12-23) rather than a true change.
Next step: Pull the log lines around the bursts of pattern 800044 and pattern 800031, particularly on 2018-01-02, and compare them with pattern 800029 and the "ifCanSync not! no cloud version" lines. — Pattern 800044 has 116 bursts and pattern 800031 has 60 bursts, and the logs do not show whether one causes the other.
Next step: Confirm in the source code what uploadStaticsToDB and "message=true" mean, and whether this path is the cloud sync. — The logs contain no explicit cloud-upload failure message, so the link to cloud sync is unverified.

baseline.text:
**The logs can't say how many users were affected, and they say nothing about business impact.** What they do show is that sync failures happened repeatedly on one app instance.

**How many users were affected**
- The log has no user, device or host field. The only identifier is the app process id.
- One process id, 30002312, appears on 253,394 of the 253,395 lines. This looks like a single app instance on a single phone, not a user population.
- The best defensible answer is "at least one device, number of users unknown". The logs can't support any percentage of users affected.
- The data ends on 2018-01-03 at 09:59. Nothing covers 3 January afternoon through 4 January.

**What the logs show about the failures**
- The app logged `sendSyncFailedBroadcast` 792 times, in 116 separate bursts. The first was on 2017-12-23 at 22:19 and the last on 2018-01-03 at 09:12.
- The daily count ranged from 13 to 159. The peak was 159 on 2 January, followed by 125 on 24 December.
- There are exactly 792 sync starts and 792 "ifCanSync not! no cloud version" lines. In this log, every sync attempt failed. A "no cloud version" configuration or availability problem is a plausible cause, but that is a hypothesis.
- Local data saving also failed in 60 bursts:
  - `ERR_DATA_INSERT` on bulk save: 212 lines.
  - Failed detail-data saves: 288 lines.
  - Failed `uploadStaticsToDB`: 212 lines.
- There were also 68 "FAILED_SCREEN_OFF block report" bursts and 5 cache-compare failures.
- All of these first appear in this period. The previous 12 days show no bursts of them.
- Some inserts did succeed: 437 `InsertCallBack onSuccess` lines. So the failures are partial on the saving side.

**Business impact**
The logs don't contain the evidence needed to state any. They have no revenue, churn, support tickets, app ratings, active-user counts or user-visible symptoms. The failure messages are internal and don't say whether the user saw stale or missing steps, or whether data was lost or just delayed. Any dollar or customer figure would be invented. Treat this as a reliability finding that needs product data to size.

**What the logs can't tell us**
- The number of distinct users, devices, app versions or regions affected. The log has no host field, so spread across devices is unknown.
- Whether the failures were retried and recovered later, or whether data was permanently lost.
- Whether the user could see the problem.
- The root cause. The "no cloud version" line and the insert errors are leads to hand to the mobile-health team, not conclusions.
- Whether this log is representative. It may be a single test or developer phone.

**To get a real answer**
- Pull the sync-failure rate from server-side or analytics data, keyed by user or device.
- Add a device or user hash and an app version to the app log lines.
- Use support-ticket and crash data to size the customer impact.

Every number above can be checked in the session report: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192701-c762

On 2017-12-15 connection sshd-16980 on node LabSZ was a login as user zachary from 218.17.80.182. It had one PAM authentication failure and two failed passwords, then an accepted password and an opened session, which was closed at 18:40:58. The logs cannot say whether this was an attack or a real user. The pattern fits a user mistyping a password, and the same IP and user appear on other days, but a stolen credential cannot be ruled out from these lines.
Scope: Dataset ssh, node LabSZ. Request sshd-16980 session 3 of 6 (10:38:55 → 10:39:04) plus the close line at 18:40:58, all on 2017-12-15. IP history for 218.17.80.182 runs from 2017-12-11 to 2017-12-21. Request-scoped and IP-scoped results were not truncated. The 'zachary' text search was truncated (30 of 34 matches shown), and I use it only for the open/close lines.
The login attempt had 5 log lines on node LabSZ between 2017-12-15T10:38:55 and 2017-12-15T10:39:04, a span of 9.0 s, with 0 problem lines by severity/status.
Step 1, 10:38:55: 'pam_unix(sshd:auth): authentication failure; logname= uid=0 euid=0 tty=ssh ruser= rhost=218.17.80.182  user=zachary'.
Steps 2 and 3, 10:38:57 and 10:39:03: 'Failed password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110 ssh2', twice, 6.0 s apart.
Steps 4 and 5, 10:39:04: 'Accepted password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110 ssh2', then 'pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user zachary by (uid=0)'.
After: the same request has one later line, at 2017-12-15 18:40:58: 'pam_unix(sshd:session): session closed for user zachary'.
The failures were for a known account (zachary) and not an 'Invalid user'. No other usernames appear in this request's lines.
Recurring, not new: IP 218.17.80.182 has 20 log lines from 2017-12-11 16:48:51 to 2017-12-21 14:07:31 on 1 node, all for user zachary. Most visits show the same sequence of auth failure, Failed password, Accepted password (2017-12-12, 12-13, 12-14, 12-19, 12-21). On those days there was 1 Failed password line, against 2 on 2017-12-15.
The first sampled line for this IP is an 'Accepted password' for zachary on 2017-12-11 16:48:51, with no preceding failure in the results.
Local: other activity on LabSZ around this connection was different request ids and different IPs. Before, 10:33:11, request sshd-16977: 'Invalid user sugon from 52.80.34.196'. After, 10:46:08, request sshd-17102: 'Invalid user butter from 185.165.29.140'.
Closest lines outside the 10-minute context window on LabSZ: before, 2017-12-15 10:24:54 'Received disconnect from 115.71.16.143: 11: Bye Bye [preauth]' (request sshd-16974), 850.0 s from the anchor. After, 2017-12-15 10:49:26 'Connection closed by 87.243.6.84 [preauth]' (request sshd-17104), 622.0 s from the anchor.
The id sshd-16980 is reused by unrelated connections. The request has 6 sessions in the logs. Nearest earlier line: 2017-12-12 05:11:00 'Connection closed by 183.238.178.195 [preauth]', 278875.0 s before. Nearest later line: 2017-12-30 07:57:40 'authentication failure ... rhost=139.219.191.138  user=root', 1286325.0 s after. Those lines are not part of the 2017-12-15 connection.
Hypothesis: A real user (zachary) mistyped the password once more than usual and then logged in. The daily pattern from the same IP, the known username, and a success within 9.0 s all fit this. Would confirm: Confirm with the account owner that 218.17.80.182 is their usual address, and check that the commands run in the 2017-12-15 10:39:04 → 18:40:58 session match their normal work.
Hypothesis: The credential could instead be compromised and used by someone else from the same IP. The logs only show that a correct password was eventually supplied. Would confirm: Check whether the IP and its geolocation match the user's usual access. Check whether the password was recently reset or exposed, and look at what the session did.
Unknown: Whether the person at 218.17.80.182 is the real zachary: these lines do not show identity, only password authentication.
Unknown: What was done during the roughly 8-hour session: command activity is not in these results.
Unknown: Whether 2 failed passwords is unusual against the normal rate: no rate baseline was computed, only the 1-failure pattern on other days in the IP's lines.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in the logs.
Next step: Review the 2017-12-15 session of zachary on LabSZ (10:39:04 → 18:40:58) in auth/shell history, using wtmp/last or the host's command audit log, and confirm 218.17.80.182 with the account owner. — The ssh logs show only authentication events, so intent can only be settled from session activity and owner confirmation (ev-6e3b9e0a76, ev-b52623e902).
Next step: Run search_logs on dataset ssh with entity ip:218.17.80.182 and pattern_id 400011 grouped by day, and compare it with the count_by of failed passwords for user zachary from other IPs. — This shows whether the 2 failed passwords on 2017-12-15 stand out against the 20 lines of history for this IP (ev-56675c50e2).
