baseline.text:
**sshd-16980 on 2017-12-15 was most likely a real user, not an attack.** The user was `zachary`, logging in from 218.17.80.182. They mistyped the password twice and then got in. The logs can't prove who was at the keyboard, but the pattern fits a person.

**What happened, step by step (host LabSZ, process sshd-16980)**

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 10:38:55 | PAM authentication failure for `user=zachary`, `rhost=218.17.80.182`. |
| 10:38:57 | `Failed password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110`. |
| 10:39:03 | A second `Failed password` on the same port, 6 seconds later. |
| 10:39:04 | `Accepted password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110`. |
| 10:39:04 | `session opened for user zachary`. |
| 18:40:58 | `session closed for user zachary`, about 8 hours later. |

The first five lines are one 9-second login attempt, and the close line comes from the same process id. The process id is reused over the 28 days, so the same id has 6 sessions in total, and the other 5 are on different days. Only the two on 12-15 belong to this question.

**Why it looks like a user**
- **Failures were few and quickly resolved.** There were 2 failed passwords, 6 seconds apart, then a success. A brute-force run would show many attempts, and it would usually try several usernames. This one stayed on a single account.
- **The session was long.** It stayed open about 8 hours, which fits someone working rather than a scanner that drops after probing.
- **It is a routine.** The same IP and user log in on 12-11, 12-12, 12-13, 12-14, 12-19 and 12-21. Almost every day has one failed attempt, or two on 12-15, then success, then a session lasting hours. That is typical of someone who sometimes mistypes a password.
- **The IP touches nothing else.** All 20 lines from 218.17.80.182 are `zachary` logins, with no other usernames and no failures that never succeed.

**Caveats**
- An attacker holding a valid or guessed password would look the same in these logs. Two quick failures then success is also consistent with a credential that was found after a short guess. The 10-day history of the same IP and user makes that less likely, but it isn't proof.
- To be sure, ask whether zachary works from that address, which is a Chinese-looking IP. Also check whether a password login is expected for that account.

baseline.text:
The warnings stayed flat for three weeks, then jumped about eightfold in the week of 1 January. Two source IPs, both sending the same single message type, caused most of the jump.

**Weekly trend** (log lines, weeks starting Monday; 19,298 lines in total):

| Week starting | Lines |
|---|---|
| 2017-12-11 | 1,291 |
| 2017-12-18 | 1,313 |
| 2017-12-25 | 1,813 |
| 2018-01-01 | 14,881 |

- **Weeks 1–2:** Volume was flat at about 1,300 lines a week.
- **Week 3:** It rose about 38% to 1,813. The rise started on 31 December, when 1,402 lines were logged in one day.
- **Week 4:** It reached 14,881 lines, about 8× the previous week and 11× the first two weeks. The week covers 1–7 January only, because the data ends on 7 January.
- **Daily pattern:** Within that week, 3 January alone had 8,724 lines. After that it fell back to roughly 100–400 lines a day (355, 271, 389 and 104 for 4–7 January).

**Owner:** security-ops owns these warnings. All of them come from the `sshd` component on the single host.

**What drove the change:** The warnings look like one burst of scanning or brute-forcing, not a gradual rise.
- **Message type:** 97.4% of the lines (18,801) are "reverse mapping checking getaddrinfo … failed – POSSIBLE BREAK-IN ATTEMPT!". The other 497 are "Address … maps to … but this does not map back to the address".
- **Week of 1 January:** Three IPs account for about 13,475 of the 14,881 lines, roughly 90%. 96 distinct IPs appear that week, and the IP counts below are lines mentioning each address.

  | Source IP | Lines | When |
  |---|---|---|
  | 183.192.189.131 | 8,670 | 3 Jan, about 00:57–12:36 |
  | 218.65.30.30 | 4,192 | 1 Jan 14:23 to 2 Jan 11:12 |
  | 183.192.189.133 | 613 | 2 Jan, about 11:03–11:54 |

- **31 December bump:** It came mainly from 218.65.30.126 (912 lines, 02:37–07:18) and 95.188.84.199 (371 lines, 08:41–09:16).
- **Weeks 1–2:** The pattern was different. 211 distinct IPs were spread across 4,418 mentions from 11 December to 31 December, with only a few sources above 300 lines. Examples are 173.82.194.233 (326 lines on 20 December) and several 51.15.x.x addresses.

Several of the heavy sources share a /16 block, 218.65.30.x or 183.192.189.x, which suggests related scanning hosts. Security-ops could check those ranges. These counts are log lines, not incidents, and the logs don't show whether any login succeeded.

Session report with every tool call and number check: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192655-13a7

hypotheses.statement: The week-over-week change may partly reflect more bursts being detected because of a logging or collection change on 2018-01-01 onward, not only a change in attacker behaviour.

baseline.text:
**The SSH log doesn't show attackers getting root access. It shows a large, ongoing attempt to guess the root password, and I found no sign that it worked.** The log only records authentication, so it can't prove what happened on the server afterwards. If you have other evidence of a root compromise, such as a change you didn't make, treat it as real and investigate the host.

**What the logs show for 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08**
- **No root login:** There is no "Accepted … for root" line anywhere in the 28-day dataset. There is no "session opened for user root" line either. I searched the week and the whole dataset.
- **Volume:** There are 102,039 "Failed password for root" lines in that week, from 214 different IP addresses, all aimed at the one server (LabSZ).
- **Heaviest sources:**

  | IP address | Failed root attempts |
  |---|---|
  | 59.63.188.30 | 28,766 (Jan 3–5) |
  | 183.63.110.206 | 17,340 |
  | 58.242.83.25 | 14,383 |
  | 183.192.189.131 | 8,670 |
  | 218.65.30.30 | 8,374 |
  | 218.87.109.156 | 7,135 |
  | 182.100.67.120 | 6,179 |
  | 182.100.67.52 | 3,389 |

- **Escalation:** Failed-password lines (all users) rose from 3,368 on Dec 31 to about 13,300 on Jan 1. They peaked at about 31,800 on Jan 3, then fell to about 1,700 by Jan 6–7. A similar campaign hit in early and mid December.
- **Server defences:** The server logged "Too many authentication failures" and "PAM ignoring max retries" over 35,000 times each in the week, so lockouts are triggering but not stopping the guessing.
- **Successful logins:** There were 94 in the week, all password logins for ordinary named accounts: curi, hxu, jmzhu, suyuxin and tzhao.
  - I read 50 of the 94 lines. Most come from the same addresses that user has used since December.
  - Of the accepted-login IPs I checked, 61.187.54.9 and 111.222.107.90 also had a few failed attempts, which could be typos or something worse.
  - 222.240.177.42, 123.255.103.215, 218.18.42.17 and 73.239.249.49 had no failures.

**What to do first**
1. **Check root directly on the host.** Look at `last`, `lastlog`, `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, recent changes to `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow`, new cron jobs, and unexpected processes. The attempts against root are certain; a compromise is not confirmed, and these checks will settle it.
2. **Turn off direct root login over SSH:** set `PermitRootLogin no` and use key-based login only (`PasswordAuthentication no`). Rotate the root password now as a precaution.
3. **Block the repeat sources:** add the top IPs above to a firewall deny list and install fail2ban or similar. Consider limiting SSH to a VPN or an allowed set of source addresses.
4. **Review the named accounts that logged in during the attack week,** starting with `curi` and `hxu`, which logged in the most. Confirm each login was the real user. Also check the other 44 accepted logins I didn't read, since one of them could be hostile.

I also generated a session report that records each step and lets you check every number: http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192723-0372. It flagged that it couldn't match any of the numbers in my summary to the tool results, so verify the figures above against the individual tool calls rather than relying on the page's check.

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2018-01-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'ssh' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'ssh' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'ssh' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE ) SELECT *, count(*) OVER () AS candidates FROM base ORDER BY bursts DESC, nodes DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 15

product.text:
The logs do not show attackers gaining root. Over 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08 there were 0 log lines matching "Accepted root", but there was very heavy brute-force pressure on root and other accounts. Treat the compromise as unconfirmed, and first have security-ops review the 94 accepted-login log lines.
Scope: Dataset ssh (OpenSSH auth log, host LabSZ, one node). Period 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08 (last log line 2018-01-07 17:22:01), compared with 2017-12-25 to 2018-01-01. Priority ranking is truncated: top 3 of 39 problem patterns are shown. Other checks are not truncated. The period is the 2018 week assumed from logs that do not record a year.
Team roll-up: security-ops owns all 39 problem patterns, with 1207 bursts (478 in the previous week, change 729) and 281388 log lines.
A search for "Accepted root" in the window returned 0 log lines.
The window contains 94 log lines matching "Accepted" and 94 matching "session opened", all on node LabSZ. The logs checked here do not show which users or source IPs these belong to.
The "failed password for root" watch fired: 102039 log lines in the window versus 13488 in the previous week, first seen 2018-01-01 00:12:30.
The "too many authentication failures" watch fired: 35318 log lines in the window versus 1329 previously. The "POSSIBLE BREAK-IN ATTEMPT" watch fired: 14881 log lines versus 1813.
Daily problem bursts over 2017-12-10 to 2018-01-08 total 3750, with first-half mean 137.33 and second-half mean 112.67. The trend reading is "no clear change".
Six problem patterns were first seen in the window, each with 1 or 2 bursts on 1 node.
1. Repeated "Invalid user <*> from <IP>" probing of non-existent accounts — owner security-ops — 108 bursts (previous week 37, change 71), 1 node, 1 week active, 4340 log lines, score 100.0 — Decide whether to fund or approve source blocking and rate limiting (for example fail2ban or firewall allow-listing) for this internet-facing host.
2. "Failed password for invalid user" attempts (password guessing) — owner security-ops — 108 bursts (previous week 37, change 71), 1 node, 1 week active, 6130 log lines, score 100.0 — Decide on moving to key-only SSH and disabling password login. Ask security-ops to confirm none of the 94 accepted logins came from these sources.
3. "input_userauth_request: invalid user" pre-authentication rejections — owner security-ops — 108 bursts (previous week 37, change 71), 1 node, 1 week active, 4340 log lines, score 95.6 — Treat as the same campaign as ranks 1 and 2 and cover it with the same decision. No separate funding is needed.
Hypothesis: The activity may be automated brute-force or credential-stuffing that has not succeeded against root. The 0 "Accepted root" lines and the rise in failure patterns are consistent with this. Would confirm: List users and source IPs of the 94 Accepted lines and check none is root or an attacker IP. Also check for root logins outside this text search.
Hypothesis: Some accepted sessions might be legitimate users, or might be a compromise under a non-root account. Would confirm: Compare the accepted sessions' users and source IPs with the known-user list. Check for activity after login on the host itself, which is not in this log.
Unknown: Whether root was actually compromised cannot be established from these logs, which only record authentication events and show 0 "Accepted root" lines in the window.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: Root cause and attacker identity are not in these logs.
Unknown: Post-login activity on the server is not in these logs.
Next step: Review the 94 accepted-login log lines in the window by user and source IP, and confirm that none is root or from an attacker IP. — The logs show 0 "Accepted root" lines but 94 accepted and session-opened lines, so this is the fastest way to confirm or refute the root compromise claim.
Next step: If any unexplained accepted login is found, rotate credentials, check the host for persistence, and treat it as an incident. Otherwise approve hardening: disable root and password login, and rate-limit or block attacking sources. — Failed root-password log lines rose to 102039 in the window from 13488 the week before, so exposure is high regardless of whether anyone got in.

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2018-01-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'ssh' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'ssh' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'ssh' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND (CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pattern_judgments jx WHERE jx.dataset = 'ssh') THEN now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ELSE now.error_lines > 0 END) ), inputs AS ( SELECT *, round(weeks_active::DOUBLE / 1, 3) AS persistence, round(problem_lines::DOUBLE / lines, 3) AS problem_share, p_problem AS severity_input FROM base ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY bursts) AS pr_frequency, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY change) AS pr_trend, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY nodes) AS pr_spread, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY persistence) AS pr_persistence, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY severity_input) AS pr_severity FROM inputs ) SELECT *, round(100 * (0.3 * pr_frequency + 0.2 * pr_trend + 0.25 * pr_spread + 0.15 * pr_persistence + 0.1 * pr_severity), 1) AS score FROM ranked ORDER BY score DESC, bursts DESC, pattern_id

Yes. 2006-01-08 had 1039 log lines (43.292 per hour) against a baseline of 1.286 per hour, a ratio of 33.7. 965 of the 1039 lines are ERROR, mostly httpd 'File does not exist' and 'script not found' lines. Three IPs sent the largest bursts, all probing for awstats.pl.
Scope: Dataset apache; 2006-01-08 00:00:00 → 2006-01-09 00:00:00 (24 h) vs the 7 earlier same-length windows, 2006-01-01 00:00:00 → 2006-01-08 00:00:00. Unit = log lines. No dataset-level filter beyond apache. The facet, top-IP and search results are truncated samples (top 8 per dimension, 15 of 27 IPs, 3 sample lines per pattern), but the counts are complete.
The window 2006-01-08 held 1039 log lines, a rate of 43.292 per hour. The previous 7 days held 216 log lines, a rate of 1.286 per hour, so the ratio is 33.7.
The busiest earlier day had 89 log lines (baseline_max_per_window). 0 of the 7 baseline windows reached 1039 lines.
In the window, 965 lines are ERROR and 74 are NOTICE. 951 lines come from component httpd, then jk2_init() with 33, mod_jk with 27 and mod_jk2 with 22.
Pattern 300021 ('File does not exist') has 599 log lines, first 2006-01-08 02:12:47, last 2006-01-08 18:39:08. Pattern 300033 ('script not found or unable to stat: …') has 132 lines. Pattern 300042 ('script not found or unable to stat') has 129 lines. Pattern 300020 ('Directory index forbidden by rule') has 42 lines.
Three IPs dominate. ip:193.19.219.217 has 253 lines between 2006-01-08 16:42:20 and 16:42:38. ip:61.134.40.151 has 233 lines between 16:35:32 and 16:36:18. ip:218.106.165.188 has 198 lines between 18:24:47 and 18:25:09. Each IP's lines fall within about a minute.
27 distinct client IPs appear in the window, with 779 IP mentions in total. Smaller bursts: ip:83.16.14.142 has 23 lines at 02:12:47-02:12:49 (File does not exist: /var/www/html/sumthin), and ip:84.155.141.86 has 17 lines between 15:13:59 and 15:14:46.
The sampled lines from the three top IPs each read '[client <ip>] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl'. The 61.134.40.151 burst also requested /var/www/html/xmlsrv, /var/www/html/wordpress and /var/www/html/blog.
Timeline around the 193.19.219.217 burst: before, '16:42:00 [client 219.147.185.1] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/' and '16:36:19 mod_jk2 Shutting down'. At, from 16:42:20, repeated '[client 193.19.219.217] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl'. The closest line before the 20-minute context window is 15:14:46 from 84.155.141.86 (5254.0 seconds earlier). The closest line after it is 18:12:42, '[client 59.58.194.229] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/' (5422.0 seconds later).
During the 84.155.141.86 burst at 15:14:05-15:14:08, the awstats 'script not found or unable to stat: /var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl' lines are interleaved with 'jk2_init() Can't find child 2725 in scoreboard', 'workerEnv.init() ok /etc/httpd/conf/workers2.properties' and 'mod_jk child init 1 -2'. The closest earlier line is 14:35:43 (2302.0 seconds before the anchor), and the closest later line is 16:35:32 (4887.0 seconds after).
The window's facet shows 1 distinct node, and the node value is blank in the facet row. The activity is therefore not attributable to a named node.
Hypothesis: The spike may be automated web scanning from a few hosts. They probe for awstats.pl, CGI scripts and common web apps (xmlsrv, wordpress, blog), which all return 'File does not exist' or 'script not found'. This fits the bursts of 253, 233 and 198 lines, each lasting under a minute. Would confirm: Check the Apache access log for these IPs, looking at their user agents, HTTP status codes (404 expected) and full request paths. Check whether the same IPs appeared on other days.
Hypothesis: The mod_jk/mod_jk2/jk2_init() lines ('Can't find child … in scoreboard', 'mod_jk2 Shutting down') may come from Apache children being respawned during the scan bursts. They would be a side effect rather than a separate fault. Would confirm: Correlate child-init and shutdown timestamps with request rate, for example with trend or count_by on patterns 300022 and 300034 per minute. Then check whether they also occur on quiet days.
Unknown: Whether pattern 300021 or the awstats probes occurred in the previous 7 days is not established; the baseline counts all lines, not per pattern.
Unknown: The 1039 lines are ERROR/NOTICE entries from the error log, so true request volume and HTTP status codes are not known.
Unknown: Root cause, whether any request succeeded, and any downtime or customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: The node name is not available, so a local-versus-spread comparison across hosts cannot be made.
Unknown: Only 15 of 27 client IPs were listed, and the 3 sample lines per pattern are not the full sets.
Next step: Run pattern_history for pattern_ids 300021 and 300033, and a count_by on pattern_id per day for 2006-01-01 → 2006-01-09 in the apache dataset. — To establish whether the awstats/File-not-found errors are new on 2006-01-08 or recurring at a lower rate. The baseline of 216 lines does not say.
Next step: Search the Apache access log (outside this dataset) for 193.19.219.217, 61.134.40.151 and 218.106.165.188 at the burst times (16:42:20, 16:35:32, 18:24:47). — These IPs account for 253, 233 and 198 error lines; the access log would show status codes and user agents.
Next step: Inspect mod_jk2 / workers2.properties and the child-init and shutdown lines (patterns 300022, 300023, 300034) around 15:14 and 16:36. — The scoreboard and child-init errors appear between the scan requests; this checks whether they are a consequence of the load.

The busiest earlier day had 89 log lines (baseline_max_per_window). 0 of the 7 baseline windows reached 1039 lines.
In the window, 965 lines are ERROR and 74 are NOTICE. 951 lines come from component httpd, then jk2_init() with 33, mod_jk with 27 and mod_jk2 with 22.

Pattern 300021 ('File does not exist') has 599 log lines, first 2006-01-08 02:12:47, last 2006-01-08 18:39:08. Pattern 300033 ('script not found or unable to stat: …') has 132 lines. Pattern 300042 ('script not found or unable to stat') has 129 lines. Pattern 300020 ('Directory index forbidden by rule') has 42 lines.

Three IPs dominate. ip:193.19.219.217 has 253 lines between 2006-01-08 16:42:20 and 16:42:38. ip:61.134.40.151 has 233 lines between 16:35:32 and 16:36:18. ip:218.106.165.188 has 198 lines between 18:24:47 and 18:25:09. Each IP's lines fall within about a minute.

27 distinct client IPs appear in the window, with 779 IP mentions in total. Smaller bursts: ip:83.16.14.142 has 23 lines at 02:12:47-02:12:49 (File does not exist: /var/www/html/sumthin), and ip:84.155.141.86 has 17 lines between 15:13:59 and 15:14:46.

The sampled lines from the three top IPs each read '[client <ip>] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl'. The 61.134.40.151 burst also requested /var/www/html/xmlsrv, /var/www/html/wordpress and /var/www/html/blog.

Timeline around the 193.19.219.217 burst: before, '16:42:00 [client 219.147.185.1] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/' and '16:36:19 mod_jk2 Shutting down'. At, from 16:42:20, repeated '[client 193.19.219.217] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl'. The closest line before the 20-minute context window is 15:14:46 from 84.155.141.86 (5254.0 seconds earlier). The closest line after it is 18:12:42, '[client 59.58.194.229] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/' (5422.0 seconds later).

During the 84.155.141.86 burst at 15:14:05-15:14:08, the awstats 'script not found or unable to stat: /var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl' lines are interleaved with 'jk2_init() Can't find child 2725 in scoreboard', 'workerEnv.init() ok /etc/httpd/conf/workers2.properties' and 'mod_jk child init 1 -2'. The closest earlier line is 14:35:43 (2302.0 seconds before the anchor), and the closest later line is 16:35:32 (4887.0 seconds after).
The window's facet shows 1 distinct node, and the node value is blank in the facet row. The activity is therefore not attributable to a named node.

hypotheses.statement: The spike may be automated web scanning from a few hosts. They probe for awstats.pl, CGI scripts and common web apps (xmlsrv, wordpress, blog), which all return 'File does not exist' or 'script not found'. This fits the bursts of 253, 233 and 198 lines, each lasting under a minute.
hypotheses.would_confirm: Check the Apache access log for these IPs, looking at their user agents, HTTP status codes (404 expected) and full request paths. Check whether the same IPs appeared on other days.

hypotheses.statement: The mod_jk/mod_jk2/jk2_init() lines ('Can't find child … in scoreboard', 'mod_jk2 Shutting down') may come from Apache children being respawned during the scan bursts. They would be a side effect rather than a separate fault.
hypotheses.would_confirm: Correlate child-init and shutdown timestamps with request rate, for example with trend or count_by on patterns 300022 and 300034 per minute. Then check whether they also occur on quiet days.

unknowns: Whether pattern 300021 or the awstats probes occurred in the previous 7 days is not established; the baseline counts all lines, not per pattern.
The 1039 lines are ERROR/NOTICE entries from the error log, so true request volume and HTTP status codes are not known.
Root cause, whether any request succeeded, and any downtime or customer impact are not in these logs.
The node name is not available, so a local-versus-spread comparison across hosts cannot be made.
Only 15 of 27 client IPs were listed, and the 3 sample lines per pattern are not the full sets.

next_steps.action: Run pattern_history for pattern_ids 300021 and 300033, and a count_by on pattern_id per day for 2006-01-01 → 2006-01-09 in the apache dataset.
next_steps.why: To establish whether the awstats/File-not-found errors are new on 2006-01-08 or recurring at a lower rate. The baseline of 216 lines does not say.

next_steps.action: Search the Apache access log (outside this dataset) for 193.19.219.217, 61.134.40.151 and 218.106.165.188 at the burst times (16:42:20, 16:35:32, 18:24:47).
next_steps.why: These IPs account for 253, 233 and 198 error lines; the access log would show status codes and user agents.

next_steps.action: Inspect mod_jk2 / workers2.properties and the child-init and shutdown lines (patterns 300022, 300023, 300034) around 15:14 and 16:36.
next_steps.why: The scoreboard and child-init errors appear between the scan requests; this checks whether they are a consequence of the load.

baseline.text:
**Yes, 2006-01-08 was unusual.** The log has 1,039 lines for that day. The previous 7 days (Jan 1–7) had 216 lines in total, about 31 a day. That makes Jan 8 roughly 34 times the usual daily volume. No earlier day in that period went above 89 lines.

The daily counts show a sharp jump:

| Day | Lines |
|---|---|
| Jan 1 | 48 |
| Jan 2–5 | 0 |
| Jan 6 | 89 |
| Jan 7 | 79 |
| **Jan 8** | **1,039** |
| Jan 9 | 763 |

Jan 9 stayed high, so this was not a one-day blip.

**What the errors were**
- 965 of the 1,039 lines were ERROR, and the other 74 were NOTICE.
- 951 lines (92%) came from the `httpd` component. The rest were `mod_jk`, `mod_jk2` and `jk2_init()` startup and shutdown noise.
- The dominant message was `File does not exist: <path>`, with 599 lines (58%).
- Next came `script not found or unable to stat`, in two variants: 132 lines with a client IP and 129 without one.
- There were also 42 `Directory index forbidden by rule` lines, which is a normal background level. These recurred at about the same rate the day before.
- 22 `jk2_init() Can't find child N in scoreboard` lines, 22 `mod_jk child init` lines and 22 `mod_jk2 Shutting down` lines also appeared. They are minor, but they suggest the web server or its Tomcat connector restarted several times that day. I haven't checked that further.
- None of these message types is new. They appear earlier in the dataset, but their volume on Jan 8 is far higher.

**Who sent the requests**
The logs name 27 distinct client IPs, and three of them account for most of the volume. Each was a short burst of repeated requests for the same missing file, `/var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl`:

| Client IP | Lines | Time on Jan 8 |
|---|---|---|
| 193.19.219.217 | 253 | 16:42:20–16:42:38 |
| 61.134.40.151 | 233 | 16:35:32–16:36:18 |
| 218.106.165.188 | 198 | 18:24:47–18:25:09 |

Smaller sources:
- 83.16.14.142 (23 lines) requested `/sumthin`.
- 70.113.52.160 (13 lines) requested `/scripts/root.exe`, `/MSADC` and other short paths. This looks like a vulnerability scan for IIS-style exploits.
- 84.155.141.86 (17 lines), 61.234.149.52 (14 lines) and 211.98.106.42 (9 lines) also appear. I did not look at what they requested.
- The `script not found or unable to stat` lines come from the same group of scanners, but I did not trace those two message types to individual IPs.

**Reading**
This looks like automated scanning for known vulnerable web applications such as awstats, not a fault in the server. The requests were all for files that don't exist, and each scanner ran for under a minute. The errors are noise created by the probes. The one thing worth checking is whether `awstats` is actually installed, since that is the main target.

The Apache log records no host or node field, so I can't say which machine handled the requests. The page at http://127.0.0.1:8767/s/20261018-192832-1346 has the session's tool calls. Its number check reported 0 of 19 numbers matched to tool results, so don't rely on that check.

Yes, it is scheduled: 'Graceful restart requested, doing restart' (pattern 300037) fired in 37 bursts, at hour 4 every time and on a Sunday in 33 of them, about every 604767 s. It is owned by web-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95). The restart line itself is judged 'not a failure' (p_problem 0.019). The ERROR lines that appear alongside each restart are the part worth a look.
Scope: Dataset apache (one Apache httpd error log), pattern 300037 across the whole corpus (2005-06-12 04:04:15 to 2006-01-22 04:10:56). Top-pattern ranking uses the period 2005-06-09 to 2006-03-01 against the previous period 2004-09-17 to 2005-06-09. Ranking lists were truncated (15 of 37 for component httpd, 10 of 28 problem patterns). The restart pattern's own periodicity, trend and ownership results were complete.
Pattern 300037 'Graceful restart requested, doing restart' has 37 log lines in 37 bursts, first seen 2005-06-12 04:04:15 and last seen 2006-01-22 04:10:56.
Gap statistics over 36 gaps: median gap 604767.0 s, MAD 249.0 s, regular_share 0.861; the tool reads this as 'regular (about every 604767 s)'.
All 37 of 37 bursts start in hour 4; by weekday: Sunday 33, Saturday 2, Monday 1, Friday 1.
Weekly trend: 1 log line in most weekly buckets, 2 in the weeks starting 2005-06-13, 2005-06-20, 2005-06-27 and 2006-01-02; no growth over time.
Owner of component httpd is web-platform (source 'curated default', confidence 0.95, area web/API); the pattern is judged p_problem 0.019, cause 'not a failure'.
'mod_jk2 Shutting down' (team app-integration) starts within ±300 s of 37 of 37 restarts (share 1.0, control share 0.081, lift 12.3).
36 of 37 restarts (share 0.973, control share 0.081, lift 12.0) are accompanied within ±300 s by 'config.update(): Can't create ...' lines and the LDAP and Digest startup lines (all web-platform).
The ERROR pattern 'config.update(): Can't create channel.jni:jni' (300006) has 45 bursts and 45 log lines over 34 weeks active, with 0 bursts in the previous period; the 'Can't create vm:', 'worker.jni:onShutdown' and 'worker.jni:onStartup' variants and the env.createBean2 'channel.jni' error show the same 45 bursts.
The corpus ends 2006-02-28 03:49:01, while the last graceful restart burst is 2006-01-22 04:10:56.
1. Investigate first: ERROR 'config.update(): Can't create channel/vm/worker.jni' and 'env.createBean2(): Factory error creating ...' lines that appear with the weekly graceful restart (mod_jk2 / JNI worker initialisation failing). — owner web-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 45 bursts and 45 log lines per pattern, 34 weeks active, 0 bursts in the previous period (change 45); p_problem 0.81 for 300006; co-occurs with 36 of 37 restarts (share 0.973, lift 12.0). — Check whether the JNI channel/vm/worker errors are expected noise from the mod_jk2 JNI setup on every restart or a real misconfiguration, and fix or silence them.
2. Weekly scheduled graceful restart (pattern 300037), judged 'not a failure'. — owner web-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 37 bursts, hour 4 in 37 of 37, Sunday in 33, median gap 604767.0 s, regular_share 0.861; p_problem 0.019. — Confirm the Sunday ~04:00 restart is a deliberate schedule (e.g. log rotation or cron) and check why the last one is 2006-01-22.
3. 'mod_jk2 Shutting down' occurs at every restart and also at other times. — owner app-integration — 113 bursts and 1336 log lines in total; within ±300 s of 37 of 37 restarts; p_problem 0.066. — app-integration to confirm that a shutdown line with each graceful restart is expected and to explain the remaining bursts not tied to a restart.
4. Highest-volume recurring pattern in the period, not tied to the restart: '[client <IP>] Directory index forbidden by rule: <PATH>'. — owner web-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 2973 bursts, 6745 log lines, 36 weeks active, 0 bursts in the previous period (change 2973); p_problem 0.66 but kind 'not a problem'. — Decide whether this is client scanning to ignore or something to block or configure.
Hypothesis: The Sunday ~04:00 graceful restart may be a cron job, for example a weekly log rotation, and the 4 off-Sunday bursts may be manual or reruns. Would confirm: Check crontab / logrotate config on the web server and compare the off-Sunday restart times with change tickets.
Hypothesis: The config.update / env.createBean2 JNI errors may be emitted by mod_jk2 re-initialising on each restart, rather than reflecting a new fault each time. Would confirm: Check whether these errors also appear on non-restart starts, and whether mod_jk2 is installed with a working JNI setup.
Hypothesis: The absence of restarts after 2006-01-22 may mean the schedule was changed or removed, or the log source stopped recording it. Would confirm: Look at the server's rotation / cron history after 2006-01-22 and the raw log around the following Sundays.
Unknown: Why the restarts happen (root cause or the job that triggers them) is not in the logs.
Unknown: Whether the restarts or the accompanying errors affected requests, and any downtime, customer impact or cost, are not in the logs.
Unknown: The logs record no node or host (nodes = 0 means unknown spread), so a single-server effect cannot be separated from a wider one.
Unknown: The previous period (2004-09-17 to 2005-06-09) has no data, so the change figures (e.g. change 45) are not a real before/after comparison.
Next step: Check crontab / logrotate on the Apache host for a Sunday ~04:00 graceful restart, and check what changed after 2006-01-22. — Restarts fall at hour 4 in 37 of 37 bursts and on Sunday in 33; the last one is 2006-01-22 04:10:56.
Next step: Review the JNI worker configuration behind 'config.update(): Can't create ...' and 'env.createBean2(): Factory error ...' and decide whether to fix or filter them. — 45 bursts each, 34 weeks active, co-occurring with 36 of 37 restarts.
Next step: Confirm that a 'mod_jk2 Shutting down' line at each restart is expected, and explain the bursts that do not coincide with a restart. — 113 bursts in total versus 37 restarts; 37 of 37 restarts have one within ±300 s.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** Yes, it runs on a schedule, about once a week. The web-platform team owns it. It looks routine and is not a problem.

**Schedule and frequency**
- The message is "Graceful restart requested, doing restart" (pattern 300037). It appears 37 times, from 2005-06-12 to 2006-01-22.
- All 37 happen in the 04:00 hour. 33 of them fall on a Sunday, and the first one was on Sunday 2005-06-12 at 04:04:15.
- The median gap between restarts is 604,767 s, which is 7.0 days, and 86% of gaps are within ±20% of that. That is a regular weekly cycle.
- 14 of the 36 gaps are longer than 7 days. Some weeks have no restart, so the schedule isn't perfectly unbroken. The data doesn't say why. It could be missing log coverage or skipped runs.
- Four restarts fell on other days (1 Monday, 1 Friday, 2 Saturday). These may be manual restarts, or the same job running slightly off schedule. I didn't check them individually.

**Owner**
- The component is `httpd`, owned by **web-platform**. The owner comes from the curated default table, with confidence 0.95, and nothing disputes it.

**Is it a problem?**
- Probably not. The lines are logged at NOTICE level, and the stored Jev judgment says "not a failure" (p_problem 0.019).
- I looked at the minute before the first occurrence on the same component and found no error lines.
- A fixed Sunday 04:04 slot looks like a cron job, for example weekly log rotation. That is my hypothesis. The logs don't name the trigger.
- A related pattern is worth a look: "child process <N> still did not exit, sending a SIGTERM" (pattern 300045). It has 168 lines in 4 bursts and p_problem 0.499, and it is also owned by web-platform. I didn't check whether it follows the restarts.

baseline.text:
Yes, four new kinds of error appeared in November 2005. None looks urgent. All four sit in the web-platform team's area.

| New error | First seen | Volume | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|---|
| `uriMap.mapUri() uri must start with /` (httpd) | 29 Nov | 27 lines, 2 bursts | Malformed requests. It appears with the "Invalid URI" error below, which has the same line count, so they look like one event. |
| `Invalid URI in request GET HTTP/1.1` (httpd) | 29 Nov | 27 lines, 2 bursts | All 27 lines come from one client IP, 210.245.233.251, between 06:09 and 09:17 on 29 Nov. |
| `File does not exist: …/~mana_` (httpd) | 10 Nov | 6 lines, 1 burst | A single client, 218.95.185.247, probed the same missing path over about 10 seconds. It looks like a scan for a missing page, not a server fault. |
| `mod_security: Access denied with code 403. Error reading POST data` on `/xmlrpc.php` (mod_security) | 20 Nov | 1 line | The 403 was a block by the mod_security module. The request came from 219.239.227.58. |

**Do they need attention?**
- **Not urgent.** The volumes are tiny: 61 lines in total across the month. Each error traces to a single outside client, and none shows a failure on the server's side.
- **Worth a quick look:**
  - The `/xmlrpc.php` line is the one the automated fault judgment rated most likely to be a real problem (0.94). `xmlrpc.php` is a common target for probing, so it is worth checking whether that endpoint exists and is exposed. mod_security blocked the request.
  - The 29 Nov malformed-request burst is probably a misbehaving client or a scanner. Blocking that IP is an option if it recurs.
- **Weaker judgments.** The judge put the two malformed-request errors at 0.43–0.50, so a real fault is less likely there. The missing-file error scored 0.27.

**Whose area?** The ownership table assigns httpd and mod_security to the **web-platform** team.

**Limit of the evidence.** The logs show frequency and source, not business impact. I only checked how often each error occurred and which clients sent it. I did not check whether the clients' requests succeeded elsewhere.

baseline.text:
Block blk_-5057834626410636236 is a 64 MiB block (67,108,864 bytes) written by task `part-00180`. On 2008-11-10 it had one failed re-replication and two read exceptions. Those are the only problem signs, and the logs don't prove why it was flagged. There are 34 lines for the block, in four bursts.

## Step by step (2008-11-10)

**1. Allocation and first write, 10:39:34–10:40:00**
- The NameNode allocated the block at 10:39:34 for `/user/root/rand/_temporary/_task_200811101024_0001_m_000180_0/part-00180`.
- Three `Receiving block` lines were logged, two on 10.251.199.245 and one on 10.251.123.33.
- The block was received in full (67,108,864 bytes) at 10:39:59–10:40:00.
- The NameNode recorded 10.251.199.245 as a holder at 10:40:00.

**2. First re-replication, 10:44:19–10:49:36 (the problem)**
- At 10:44:19 the NameNode asked 10.251.199.245 to copy the block to 10.250.17.225 and 10.251.67.225. The node started the transfer thread.
- Neither target ever logged the block as stored.
- At 10:46:06 the NameNode recorded 10.251.199.225 as a holder. That host was not one of the two targets.
- At 10:49:36 `PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block …` was logged at WARN. It is the only abnormal line in this early phase, and it comes about 5 minutes after the request.

**3. Second re-replication, 10:49:41–10:57:46**
- At 10:49:41 the NameNode asked 10.251.199.245 to copy the block to 10.251.43.115.
- That copy finished at 10:50:22, with `Transmitted block` and `Received block … of size 67108864`, and the NameNode recorded 10.251.43.115 as a holder.
- At 10:57:46 the NameNode recorded 10.251.123.33 as a holder. This is the node that received the original write at 10:39:59, so the log doesn't show why it is registered this late.
- At 10:57:50 `FSDataset` logged `Deleting block … file …/subdir0/blk_…`. The line has no node, so I can't say which datanode it was.

**4. Read errors, 12:48–12:49 (the second problem)**
- 12:48:28, WARN `Got exception while serving` on 10.251.199.225, for a read by client 10.250.9.207.
- 12:48:47, the same WARN on 10.251.43.115, for a read by client 10.250.14.143.
- 12:48:59, 10.251.43.115 logged `Served block … to /10.250.14.143`. That is the retry succeeding, which suggests it was a transient failure.

**5. Verification, 16:49:12 and 16:54:24**
- `DataBlockScanner` logged `Verification succeeded` twice, so the stored replicas were not corrupt.

**6. Deletion, 21:01:40–21:05:04**
- At 21:01:40 the NameNode added the block to the invalid set on three datanodes: 10.251.199.225, 10.251.199.245 and 10.251.43.115.
- `FSDataset` then deleted block files at 21:03:54, 21:04:56 and 21:05:04, in three different directories. The three delete lines carry no node, so I can't match each to a datanode.

## Datanodes involved
- **10.251.199.245** was the write source and the re-replication source.
- **10.251.123.33** received the original write.
- **10.251.199.225** was recorded as a holder at 10:46:06 and threw a read exception at 12:48.
- **10.251.43.115** was the second re-replication target, threw a read exception at 12:48 and then served the block.
- **10.250.17.225** and **10.251.67.225** were the failed first replication targets.

## Caveats
- The `Deleting block` line at 10:57:50 comes only 4 seconds after the last `addStoredBlock` and well before the 12:48 reads and the 21:01 invalidation. It may be a delete of a stale or excess replica, but the logs don't say. I would check that first if you want to explain the flag.
- This is a timeline of what was logged, not a diagnosis. The timed-out replication and the read errors are the likeliest reasons for the flag.
- Time is only to the second, and the dataset has no ERROR-level lines for this block.

baseline.text:
**Summary:** In your window, pending replications timed out on 47 log lines. Those lines hit 46 distinct blocks. It started at 2008-11-10 10:49:36. It comes in bursts but not on a schedule. The owner is storage-platform.

- **How often:** The message is `PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block blk_…` (pattern 500054). It is logged at WARN level. All 47 lines fall inside your window, and the dataset has none outside it. They form 7 bursts, where a burst is lines separated by less than 30 minutes of quiet. The bursts are:

| Burst start | Lines |
|---|---|
| 11-10 10:49 | 1 |
| 11-10 21:24 | 5 |
| 11-10 22:29 | 8 |
| 11-11 05:09 | 6 |
| 11-11 07:14 | 16 (includes follow-up lines at 07:24 and 07:29) |
| 11-11 08:19 | 8 |
| 11-11 09:24 | 3 |

- **Blocks hit:** 46 distinct blocks. The only repeat is `blk_508142918386110029`, which timed out at 07:14:34 and again at 07:24:33.
- **Start:** The first timeout was at 2008-11-10 10:49:36 (block `blk_-5057834626410636236`). The message never appeared earlier in the dataset, so it is new rather than long-running. The last occurrence is 2008-11-11 09:24:33. After that the dataset has none up to its end at 11:16.
- **Schedule:** There is no regular schedule. The gaps between burst starts are about 10.6 h, 1.1 h, 6.7 h, 2.1 h, 1.1 h and 1.1 h. The median is about 95 minutes and none of the gaps are regular within ±20 %. No hour of the day dominates. The bursts are more frequent on 11-11 (4) than on 11-10 (3), and their sizes also grow.
- **Owner:** The team is **storage-platform**. The component is `dfs.PendingReplicationBlocks$PendingReplicationMonitor`. Ownership comes from the curated default row, with 0.95 confidence, so it is solid but not a hand-assigned component entry.

**Caveats:**
- The stored judgment gives p_problem 0.67, cause "network or I/O". This is a hint, not a diagnosis.
- Similar socket-timeout errors from datanode-ops components appear in the same period. I did not test whether they are related.
- The HDFS log carries no node field, so I could not say whether the timeouts come from one machine.

baseline.text:
**Short answer:** The logs show no sign of lost or corrupted data. The warnings are fleet-wide, not one bad machine. Treat the main warning as a read-path problem to investigate, not an emergency. Two caveats: the logs can't prove nothing was lost, and they end at 2008-11-11 11:16, not 12:00.

**Did we lose or corrupt data?**
- **No direct evidence.** The words corrupt, checksum, lost and missing never appear in the HDFS lines. Every warning (362,793 of 11,175,629 lines) comes from six message types, and none of them reports a checksum failure or a lost block.
- **The blocks I traced were intact.** One block hit by the main warning was written to three replicas, then served successfully to a client. A second block (replication timeout) and a third (failed transfer) each showed at least two replicas registered, and the second was deleted normally afterwards.
- **I checked only a handful of blocks.** I did not audit every block, so I can't prove nothing was lost. To confirm, run an HDFS fsck (the built-in consistency check) for under-replicated or missing blocks.
- **Two minor signs of replication stress:**
  - 47 "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" warnings. These are re-replication attempts that took too long. The one block I followed was retried and completed.
  - 9 "Failed to transfer … Connection reset by peer" warnings, each on a different node. In the one I traced, the target already held a valid copy.

**One machine or the whole fleet? The whole fleet.**
- 356,207 of the warnings (98.2%) are "Got exception while serving blk_… to /<client>". They come from 202 datanodes, and the busiest node has only 0.5% of them.
- They arrive in 8 bursts, with the heaviest hours at 2008-11-09 21:00–23:00 and 2008-11-10 12:00–14:00. The last one was at 2008-11-11 02:39.
- The pattern points to the cluster's read or serving path, or to client and network behaviour. It does not point to a failing host.
- These bursts coincide with replication and block-deletion activity (co-occurrence in all 8 bursts). That is an association, not a proven cause.
- Replacing a single machine would not help.

**What to prioritise**
1. **"Got exception while serving block" (datanode-ops).** Find the underlying exception behind this message. It is logged without the exception text. Check what the clients were doing and whether the network was dropping connections during the 8 bursts. It is the largest source of warnings and covers the whole fleet. The system's own judgment rates it a likely network or I/O failure, with moderate confidence (0.71).
2. **"Unexpected error trying to delete block … BlockInfo not found in volumeMap" (storage-platform).** There were 5,545 warnings in 18 bursts, still occurring at 11:06 on the last day. The datanodes are being told to delete blocks they have no record of. That suggests the NameNode and datanode block records are out of step, which is worth fixing because it could hide real problems. It ranks first in the computed priority table (score 85, versus 82.5 for item 1).
3. **Replication timeouts and failed transfers (storage-platform).** These are low in volume but are the warnings closest to a durability risk. Confirm via fsck that all blocks are back at full replica count.

**Limits of this analysis**
- Counts are log lines, not incidents.
- The severity judgments are model-assigned estimates.
- This is a scale-test cluster, and the logs don't show impact on users or jobs.
- Ownership of the replication components is a default assignment, and the datanode-ops team may be the better owner.

baseline.text:
**Summary:** The member is `myid=1` (10.10.34.11). The warnings began at 15:26:57 on 2015-08-24, right after it restarted. It first rejoined a quorum at 11:14:51 on 2015-08-25, and the quorum had settled with it as a follower by 11:23:56. The log shows no cause for the restart.

The three ensemble members share this log, so the lines come from `myid=1`, `2` and `3`.

**When it started**
- The first warning is at 2015-08-24 15:26:57.688: "Cannot open channel to 2 at election address /10.10.34.12:3888".
- The matching warning for peer 3 follows at 15:27:03.681.
- There are 2,417 such lines from 08-24 through 08-25. The last two are from `myid=3` at 11:23:57 (peer 2) and from `myid=1` at 11:23:07 (peer 3).
- This message is not new. There are 167 earlier occurrences, from 2015-07-29 17:41 (the start of the log) to 08-18 16:09. The 08-24 episode is a long, unbroken run of it.

**Which peers it could not reach**
- **Peer 2:** 10.10.34.12:3888, with 1,211 lines. The last is at 08-25 11:23:57.
- **Peer 3:** 10.10.34.13:3888, with 1,206 lines. The last is at 08-25 11:23:07.
- Almost all lines (2,397) come from the `QuorumPeer[myid=1]` thread, about every 3 seconds. A few come from the `WorkerSender` threads.
- Some of the 2,417 lines are `myid=3`'s `WorkerSender` complaining about peer 2. That is 3 lines through the whole period, including the last one at 11:23:57.

**What happened just before**
- At 15:26:54 `myid=1` restarted. In 0.3 seconds it logged "Reading configuration from /etc/zookeeper/conf/zoo.cfg" (15:26:54.374), then "Starting quorum peer" and "Reading snapshot …/snapshot.c00000001". It then bound election port 3888 and went to LOOKING with "New election … proposed zxid=0xc0000018f" at 15:26:54.674.
- The first "Cannot open channel" came 3 seconds later, because the peers' election ports were not accepting connections.
- The log has no shutdown or error line before the restart. The previous line from any member is a batch of session expiries on `sid:2` at 10:21:46, about 5 hours earlier. Why it restarted, and why peers 2 and 3 were unreachable, is not in these logs.

**Rejoining a quorum**
- **08-25 11:14:51:** `myid=1` logs FOLLOWING, with node 2 as leader. Leader election took about 71,276,526 ms, roughly 19.8 hours, which fits the whole outage. Peer 2 logs LOOKING at 11:14:51.8 and LEADING at 11:14:52.0, and peer 3 joined as a follower at 11:16:08. The clocks of the members are slightly out of step, since `myid=1` logs FOLLOWING 0.6 s before node 2 logs LOOKING. Read this as roughly the same moment.
- **11:19:47:** "Exception when following the leader", back to LOOKING, then FOLLOWING again a fraction of a second later. Node 3 became leader after its own exception, with peer 2 apparently still unreachable.
- **11:20:12:** a second exception. It sat in LOOKING for about 3.7 minutes, with only its own vote being re-sent (11:20:12–11:21:12), and no quorum.
- **11:23:56.366:** FOLLOWING again, with node 3 as leader, after a 223,897 ms election. That is the last rejoin in the data.
- **Unresolved:** the last log line is at 11:26:28, so I can't say whether `myid=1` stayed in the quorum.
  - At 11:23:56 `myid=1` logged "Unexpected exception, tries=0, connecting to /10.10.34.13:2888".
  - At 11:23:58 the leader on node 3 logged "Commiting zxid 0xf00000000 … not first!" and "First is 0x0" for the learner at 10.10.34.11.
  - At 11:26:26 `myid=1` was still in the FOLLOWING state, and node 2 became a follower at 11:26:28.

I did not check whether `myid=1` reached a quorum again before 08-26 beyond the log's end, since the data stops at 08-25 11:26.

baseline.text:
**It isn't new, but the 24/25 August episode is far larger and longer than any earlier one.**

The message is "Cannot open channel to N at election address /10.10.34.x:3888". It is a WARN from the `QuorumCnxManager` component (pattern 200018). The logs don't show a cause for any episode.

**History since 2015-07-29**
- Seven earlier bursts, 167 lines in total, before 24 August. A burst is a recurrence separated from the next by more than 30 minutes of quiet.
- The first line is 2015-07-29 17:41:41, seconds after startup logging.
- The last earlier burst is on 2015-08-18, so the pattern recurred about 8 times in 4 weeks.
- Overall there are 8 bursts and 2,584 lines. The 24/25 August episode is burst 8.

**Comparison with earlier bursts**

| Burst | Lines | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| 29 Jul | 28 | about 4 min (17:41–17:45) |
| 30 Jul (2 bursts) | 71 | a few minutes each, around 17:52–17:56 |
| 31 Jul | 36 | about 5 min (15:31–15:36) |
| 7 Aug | 14 | about 20 s |
| 10 Aug | 8 | about 1.5 min |
| 18 Aug | 10 | about 12 s |
| **24 Aug 15:26:57 → 25 Aug 11:23:57** | **2,417** | **about 20 hours** |

- The latest burst has about 14 times as many lines as all earlier bursts combined.
- It ran at a flat 120 lines per hour for almost 20 hours, rather than clearing within minutes.
- Earlier bursts looked like short flaps during startup or restart.
- Timing is irregular: gaps average a few days and the longest is about 8 days. There is no schedule or time-of-day pattern.

**What happened at the start of the latest burst**
- Just before it, the member with myid=1 logged a fresh start: tickTime, snapshot read, election port bound, LOOKING and a new election.
- From 15:26:57 it could not open channels to peers 2 (10.10.34.12) and 3 (10.10.34.13). Those two peers are the ones that failed in the earlier bursts.
- Election notification timeouts doubled as it retried.
- The pattern's last line is 11:23:57 on 25 August. Follower and leader "ELECTION TOOK" lines are logged within the same seconds, so the ensemble probably settled then. That timing is suggestive, not confirmed.
- Whether this was a restart or a peer or network outage is a hypothesis. I didn't check the other members' logs.

**Owner:** `coordination-platform`. This is the curated default owner for the `QuorumCnxManager` component, with confidence 0.95. It comes from the table's default row for unlisted classes, not a class-specific entry. The area is orchestration (ZooKeeper quorum and leader election).

**Caveats**
- These are log-line counts, not confirmed incidents.
- The dataset has no node field, so I could not break the burst down by host.
- The model-based problem score for the pattern is 0.73, labelled "network or I/O".

Not new: the 'Cannot open channel … at election address' pattern (200018) was first logged 2015-07-29 17:41:41.733 and recurred on several earlier days. The 2015-08-24/25 episode is far larger in log lines than any earlier one (1039 and 1378 lines on the two days, against a previous daily maximum of 71). Ownership is coordination-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95, no dispute listed).
Scope: Dataset zookeeper, 2015-07-29 → 2015-08-26 (pattern history from corpus start 2015-07-29 17:41:41.733 to corpus end 2015-08-25 11:23:57.731). Compared with the previous period 2015-07-01 → 2015-07-29 and the 2015-08-22 → 2015-08-24 window. Filters: pattern_id 200018 and problem patterns with p_problem >= 0.5. The pattern trend and the top_patterns results are not truncated. The raw-line sample is truncated (10 of 2417 lines). The top_patterns result for the full period shows 10 of 11 candidates.
Pattern 200018 'Cannot open channel to <N> at election address /<IP>' has 2584 log lines and 8 bursts in total, first seen 2015-07-29 17:41:41.733000 and last seen 2015-08-25 11:23:57.731000.
Daily log lines before the episode: 28 on 2015-07-29, 71 on 2015-07-30, 36 on 2015-07-31, 14 on 2015-08-07, 8 on 2015-08-10 and 10 on 2015-08-18. Every other day from 2015-08-01 to 2015-08-23 shows 0 log lines.
Daily log lines during the episode: 1039 on 2015-08-24 and 1378 on 2015-08-25.
In the window 2015-08-24 → 2015-08-26 the pattern has 2417 log lines in 1 burst, against 0 bursts in the previous window 2015-08-22 → 2015-08-24.
Over 2015-07-29 → 2015-08-26 the pattern has 8 bursts, active in 5 weeks, against 0 bursts in the previous period 2015-07-01 → 2015-07-29. Its first_seen is 2015-07-29 17:41:41.733000.
Burst timing shows no regular schedule: median gap between burst starts is 298582 seconds, and regular_share is 0.143. One gap is longer than 7 days.
The first sampled log lines of the episode (2015-08-24 15:26:57.688 onward, WARN) come from myid=1 and show failed connections to peer 2 at /10.10.34.12:3888 and peer 3 at /10.10.34.13:3888.
The pattern is judged 'network or I/O failure' with p_problem 0.733. The component QuorumCnxManager maps to team coordination-platform, source 'curated default', confidence 0.95.

It is a recurrence of an older pattern, but this episode is the largest. — owner coordination-platform (curated default, confidence 0.95) — 2417 log lines in 1 burst on 2015-08-24/25 (1039 and 1378 per day) versus a previous daily maximum of 71. 8 bursts in total, 5 weeks active, change vs previous period +8 (0 bursts before). Nodes = 0 (spread unknown). — Check reachability and health of the peers at /10.10.34.12:3888 and /10.10.34.13:3888 around 2015-08-24 15:26 and why the episode lasted until 2015-08-25 11:23.

baseline.text:
**The logs don't support the claim.** I found no disk or snapshot problems, so I wouldn't put the storage-persistence team's fixes first.

**What the storage-persistence team's logs show (2015-07-29 to 2015-08-25)**
- The team owns 284 of the 74,380 log lines, about 0.4%. All 284 are INFO level, with no WARN or ERROR lines.
- They come from five components: DatadirCleanupManager (108 lines), FileTxnSnapLog (65), FileSnap (60), SyncRequestProcessor (26) and FileTxnLog (25).
- The snapshot messages are routine housekeeping. Examples are "Reading snapshot …", "Snapshotting: … to …", "autopurge.snapRetainCount set to …" and "Purge task is not scheduled." The stored judgment rates each of these as "not a failure", with a problem probability of 0.02–0.04.
- Searches for disk, "no space", corrupt, fsync, "I/O error" and "unable to load database" returned 0 lines. Searching ERROR-level lines for snapshot-related words also returned 0.
- The priority ranking produced no storage-persistence problem patterns for this period. The team-risk tool refused to run for them, because the only teams with problem patterns are coordination-platform and client-connectivity.

**Where the problems are**
Over the period there were 65 problem bursts. A burst is a recurrence of one message pattern after more than 30 minutes of quiet. None of them are from storage-persistence.

| Team | Problem bursts | Main issues |
|---|---|---|
| coordination-platform | 35 | Quorum connection failures, such as "Cannot open channel to … at election address" (8 bursts, active all 5 weeks, 2,584 lines) |
| client-connectivity | 30 | "caught end of stream exception" (18 bursts, 1,670 lines), the top-ranked item with a score of 89.5 out of 100 |

- The largest single volume is "Connection broken for id …" (10,356 lines in one burst, coordination-platform).
- Most of these items are network or connection failures rather than storage failures. All of them first appear in this period, with no bursts in the previous four weeks.

**Recommendation**
Start with the coordination-platform quorum and election connectivity failures. Then take the client-connectivity stream exceptions.

**Caveats**
- The logs come from one ensemble member and the data ends on 2015-08-25.
- They don't record cost, downtime or customer impact.
- Whoever reported "disk and snapshot problems" may have been looking at something outside these logs, or at the routine snapshot messages. If you can get their source, I can check it.

I can't walk through this trace because its logs aren't in the database, so I have no evidence on which service failed first or with what error.

- **No matching dataset:** Ten datasets are loaded: bgl, openstack, zookeeper, apache, ssh, hdfs, linux, healthapp, android and proxifier. They date from 2005 to 2018, so none is an OpenTelemetry demo log from 2025-09-23.

- **Not in the loadable catalog:** The catalog has no OpenTelemetry demo or checkout-service logs either.

I haven't guessed at a service or error from general knowledge of the demo's checkout flow. Any such answer would be invented.

If you have the OTel demo logs as a file, for example a collector export or the container logs from the checkout, cart, payment, shipping, email, currency and product-catalog services, give me the path. I can load it with `load_logs`. It loads only if the format is detected with at least 95% coverage, and otherwise it is refused. I'd then:

1. Pull every line for trace `559cdb671a24df91566226b0d22afa4f` with `request_timeline`.
2. Order the steps by service and time.
3. Name the first service with an error-level line and quote its message.
4. Use `get_context` on that line to separate the originating failure from downstream errors.

Two things to check in the export. The trace ID has to appear in the log lines as a field or in the text. All services also need to be in the file, or the first failure may be missing.

**What I checked**
- Ten datasets are loaded: bgl, openstack, zookeeper, apache, ssh, hdfs, linux, healthapp, android and proxifier.
- None is a webshop or payment log. They are a supercomputer, a cloud platform, a coordination service, a web server error log from 2005, SSH auth, a file system, Linux syslog, a health app, an Android framework log and a proxy client.
- None covers 2025-09-23. The newest data ends in early 2018.
- The loadable catalog has no webshop dataset either.
- The only dataset the tools describe in detail is the BGL supercomputer log. It has no payment or checkout components, and its teams are cluster-control, hpc-workloads and node-platform. Any answer from it would be made up.

**What I need from you**
Give me the path to the webshop log file, for example `~/logs/webshop.log`. If the format needs a year, tell me which. I can load it, and the load will only go ahead if the format is recognised.

Once it's loaded, I would:
1. Count failed card payments per minute across 00:00–00:30. That shows whether they are a single spike or spread across the whole window.
2. Look at spread, to see whether it is one node or the whole fleet.
3. Check whether the failure message is new or has happened before. A 30-minute sample limits what this can show, so I'd say so plainly.
4. Look up which team owns the component that logs the failures, and how reliable that ownership record is.

If you mean a different loaded dataset, tell me which one. I won't relabel an unrelated dataset as the webshop.

baseline.text:
**The slowest nova-api endpoint is `POST /v2/servers` (create a server).** It returned HTTP 202 and has the highest typical (median) request time of any endpoint.

I compared 2017-05-14 to 2017-05-18, though the data only runs to 2017-05-17 12:02. I left out the "Took N seconds to build/spawn/destroy" lines, because those are VM lifecycle steps and not HTTP requests.

| | Requests | Median | p95 | Max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /v2/servers` | 2,065 | **0.504 s** | 0.648 s | 1.79 s |
| `GET /v2/servers/detail`, the most common request | 67,361 | 0.265 s | 0.365 s | 1.30 s |
| All timed lines in the period, HTTP and lifecycle combined | 106,994 | 0.261 s | 1.01 s | – |

- **Against the typical request:** `POST /v2/servers` has a median about 1.9 times the most common request and about 1.9 times the all-lines median. It is also about 2 to 5 times slower than the metadata, DELETE and external-events endpoints, which sit at 0.09 to 0.27 s.
- **Consistently slow:** its p95 and p99 (0.765 s) are also higher than those of every other HTTP endpoint. Its slowness is not caused by a few outliers.
- **Worst single requests:**
  - The worst single request was a `GET /v2/servers/detail?all_tenants=True&changes-since=…&host=cp-….slowvm…` call. It took 4.16 s, although its median is only 0.33 s across 176 requests.
  - The metadata endpoints `meta_data.json` and `vendor_data.json` each had a worst case of about 2.2 s, against a median of about 0.22 s.
  - `os-server-external-events` also reached 2.1 s, against a median of 0.095 s.

  These are occasional spikes, not endpoints that are slow in general.
- **Errors:** none of these endpoints had a problem-level or 5xx error rate above 0.

The "overall" median in the table mixes HTTP requests with VM lifecycle timings, so it is only a rough benchmark. The lifecycle steps are far slower than any HTTP call: build takes a median of about 20.6 s and spawn about 19.7 s.

baseline.text:
**The recurring error** is a failed periodic image-cache task in nova-compute: `Error during ComputeManager._run_image_cache_manager_pass`.

- **Cause:** The task fails with `InvalidDiskInfo: Disk info file is invalid: qemu-img failed to execute on /var/lib/nova/instances/<uuid>/disk`. The command exits with code 1 and says `No such file or directory`. In the one occurrence I read in full (16 May 03:19), the missing disk belonged to instance `16797a0f-32fb-494c-8f36-38588148c35d`. I did not read the other seven tracebacks, so I can't say they all name the same instance.
- **Where it fails:** The traceback runs through `ComputeManager._run_image_cache_manager_pass`, then `libvirt/imagecache.py`, `_list_backing_images`, `get_disk_backing_file` and `qemu_img_info`.
- **How many times:** It occurred **8 times**. Each occurrence logs a 24-line traceback, so the 192 ERROR lines from nova-compute in the window are these 8 occurrences, not 192 separate errors.
- **Period:** First 2017-05-16 03:19:45, last 2017-05-17 05:24:15, about 26 hours. The other six occurrences were at 16:30, 17:41, 19:33, 20:31 and 22:16 on 16 May, and 00:15 on 17 May. The dataset ends at 2017-05-17 12:02, so nothing in the logs falls between 17 May and your 18 May cutoff.
- **Owner:** **cloud-compute**. Ownership of `nova-compute` is curated (confidence 1.0), and the area is compute/virtualisation.

This is a hypothesis, not something the logs prove. The disk file for a VM is missing on the host while the cache manager scans for backing images. That could be a deleted or half-built instance leaving stale state.

baseline.text:
There was no kernel panic on R52-M0 in that window. The panic in the logs is on a different midplane, R52-M1, and the logs show a likely trigger but not a confirmed root cause.

**The premise doesn't match the logs**
- R52-M0 has zero log lines on 2005-10-12, including 13:00–15:00. A search for "kernel panic" there returned nothing.
- The only R52 activity in your window is 46 lines between 14:02:13 and 14:03:26, all on one node of R52-M1. The rack's other lines that day fall outside your window, at 09:00 and from 15:00 on.
- You may have the wrong midplane, or R52-M0 may be a typo for R52-M1.

**Which node went down first**
- **Node:** `R52-M1-N9-C:J04-U11` is the only node with lines in the window, so it is the first and only node down. It is not a first-among-several result.
- **Timing:** It logged FATAL KERNEL lines from 14:02:13.7, and the last line, `rts panic! - stopping execution`, came at 14:03:26.1.
- **No warning beforehand:** The node's previous log line was an INFO line on 2005-08-28. No other line anywhere in the dataset appears in the 15 minutes before the first FATAL line.

**Likely cause (my reading of the dump, not a stated root cause)**
- **Sequence:** The node logged `machine check interrupt` first, then `machine check status register: 0x81000000`, then a register dump ending in the panic.
- **Parity error:** In the dump, `d-cache flush parity error` is the only error counter showing 1 (the `summary` line also reads 1). The other error counters (instruction PLB, data read/write PLB, TLB, i-cache parity, d-cache search parity) all read 0.
- **Hypothesis:** A data-cache parity error on that node's CPU raised a machine check, and the runtime system (RTS) stopped execution. I'd treat this as a hardware fault on that node.
- **Not checked:** I didn't check whether the same node has failed this way before or whether other nodes in the midplane were affected.

I haven't generated the session report page.
